Section 6. 중지미수에 관한 위법
Section 7. 위법성저각사유
1. 정당행위
(1) 저항권 이론
(2) 정당한 직무집행
(3) 상관의 명령
2. 정당방위
3. 긴급피난
(1) 피고인 A의 경우
(2) 피고인 C의 경우
Section 8. 책임저각사유
Section 9. 양형부당
Section 10. 결론
Section 11. 소수의견
1. 대법원판사 민문기의 의견
2. 대법원판사 양병호의 의견
3. 대법원판사 임항준의 의견
4. 대법원판사 김윤행의 의견
5. 대법원판사 정태원의 의견
6. 대법원판사 서윤홍의 의견

Section 1. 공소 기각의 결정을 간과한 위법

Among the grounds of appeal, it is argued that, even based on the facts stated in the indictment, there is no statement of specific facts concerning the purpose of subverting the Constitution, the riotous acts, and the contents of the conspiracy, which are constituent elements of the crime of insurrection, or concerning the division of execution in the co-principal offense of murder; thus, because the facts charged are not specified, an order dismissing the prosecution should have been entered pursuant to Article 373(1)4 of the Military Court-Martial Act, but the lower court overlooked this and thereby erred in misunderstanding the above legal principles. We shall first consider this point.

Upon review, this point was already lawfully considered by the lower court. In addition, the facts charged against the Defendants, as organized from the indictment in this case and the applications to amend the indictment made on two occasions, are sufficiently specified on their face to be recognized as the relevant offenses, and it is admitted that they are specifically stated. Further, as to the murder of Defendant C, the indictment clearly charges co-principal liability by conspiracy; accordingly, in that case, the omission of facts concerning the division of execution in co-principal liability cannot be deemed a defect. Therefore, this argument is without merit.

Section 2. Procedural illegality

1. Violation of the principle of accusation and adjudication

Among the grounds of appeal, it is argued that, according to the indictment and the application to amend the indictment, Defendant G was prosecuted for killing T and U with the purpose of subverting the Constitution, but the lower judgment found Defendant G to have killed six persons, namely B, T, V, W, X, and U; this, it is argued, is a violation of the principle of accusation and adjudication and thus a violation of law. We consider this argument.

Upon review, according to the application to amend the indictment lawfully granted at the first trial date in the lower court trial transcript p. 1458, it is clear, as argued, that Defendant G was prosecuted for having killed T and U, among the six deceased persons in this case, for the purpose of subverting the Constitution. However, in the reasoning of the lower judgment, in the conclusion portion concerning the facts of the offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose, the court stated that from around 19:40 to 20:05 on the same day, former President B, the said T, the said V, the said W, the said X, and the said U were each caused to die, thereby the Defendants jointly murdered the above victims for the purpose of subverting the Constitution. This appears, on its face, to have committed the illegality alleged. Nevertheless, the lower court had previously stated that, on October 26, 1979, around 19:40, Defendant G, after the other Defendants had fired at the above deceased persons, received at around 20:05 that day an instruction from Defendant E to carry out a confirmation shot on persons not yet fully dead and agreed to participate in that killing. Not only that, but the lower court also stated that, with respect to the shooting pursuant to that instruction, it was done by firing one shot at the said W lying fallen, two shots at the said V, two shots at the said T groaning, and one shot at the said U lying fallen and groaning. In view of this point, although the expression in the conclusion portion of the lower judgment is somewhat inaccurate, it is still recognized that the lower court judged within the scope of the prosecution. The argument is without merit.

2. Violation of public trial

Among the grounds of appeal, it is argued that the court-martial of first instance, at the second trial date on December 8, 1979, conducted the defense counsel’s statements and questioning of Defendant A in closed session without satisfying the prescribed requirements, and also, at the ninth trial date on December 18, 1979, effectively prohibited public access and proceeded with Defendant A’s final statement without even entering a decision of closure; thus, it is argued that the closed proceedings were plainly illegal in their grounds and procedure. We consider this argument.

Upon review, according to the record trial transcript p. 223, at the second trial date on December 8, 1979, during the defense counsel’s cross-examination of Defendant A, the court ordered a closed proceeding on the ground that Defendant A, as former Director of the Central Intelligence Agency, has performed important duties concerning foreign intelligence and domestic security intelligence, security affairs pertaining to state secrets, insurrection, foreign relations, the investigation of crimes prescribed in the National Security Act, the Anti-Communist Act, and similar laws, and the coordination and supervision of intelligence and security affairs, and the content of the defendant’s statements in this court pursuant to the defense counsel’s cross-examination substantially includes matters that may interfere with the security or public order of the State. It then proceeded in camera thereafter. This was based on Article 67 of the Military Court-Martial Act, which provides that the oral proceedings and judgment in trial shall be public; provided, however, that where public order may be disturbed, morals harmed, or where necessary for military secrecy, the military court may decide not to hold them publicly. Even in light of the record, the reason is fully understandable. Therefore, the first-instance court’s measure was proper and cannot be said to have been mistaken. Accordingly, this portion of the argument is without merit.

Further, whether any stage of the trial proceedings was public is to be recorded in the trial transcript pursuant to Article 85(2)5 of the Military Court-Martial Act, which prescribes the entries in the trial transcript. Article 89 of the same Act provides that matters recorded in the trial transcript as procedural acts on a trial date are proved by that transcript alone. Thus, the public or private nature of the proceedings on December 18, 1979, the ninth trial date in the first instance, can be established only by the trial transcript in this case. The first-instance ninth trial transcript trial transcript p. 769 states in the column for public or private that the trial was public in court. Therefore, it can be recognized that the proceedings on that date were conducted in a public courtroom. Accordingly, this argument also lacks merit.

3. Illegality of limiting examination

Among the grounds of appeal, it is argued that the first instance and the lower court, though under Article 344 of the Military Court-Martial Act they could limit examination only to the extent that the essential rights of parties to the litigation were not harmed, nevertheless restricted examination and statements whenever specific references were to be made in the course of examining Defendant A concerning the motive and purpose of this act, the domestic political situation immediately before the act, and the inevitability of the act, and also frequently imposed limitations during the examination of Defendants E and F; this, it is argued, constituted a grave infringement of the Defendants’ and counsel’s right of defense beyond the permissible bounds of examination restriction. We consider this argument.

Upon review of the first-instance and appellate trial transcripts, it can be recognized that the first instance and the lower court afforded the above Defendants necessary and sufficient opportunities to make statements, and that each defense counsel was granted the necessary right to examine the Defendants and other parties to the litigation; further, it is sufficiently recognized that each defense counsel had necessary and sufficient opportunities to defend the Defendants, which were realized, and that each Defendant had a full opportunity to make final statements. In particular, in the case of Defendant A, from the content of the Defendant’s statements in response to examinations by the prosecutor, defense counsel, and legal officer in the first-instance and appellate courts, as well as the supplemental statement of reasons for appeal submitted by Defendant A himself trial transcript p. 1695, and the statements of reasons for appeal and grounds of appeal submitted by his counsel, it can be recognized that the defense content alleged by the appellant is sufficiently reflected. Therefore, the contrary argument lacks merit.

4. Illegality of ordering withdrawal from the courtroom

Among the grounds of appeal, when questioning Defendant C and others at the third trial date on December 10, 1979, the first-instance court, invoking Article 343(2) of the Military Court-Martial Act, ordered Defendant A to withdraw from the courtroom on the ground that he could not make sufficient statements in Defendant A’s presence; this, it is argued, was done without just cause solely upon the application of the prosecutor, and furthermore, when Defendant C’s statement ended in that case, Defendant A, who had been withdrawn, should have been brought back into the courtroom and informed of the substance, and Defendant A should have been allowed to question Defendant C directly, but instead the proceedings were simply closed without Defendant A being brought back into the courtroom that day; this is said to be illegal. We consider this argument.

Upon review, according to the first-instance third trial transcript, before the examination of Defendant C at the said third trial date, the first-instance court, ex officio, ordered the remaining Defendants including Defendant A to withdraw from the courtroom on the ground that they were deemed unable to make sufficient statements in the presence of co-defendants trial transcript p. 237. This measure was based on Article 343(2) of the Military Court-Martial Act, which provides that the presiding judge may order the defendant to withdraw and be questioned when, on his own motion or upon application by the prosecutor, the defendant is deemed unable to make sufficient statements in the presence of another defendant or .... In light of the record, this was reasonable. It is true, as argued, that after Defendant C’s statement ended at that date, the proceedings were closed without Defendant A being brought back into the courtroom. However, according to the first-instance fourth trial transcript, when the first-instance court resumed and, at the fourth trial date, the legal officer informed the parties in the courtroom, which included all defendants in this case including Defendant A and all their counsel, of the substance of the previous court hearing on Defendant C, and asked the parties for their views, the parties stated that they had no particular opinion; this is clearly shown in the record trial transcript p. 318. Further, according to the first-instance sixth trial transcript, it is clearly shown in the record that Defendant A’s assigned counsel O and Y cross-examined Defendant C on behalf of Defendant A trial transcript pp. 518, 520. Therefore, this argument lacks merit.

5. Illegality in witness examination procedure

Among the grounds of appeal, first, according to the witness examination record of Z adopted by the lower court, it is clear that Defendant A was not allowed to participate in the examination of that witness. This, it is argued, violated the law guaranteeing a defendant’s right to participate in witness examination and, through that, the right of cross-examination. Second, it is argued that, in examining witnesses, there was no service of summons by the prescribed procedure under Articles 106 through 108 of the Military Court-Martial Act; moreover, in some cases, witnesses were made to wait in advance before the prosecutor had even applied for evidence, and then were taken up and examined immediately upon application; this, it is argued, was not only a procedural violation but a grave illegality depriving the Defendants and their counsel of the opportunity to prepare for cross-examination. We consider this argument.

Upon review, first, according to the first-instance trial record, at the eighth trial date at which all the Defendants in this case and their counsel were present, regarding witness Z who failed to appear, the first-instance court instructed the legal officer that he would conduct the examination outside the courtroom and ordered the attendance of the relevant persons trial transcript p. 707. Thereafter, on December 17, 1979, legal officer AA examined the witness at the Army Headquarters Judge Advocate General’s Office, where Defendant C and his counsel and the counsel for Defendants A and D were present trial transcript p. 749. In the manner of that witness examination, it cannot be said that Defendant A was not notified and thus was denied an opportunity to participate. Moreover, the witness’s testimony primarily concerned the criminal facts of Defendant C, so it cannot be said that there was any illegality in the procedure. In addition, according to the same trial record, at the ninth trial date resumed on December 18, 1979, the first-instance court, after the legal officer informed the courtroom that witness Z had been examined, presented the substance and asked the parties for their opinions; the parties stated that they had no particular opinion, as clearly shown in the record trial transcript p. 771. Therefore, even if there were a mistake as alleged, the Defendants and their counsel stated at the evidence examination that they had no particular opinion, so the mistake would be cured by waiver of the right to object. Accordingly, this part of the argument is without merit.

Second, according to the first-instance trial record, after the first-instance court selected eight witnesses at the sixth trial date, it examined the two selected witnesses who appeared at the seventh trial date trial transcript p. 571, and at the eighth trial date it newly selected nine witnesses present at the court and examined those witnesses and the five witnesses selected earlier who appeared trial transcript p. 629. Also, one witness examination was conducted outside the courtroom by legal officer AA on December 17, 1979, all of which is clear from the relevant trial transcripts and witness examination records. Under the proviso of Article 192 of the Military Court-Martial Act, witnesses present in court may be examined without summons, so it cannot be illegal that the nine present witnesses were not summoned. Nor can it necessarily be faulted that those witnesses were examined immediately upon application. As to the remaining witnesses, although summons procedures should have been taken, no trace of the issuance of summons can be found in the record except that the trial transcripts state that they were summoned and appeared. However, after examining those witnesses and the witness outside the courtroom, the first-instance court afforded the Defendants and their counsel the opportunity to state their opinions in court or at the next trial date, and they stated that they had no particular opinion. Moreover, it is clearly shown in the record that the Defendants and their counsel conducted sufficient and necessary cross-examination of those witnesses. Therefore, the defect of non-issuance of summons cannot be said to be a case affecting the outcome of the judgment, and this portion of the argument also cannot be accepted.

6. Illegality in opening the proceedings without counsel

Among the grounds of appeal, in military court cases, counsel is mandatory under Articles 62 and 315 of the Military Court-Martial Act, and therefore proceedings cannot be opened without counsel’s appearance. Nevertheless, on January 22, 1980, at the first trial date, as a measure under Article 416 of the Military Court-Martial Act rather than severance of trial, the lower court opened proceedings with only Defendants C and G present and without the appearance of Defendants A, E, and F and their counsel, and is alleged to have illegally examined matters concerning the motives and circumstances of the co-defendants’ offenses. We consider this argument.

Upon review of the appellate trial record, after notifying Defendants A, E, and F and their counsel that the first trial date was set for January 22, 1980 trial transcript pp. 1007, 1009-1011, 1019-1021, 1024, 1040-1044, the court later re-designated and notified the trial date as January 23, 1980 trial transcript p. 1381. Then, at the first trial date on January 22, 1980, the court, pursuant to Article 416 of the Military Court-Martial Act, deemed that some of the Defendants including Defendants A, E, and F need not appear at trial and did not order their appearance, but proceeded with the hearing with only Defendants C and G present trial transcript p. 1383. Article 416 of the Military Court-Martial Act is only the provision that in appellate proceedings under the Military Court-Martial Act, the appeal instance is not a de novo trial of the first instance, but rather a post hoc review of specific factual and legal issues in the first-instance judgment, and thus as a rule the defendant need not appear at appellate trial dates. It is not a provision allowing only some co-defendants to appear selectively, as in this case, and excusing the appearance of the others. Therefore, the above measure of the appellate court was mistaken. However, at the continued second trial date on January 23, 1980, the legal officer informed the substance of the important matters of the previous trial hearing trial transcript p. 1469, and thereafter sufficient opportunity for cross-examination was afforded. Moreover, the record shows that the first instance had already conducted sufficient hearings on the matters alleged in the appeal grounds, and at the first appellate trial date there is no indication that new matters were examined on that point. Accordingly, the error was not such as to affect the outcome of the judgment. The Supreme Court decisions cited by the appellant are not apt to this case. Thus, this argument also cannot be accepted.

7. Deprivation of the right to counsel

Among the grounds of appeal, the Defendants’ lineal family members and spouse have, under Article 59 of the Military Court-Martial Act, an independent right to appoint counsel. Thus, even if the defendant himself refuses to argue, the right of counsel appointed by the lineal family members and spouse does not extinguish. Nevertheless, counsel AB and others appointed by Defendant A’s lineal family members and spouse were denied entry into the courtroom by military police serving as courtroom order personnel pursuant to the judge’s order at the first-instance fifth trial date on December 12, 1979, and it is argued that thereby their right to counsel was deprived, and that the court committed illegality in failing to decide on the objection to this point. We consider this argument.

Upon review, even if, pursuant to Article 59(2) of the Military Court-Martial Act, the defendant’s lineal family members and spouse may independently appoint counsel, the appointing party is one who independently exercises the appointing right of the principal, so the effect of the appointment extends to the principal, and the principal must be understood as being able to revoke the appointment. In this case, according to the first-instance fourth trial transcript, while the hearing at the fourth trial date proceeded under the participation of privately retained counsel including attorneys AB and others appointed by Defendant A’s mother and spouse, Defendant A stated, From now on, I refuse the defense by the private defense team for this defendant. At that time the legal officer informed him of the fact that the military court requires counsel and, if the privately retained counsel must be dismissed, the military court must decide to appoint assigned counsel. Defendant A then stated, Please appoint assigned counsel for this defendant; I will revoke all privately retained counsel for myself. This is clearly shown in the record trial transcript pp. 346-347. Therefore, the above private counsel were lawfully revoked, and the fact that they were later denied entry to the courtroom as counsel at the first-instance fifth trial date on December 12, 1979, cannot be regarded as deprivation of the right to counsel. Nor can it be said that any illegality occurred merely because the objection thereto was not decided. The argument is without merit.

8. Deficiency in the trial transcript and deprivation of the rights of inspection and copying

Among the grounds of appeal, even if the Military Court-Martial Act does not have a provision like Article 54 of the Criminal Procedure Act that trial transcripts must be promptly prepared within five days after each trial date, considering Articles 89 probative force of the trial transcript, 86 special provisions concerning the trial transcript, and 64 inspection and copying of documents and evidence, etc., the trial transcript in military court proceedings should also be prepared before the next trial date or, at the latest, before the factual hearing ends. Nevertheless, it is argued that the first instance and the appellate court did not promptly prepare the trial transcripts, thereby effectively depriving counsel of the right under Article 64 of the Military Court-Martial Act to inspect and copy the transcripts, etc. We consider this argument.

Upon review, the Military Court-Martial Act does not contain a provision like Article 54 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which sets a statutory period for preparing trial transcripts. Of course, military court trial transcripts must also be prepared promptly, but one cannot definitively say by when they must be completed. In particular, even the statutory period set by the Criminal Procedure Act is only a directive provision, and merely failing to complete the transcript within that period cannot by itself be regarded as rendering the trial transcript void. Therefore, no fault can be found with respect to the timing of preparation of the first-instance and appellate trial transcripts; nor can it be said that there was illegality in depriving the right of inspection and copying of transcripts. The gist of the argument is that it concerns the defendants’ right of defense. Upon review of the first-instance and appellate trial records in this case, it is recognized that the defendants’ right of defense was fully protected; accordingly, this argument cannot be accepted.

9. Infringement of the independence of the trial

Among the grounds of appeal, it is argued that the first instance and appellate court pressed ahead with the hearing as though there were a fixed, predetermined schedule under the aforementioned unlawful procedures infringing the defendants’ right of defense and right to counsel, and that even during the hearing, there were cases in which notes of contact from outside were publicly and repeatedly handed to the judges through the back door behind the judges’ bench; this, it is argued, violated Article 102 of the Constitution and Article 28 of the Military Court-Martial Act, which guarantee judicial independence. We consider this argument.

As to the arguments alleging that the above first-instance and appellate trial procedures were illegal, we have already found them to be without merit. Even in light of the record, it is not recognized that the factual hearings in the first instance and appellate court were pressed ahead under some fixed schedule as alleged. Rather, the record only shows that the first instance conducted sufficient factual hearings eight times across the second through ninth trial dates, and the appellate court did so three times across the first through third trial dates, while ensuring the defendants’ right of defense and right to counsel. No other illegality is found. Furthermore, there is absolutely nothing in the record suggesting that contact notes were delivered to the judges during the hearing, and especially whether their content infringed judicial independence is wholly unknown. This point is too abstract and fabricated to require further discussion. Therefore, the argument lacks merit.

Section 3. Issue of voluntariness regarding the suspect-interrogation record prepared by the prosecutor

Among the grounds of appeal, it is argued that the suspect-interrogation records concerning the Defendants prepared by the prosecutor were merely an extension of the records prepared by the military police investigators because, at the time of the prosecutor’s interrogation, the Defendants were physically and mentally exhausted by numerous acts of torture at the joint investigation headquarters under martial law, and in particular Defendant A made statements involuntarily, under the prosecutor’s earnest persuasion, while his consciousness was dim due to aggravation of his chronic liver disease; or because the prosecutor conducted the interrogation at the place where the military judicial police had investigated after receiving the case, under a state in which access and communication with counsel and family were completely prohibited, and the record content was the same as the military judicial police records except for legal refinement, so that it lacked voluntariness. It is argued that the lower court nevertheless used this as evidence of guilt, thereby committing an error of law concerning evidentiary capacity or a defect for failure to provide reasons, and also erred by omitting consideration of the grounds of appeal. We consider this argument. This point is related to the argument below that the fact-finding violated the rules of evidence, and for convenience it is considered separately.

Upon review, in general, the absence of voluntariness in a statement means that the person being interrogated by an investigative authority did not make the statement under free conditions because of threats, torture, or other means. The determination of voluntariness is made within a reasonable scope by the free conviction of the judge without violating the rules of experience. It suffices that the adjudicating panel makes a reasonable judgment in all respects of the litigation process namely, the preparation and content of the document, the defendant’s explanation and demeanor, the prosecutor’s elucidations, and the testimony of witnesses involved in the preparation of the document. On that basis, the record shows the following:

(1) In the prosecutor’s direct examination of Defendant A at the second trial date in the first instance:
Q: When the prosecutor investigated, I wrote the record and made you verify it item by item, did I not?
A: Yes.
Q: After confirming the contents, you signed and affixed your seal, did you not?
A: Yes.
Trial transcript p. 210

(2) During the prosecutor’s direct examination of Defendant A at the third trial date in the first instance:
Q: During the prosecutor’s investigation, was there any instance in which you made a statement under compulsion or threat?
A: I said, please write it as it was.
Trial transcript p. 247
And:
Q: When the prosecutor investigated, was there any threat or coercion?
A: No.
Q: You reviewed the record prepared at that time, confirmed the contents, and signed and affixed your seal, did you not?
A: Yes.
Trial transcript p. 256

(3) During the cross-examination of Defendant A by defense counsel AC at the first appellate trial date:
Q: Looking at the prosecutor-prepared suspect-interrogation record concerning the defendant, it says that during a conversation at the curb in front of the entrance you nodded your head and thought you would kill T, and where was that record prepared?
A: I do not know the exact location, but the prosecutor came to the Joint Investigation Headquarters and took the record for two days.
Q: Was there no investigation at the Prosecutor’s Office?
A: There was. After that, they came to the Judge Advocate General’s Office twice and investigated me.
Q: Then, did the prosecutor investigate you on the spot immediately after the Joint Investigation Headquarters investigation?
A: No. After the case was transferred to the Prosecutor’s Office, the prosecutor came to that place and investigated me.
Q: At that time, did you clearly know that the case had been transferred to the prosecutor?
A: I clearly knew that the case had been transferred to the prosecutor and that he was a military prosecutor.
Trial transcript pp. 1398-1400

(4) During the cross-examination of Defendant F by his counsel Y at the fifth trial date in the first instance:
Q: When you were investigated before the prosecutor, did you tell the truth and read the contents?
A: Yes.
Trial transcript p. 430

(5) During the cross-examination of Defendant G by his counsel P at the same trial date:
Q: Did the prosecutor write the record as you said?
A: Yes.
Trial transcript p. 435

(6) Through the hearings in the first instance and appellate court, there is no statement to be found that the Defendants were investigated under a non-free atmosphere such as assault or deception during the prosecutor’s interrogation of suspects.

(7) According to the prosecutor-prepared suspect-interrogation records for the Defendants, the statements of the Defendants are almost identical in content concerning the circumstances and details of the offense in this case, with only some differences in expression, and in particular, as for Defendants C, D, E, and G, they were investigated on two occasions and the statements on both occasions are consistent.

(8) In the trial hearings in the first instance and appellate court as well, the Defendants’ statements in court are largely the same as the contents of the prosecutor’s statements regarding objective facts, differing only as to some subjective matters such as motive, and this becomes even more pronounced as the proceedings progress. These facts are apparent from the record. Taking these together with other circumstances appearing in the record, the prosecutor-prepared suspect-interrogation records for the Defendants are all admitted to have voluntariness. Therefore, the lower court’s use of them as evidence of guilt was proper, and there is no illegality as alleged. Accordingly, this part of the argument lacks merit.

And although Defendant C’s counsel AC raised this point in the statement of grounds of appeal submitted, the lower court’s failure to decide it was mistaken trial transcript p. 1128; however, since the argument is plainly without merit as above, the mistake could not have affected the outcome of the judgment. Therefore, this point also lacks merit.

Section 4. 범죄구성요건에 관한 위법

1. 국헌문란의 목적

Among the grounds of appeal, the subversion of the Constitution prescribed in Article 91 of the Criminal Act, as the purpose element of the offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose and attempted insurrection, ultimately means everything that unlawfully destroys the State’s political basic order itself. The political basic order of our country is, needless to say, a liberal democratic political system; therefore, only acts that substantially or formally destroy the principle of popular sovereignty and the people’s fundamental freedoms and equality would constitute subversion of the Constitution. Accordingly, the overthrow of a specific government or cabinet, or an act of shouting slogans of overthrow, or whether the means of overthrowing is violence, or the killing of a specific constitutional organ as a natural person and the planning of succession or improvement thereof, would not fall under this.

First, in the case of Defendant A, the Yushin system, by its establishment and continuance alone, was not only an illegal criminal state in which sovereignty was usurped, but its content and operation produced a continuing condition that destroyed the political basic order of a democratic state. Therefore, for Defendant A, the killing of the President, a natural person, was unavoidably done according to a plan long prepared for the restoration of democracy. Even if not so, since after this offense he intended to enact a democratic constitution and organize the National Assembly and Government by democratic methods, there was no purpose to subvert the Constitution.

Second, in the case of Defendant C, it is difficult to conclude, merely because he killed T, the head of the Presidential Security Service, who was not even a state organ established by the Constitution, that he had a purpose of subverting the Constitution like the co-defendants; and as to Defendant C, neither his own statement nor his external behavior can be said to show a purpose of subverting the Constitution.

Third, in the case of Defendant D, he merely thought that only a few persons would be killed and the President abducted in this offense, and the killing of security officer V and the like, which he admits was done pursuant to the order of his superior, would not amount to subversion of the Constitution. Moreover, Defendant A’s explanation also states that he reached this offense in order to restore liberal democracy, so it cannot be said that there was a purpose to subvert the Constitution.

Fourth, in the case of Defendants E, F, and G, the Defendants were merely security guards or drivers of the Central Intelligence Agency restaurant and, having no choice, blindly and mechanically carried out the orders of Defendant D, the chief responsible person there. They could not even imagine the specific harm and consequences. In particular, Defendant G did not know of the murder of the President or even of its plan. Nevertheless, the lower court found, contrary to Defendant C’s explanation, that the facts it held satisfied the purpose of subverting the Constitution, and as to the other Defendants, it found that they had carried out riots or killings with the purpose of subverting the Constitution, on the ground that they knew a state of national upheaval had occurred. It is argued that this was a fact-finding without evidence, a violation of the rules of evidence contrary to logic and experience, a failure of hearing, and a defect for lack of reasons, or that the legal principles concerning the purpose of subversion of the Constitution in the offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose and attempted insurrection were misunderstood. We consider this argument.

(1) First, we examine the legal principles concerning the purpose of subversion of the Constitution.

Article 91 of the Criminal Act provides: In this Chapter, purpose of subverting the Constitution means any of the following: 1. abolishing the functions of the Constitution or laws without following the procedures prescribed by the Constitution or laws; 2. overthrowing, by force, a state organ established by the Constitution or making the exercise of its functions impossible. Thus it defines subversion of the Constitution. This ultimately means unlawfully destroying the political basic order prescribed by the present Constitution or laws. As argued, it does not necessarily have an extra-legal meaning, and certainly does not mean changing to a communist, monarchical, or dictatorial system. Of course, as argued, killing only a natural person who is a specific state organ, or planning his succession, does not fall under it. Further, since the crime of insurrection is a crime with a specific purpose, the general principles concerning crimes with specific purpose apply. The purpose belongs to matters requiring strict proof and must be direct, but it cannot be said that it requires a desire or will for the result to occur, nor does it require definite knowledge; a conditional awareness is sufficient see Supreme Court decision dated April 2, 1968, 68DO61.

(2) Next, we examine the lower court’s factual findings on this point regarding the Defendants.

(A) Part concerning Defendant A

The lower judgment stated the following as the facts of Defendant A’s purpose of subverting the Constitution: While performing his duties as Director of the Central Intelligence Agency, Defendant A’s plans for stabilizing the political situation repeatedly failed, exposing his incompetence in carrying out his duties, and after being reprimanded by former President B, rumors of a dismissal for taking responsibility circulated, causing him to feel insecure in his position. Meanwhile, although he resented the President’s greater trust in T, then head of the Presidential Security Service, who was junior to him and younger, despite T’s arrogant attitude and interference in matters beyond his authority, he planned to seize power after killing the President, and, for secrecy, independently devised the concrete plan for the act, after assassinating the President, he planned to declare martial law on the ground of national security and public disorder, to use the authority and organizational power of the Central Intelligence Agency to take control of the martial law forces and suppress the situation by force, to constitute a revolutionary committee that would oversee legislative, judicial, and executive powers, to assume the chairmanship himself and secure a basis of power, and then to run for President. Examining the important basis of this conclusion from the evidence lawfully admitted and cited by the lower court:

question: Which of the following statements concerning 압수 and 수색 are incorrect? (In cases of dispute, pursuant to case law)
A: (a) If the 피압수자 expressly indicated to the 수사기관 that he would not participate in the 집행 of the 압수/search warrant, then, except in special circumstances, it is permissible not to separately guarantee his 변호인 an opportunity to participate in the 집행 of the 압수/search warrant.
B: (b) If, after the 수사기관 has selectively 압수한 정보 related to the alleged 범죄 and is retaining the remaining 정보 unrelated thereto without deleting, discarding, or returning it, then, as to the portion unrelated to the alleged 범죄, it has unlawfully 압수 and searched 전자정보 beyond the scope of 전자정보 subject to 압수 without a 영장, and such 위법성 cannot be deemed cured merely because a 압수/search warrant was later issued by a 법원 or because the 피고인 or 변호인 consented to its use as evidence.
C: (c) The term "an 정보저장매체 belonging to the 피의자's 소유 or 관리," for which the right of 참여 should be guaranteed not only to the 피압수자 who voluntarily submitted the 정보저장매체 but also to a 피의자 who is not the 임의제출자, means a case in which the 피의자, at the time of the 압수/search or up to a temporally proximate time, actually controlled and managed the 정보저장매체 and possessed and exercised exclusive authority to 관리 and dispose of all 전자정보 within that 정보저장매체, and did not otherwise transfer or relinquish it to a 제3자 according to his own 의사, so that the 피의자 can be evaluated as the 실질적 피압수자 with respect to the 전자정보 stored in that 정보저장매체.
D: (d) Whether a person qualifies as the 실질적 피압수자 must be determined on the basis of the externally and objectively recognizable 사실상의 상태 at the time of the 압수/search; thus, if the 피의자 or any other 제3자 had, in the past, been involved in the 사용 of that 정보저장매체 or the 생성 or 사용 of individual 전자정보, or if they are the 정보주체 identified by 전자정보 created in the course thereof, then they must be treated as the party 실질적으로 subjected to 압수 and 수색.
E: (e) If, while voluntarily 제출ing a 휴대전화, the 피의자 voluntarily provided the 수사기관 with the ID and 비밀번호 for accessing 클라우드 services or the like, with the intent of submitting to the 수사기관 전자정보 stored not in the 휴대전화 but in remote locations managed by a 제3자 such as the 클라우드, then the 전자정보 stored in the 클라우드 or the like may be regarded as having been voluntarily 제출되었다.

{"[2020DO10729]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.

1. a. When investigative agencies execute a warrant of seizure and search, the person from whom items are seized or the defense counsel may participate in its execution (Articles 219 and 121 of the Criminal Procedure Act). Even where, in the course of a seizure and search of 저장매체, it is impossible to print and duplicate within the scope fixed, or where exceptional circumstances are recognized in which it is markedly difficult to accomplish the purpose of seizure, and the storage media containing electronic information, hard copies, or imaging and other forms (hereinafter referred to as the “duplicate copy”) are moved to the investigative agency’s office, etc. for duplication, examination, and printing, the principles of warrant issuance and 적법절차 must still be observed by guaranteeing the opportunity for the person from whom items are seized or the defense counsel to participate and by taking appropriate measures to prevent arbitrary duplication, etc. of electronic information unrelated to the alleged facts. If such measures were not taken, then, unless there are special circumstances such as where the side of the person from whom items were seized explicitly indicated an intention not to participate in the above procedures or process, or where it cannot be said that the purpose of guaranteeing participation in the procedure was substantially infringed in light of the nature and content of the process in which the procedural violation occurred, the seizure and search cannot be said to be lawful. The same applies even where the investigative agency duplicated and printed only the electronic information related to the alleged facts from the storage media or the duplicate copy (see Supreme Court en banc Decision dated 2015. 7. 16. in 2011MO1839, Supreme Court Judgment dated 2017. 9. 21. in 2015DO12400, etc.).

Meanwhile, the defense counsel’s right to participate, as provided in Articles 219 and 121 of the Criminal Procedure Act, is an inherent right granted to the defense counsel for the protection of the person from whom items are seized. Therefore, even if the person from whom items were seized explicitly indicated to the investigative agency an intention not to participate in the execution of the warrant of seizure and search, the defense counsel must, unless special circumstances exist, be separately guaranteed an opportunity to participate in the execution of the warrant of seizure and search by being notified in advance of the time and place of execution pursuant to Articles 219 and 122 of the Criminal Procedure Act.

b. Article 308-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “evidence collected in violation of lawful procedures shall not be admissible as evidence.” This explicitly sets forth the exclusionary rule for illegally obtained evidence in order to realize the constitutional ideal of guaranteeing the fundamental human rights of the people by suppressing unlawful acts in investigative processes, including unlawful seizure and search, and preventing their recurrence (see Supreme Court Judgment dated 2013. 3. 14. in 2010DO2094, Supreme Court Judgment dated 2019. 7. 11. in 2018DO20504, etc.). Article 12 of the Constitution declares the principles of due process and warrant issuance with respect to seizure and search in order to guarantee fundamental human rights, and the Criminal Procedure Act inherits this and establishes specific standards concerning seizure and search procedures so as to harmoniously realize the ideals of discovering substantive truth and protecting individual rights. Since it is necessary to firmly maintain the normative force of the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act and to suppress unlawful acts in investigative processes, evidence collected not only in violation of lawful procedures but also secondary evidence obtained on the basis thereof should be regarded as having been secured without lawful procedures prepared for the protection of fundamental human rights and, in principle, cannot be used as evidence for conviction.

However, uniformly denying evidentiary admissibility merely because evidence was collected without following the procedures prescribed by law does not accord with the purposes of the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act. This is because the realization of legitimate punitive power through the discovery of substantive truth is also an important goal and ideal that the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act seek to achieve through criminal procedure. If the investigative agency’s procedural violation does not amount to an infringement of the substantive content of due process, and rather it is an exceptional case in which excluding evidentiary admissibility would be evaluated as producing a result contrary to the intent of the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act in establishing procedural provisions for criminal procedure so as to seek harmony between the principle of due process and the discovery of substantive truth and thereby realize criminal justice, the court should find that such evidence may be used as evidence for conviction. Whether this applies must be determined by comprehensively and holistically examining all circumstances relating to the procedural violation committed in the course of the investigative agency’s collection of evidence, namely, the purport of the procedural provision, the content and degree of the violation, the specific circumstances and avoidability of the violation, the nature of the rights or legal interests that the procedural provision seeks to protect and the degree of infringement, the relationship between such rights or legal interests and the defendant, the relationship between the procedural violation and the collection of evidence, and the investigative agency’s awareness and intent. Since this legal principle applies equally to secondary evidence obtained on the basis of evidence collected without lawful procedures, secondary evidence may also be used as evidence for conviction in exceptional cases by comprehensively and holistically considering all circumstances relating to the collection of secondary evidence, focusing on whether the causal relationship between the collection of evidence without procedure and the collection of secondary evidence has been attenuated or severed (see Supreme Court en banc Decision dated 2007. 11. 15. in 2007DO3061, Supreme Court en banc Decision dated 2015. 1. 22. in 2014DO10978, Supreme Court Judgment dated 2019. 7. 11. in 2018DO20504, etc.).

2. a. The gist of the charged facts at issue in this case is as follows.

The Defendant, at an unknown time in or before 2019, in the restroom of “○○ Singing Practice Room” located in Uijeongbu-si (address omitted), attached, by using tape, a small camera wrapped in vinyl to the outside of a trash can inside the toilet stall there, attached a portable battery connected to the above camera to the inside of the trash can, and then pressed the record button, thereby filming the buttocks and genitals of an unidentified female who was using the toilet in that restroom; in addition, from around 2013 to around 2019, the Defendant filmed the victims using the toilet in restrooms on a total of 296 occasions as set forth in numbers 1 through 296 of the crime list table cited in the judgment below. In this way, the Defendant, by using a camera or any other mechanical device with a similar function, filmed the body of another person that may arouse sexual desire or cause shame, against that person’s will.

b. The lower court, for the following reasons, found that this portion of the charged facts fell under a case in which the facts constituting the offense were not proven, and thus reversed the first-instance judgment that had found the Defendant guilty and held him not guilty.

1) The investigative agency violated due process by executing the warrant of seizure and search on 2019. 10. 30. in the investigative agency’s office by searching, duplicating, and printing the storage media, without having previously notified the Defendant’s court-appointed defense counsel of the time and place of execution.

2) Considering that the Defendant was then in custody and the importance of the participation procedure prescribed in Articles 219 and 121 of the Criminal Procedure Act, the above violation of due process was serious in degree.

3) Therefore, video capture printouts, etc. collected through the unlawful seizure and search cannot be used as evidence pursuant to Article 308-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and the Defendant’s confession is also a product based on those pieces of evidence or the only evidence for this portion of the charged facts, so it cannot be used as evidence of guilt pursuant to Article 308-2 or Article 310 of the Criminal Procedure Act.

3. The lower court’s above determination cannot be accepted as is for the following reasons.

a. According to the reasoning of the lower court judgment and the record, the following facts may be found.

1) A judicial police officer affiliated with the Gyeonggi Uijeongbu Police Station, Police Lieutenant Nonparty 1, on 2019. 10. 25. at around 09:00, removed from the Defendant’s residence to the police station, by way of taking them out, one computer main unit owned by the Defendant (hereinafter referred to as the “computer at issue”) and one Galaxy Note8 mobile phone (hereinafter referred to as the “mobile phone at issue”), on the basis of the search, seizure, and inspection warrant dated 2019. 10. 24. issued by a judge of the Uijeongbu District Court (hereinafter referred to as the “warrant at issue”).

2) At that time, the Defendant handwrote a “V” mark and signed and affixed his thumbprint on the portions of the confirmation forms for removal of the original for the computer at issue and the mobile phone at issue stating, “I participated in the process of sealing the digital device and storage media and confirmed that there was no problem with the sealing; I was notified that I may participate in the process of unsealing, obtaining the duplicate copy, and searching, duplicating, and printing the digital device, storage media, or duplicate copy; and I will not participate in the above process.”

3) In the first police interrogation of the suspect immediately thereafter, the Defendant stated, “Since 4 to 5 years ago, I installed a hidden camera purchased online in trash cans in restrooms of PC rooms, singing rooms, etc. and filmed women’s genitals, etc., and stored the videos on the hard disk of the computer at issue.”

4) Police Sergeant Nonparty 2, affiliated with the Gyeonggi Uijeongbu Police Station, searched the hard disk of the computer at issue on 2019. 10. 25., discovered a number of video files that appeared to have been filmed by the Defendant with a hidden camera, prepared an investigative report to that effect, and attached thereto photographs of the folder screen where the video files were stored.

5) Meanwhile, the Prosecutor filed an application for an arrest warrant against the Defendant on 2019. 10. 25., and a judge of the Uijeongbu District Court, after appointing Attorney Nonparty 3 as the Defendant’s court-appointed defense counsel on 2019. 10. 26., conducted a pre-arrest suspect interrogation of the Defendant and issued the arrest warrant.

6) In the second police interrogation of the suspect on 2019. 10. 29., the Defendant stated, “From around 2011 to around 2019, I installed hidden cameras in the restrooms of six places in total, including the places of offense stated in the charged facts at issue in this case, such as PC rooms, hospitals, and singing rooms, and filmed other persons’ bodies,” while specifying the places of offense by year.

7) Police Lieutenant Nonparty 1, Police Sergeant Nonparty 4, and Police Corporal Nonparty 2, affiliated with the Gyeonggi Uijeongbu Police Station, each took charge of one of the three hard disks built into the computer at issue and searched them in their office on 2019. 10. 30., then captured the playback scene of the illegal filming video they each found (one scene per video file) and printed it together with the captured image of the corresponding video file information (all such printouts are hereinafter referred to as the “printouts at issue”).

8) However, the investigative agency did not give advance notice to the Defendant’s court-appointed defense counsel concerning the above search and duplication of the computer at issue and the procedure for creation of the printouts at issue, and neither the Defendant nor the above court-appointed defense counsel participated in those procedures.

b. In light of the foregoing legal principles, when examining the above factual relationship, even if the Defendant indicated to the investigative agency an intention not to participate in the process of searching, duplicating, and printing the computer at issue, the investigative agency should have provided the Defendant’s court-appointed defense counsel with an opportunity to participate in the above procedure by notifying him in advance of the time and place of execution before searching, duplicating, and printing the storage medium, namely, the computer at issue, in the investigative agency’s office on 2019. 10. 30.; yet it did not do so. Therefore, the lower court’s determination that the investigative agency executing the warrant at issue violated the seizure procedure is proper, and there is no illegality in the lower court’s above determination that violated no rules of logic or experience, did not exceed the limits of free evaluation of evidence, and did not misapprehend the legal principles regarding the nature of the defense counsel’s right to participate.

c. 1) However, when all of the following circumstances ascertainable through the above factual relationship and the record are comprehensively considered, the above procedural violation by the investigative agency does not amount to an infringement of the substantive content of due process, and rather there is ample room to view this as an exceptional case in which excluding the admissibility of evidence collected through the execution of the warrant at issue would produce a result contrary to the intent of the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act in establishing procedural provisions regarding criminal procedure so as to seek harmony between the principle of due process and the discovery of substantive truth and thereby realize criminal justice.

a) On 2019. 10. 25., the investigative agency, after confirming from the Defendant, who was then the only person entitled to participate as the person from whom items were seized, that he did not wish to participate in the process of searching, duplicating, and printing the computer at issue, began the search of the computer at issue. At the time of the search, the Defendant had already stated that “illegal filming videos are stored on the hard disk of the computer at issue.”

b) By the time the Defendant’s court-appointed defense counsel was appointed, it appears that the investigative agency had already carried out the search of the computer at issue to some extent and had identified at least the location of the folder where the seized electronic information was stored.

c) The Defendant’s court-appointed defense counsel had not inquired of the investigative agency about the status of execution of the warrant at issue, nor had he requested participation in the process.

d) At the time of execution of the warrant at issue, there was no established precedent or internal guideline of the investigative agency that the defense counsel appointed or selected after the commencement of the seizure and search procedure had to be separately notified in advance notwithstanding the person from whom items were seized having waived or refused participation.

e) In the course of executing the warrant at issue, the investigative agency seized videos that the Defendant had recorded, through hidden cameras installed in restrooms of PC rooms, singing rooms, etc. since around 2011, of the bodies of hundreds of victims, and indicted him for 296 of those acts (the charged facts at issue in this case). The Defendant confessed to all of those offenses in the investigative agency and in court.

2) If so, the lower court should have carefully determined, by comprehensively considering the circumstances of the seizure and search pursuant to the warrant at issue, the provisions relating to seizure procedures for electronic information in force at the time of execution of the warrant at issue, the probative purpose of the seized evidence, the circumstances that led to the procedural violation and the investigative agency’s awareness and intent regarding it, and the content and nature of the offense in this case, whether this case falls under an exception to the exclusionary rule for illegally obtained evidence.

Nevertheless, the lower court, based solely on the reasons stated in its opinion, concluded that the evidence collected through the seizure and search pursuant to the warrant at issue could not be used as evidence of guilt and found the charged facts at issue in this case not guilty. In this respect, the lower court erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the exception to the exclusionary rule for illegally obtained evidence and by failing to conduct the necessary examination. The Prosecutor’s ground for appeal pointing out this error is well-founded.

4. Therefore, the portion of the lower court judgment finding not guilty is reversed, and the case is remanded to the lower court for retrial and reconsideration of this portion, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2020DO14654]": "The grounds for final appeal are examined.

1. Summary of the charges at issue

The Defendant, ① from around 2018. 1. 2. to around 2018. 12. 10., committed sexual abuse acts such as sexual harassment causing sexual humiliation against each of the 14 child and juvenile victims in the Attached Sheet of the judgment of the court below, ‘Amended Crime List I,’ and at the same time produced obscene materials by using them; ② on 2019. 3. 1., distributed obscene materials using children and juveniles by transmitting photographs taken of the victim’s genital area, etc.; and ③ from around 2018. 6. 14. to around 2019. 1. 5., possessed a total of 229 items of obscene materials using children and juveniles.

2. Judgment concerning the seizure pursuant to the warrant in this case

A. The judgment of the court below

The court below, based on the reasons stated in its holding, determined that the procedure by which the mobile phone in this case, etc., owned by the Defendant, was seized from the Defendant’s residence pursuant to the warrant in this case was not unlawful, such as by violating the warrant principle or infringing the Defendant’s right to participate in the seizure and search proceedings.

B. Judgment of the Supreme Court

(1) Article 215(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides: “When necessary for a criminal investigation, the prosecutor may conduct seizure, search, or inspection by a warrant issued upon application to a judge of a district court, limited to property for which there are circumstances sufficient to suspect that the suspect committed the offense and which may be recognized as related to the case concerned.” Accordingly, if separate evidence unrelated to the criminal facts that formed the ground for issuance of the warrant is seized, such evidence cannot, in principle, be used as evidence of guilt. However, in the case of an offense that was the object of the seizure and search, or an offense related thereto, the results of such seizure and search may be used as evidence of guilt. A “crime related to the criminal suspicion stated in a seizure and search warrant” means a crime that has an objective connection with the suspected facts stated in the seizure and search warrant and a personal connection between the person subject to the warrant and the suspect. Among such crimes, “objective connection” with the suspected facts means a case directly related to the suspected facts themselves stated in the seizure and search warrant or to an offense having the same basic factual relationship as such facts; however, it may also be recognized where the evidence can be used as indirect evidence or circumstantial evidence to prove the motive and background of the offense, the means and method of the offense, the time and place of the offense, etc. At this time, objective connection should be recognized only where, taking into comprehensive consideration the content of the suspected facts stated in the seizure and search warrant, the object of the investigation, and the course of the investigation, there is a concrete and individual relationship, and such connection should not be deemed to exist merely because the suspected facts and the offense are of the same kind or similar. And the personal connection with the suspect refers to the offense of the person stated in the seizure and search warrant, but it may also be recognized in criminal cases against accomplices such as co-principals, instigators, and indirect principals, as well as necessary accomplices (see Supreme Court Decision 2016DO13489, decided 2017. 1. 25.; Supreme Court Decision 2017DO13458, decided 2017. 12. 5., etc.).

(2) According to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.

(a) The police, based on the results of seizure and search regarding the Defendant’s Facebook account through which the victim communicated, confirmed that the subscriber to the access IP address of the account through which the offender conversed with the victim via Facebook Messenger was Non-Indicted Person 1 the Defendant’s mother. The police further confirmed that Non-Indicted Person 2 the Defendant’s father and Non-Indicted Person 3 the Defendant’s younger brother were residing together on the resident registration record of Non-Indicted Person 1. At the time, the Defendant was residing at the above Facebook access location, but because his resident registration address was different, he did not appear on Non-Indicted Person 1’s resident registration record. The police, after identifying Non-Indicted Person 3 as the suspect, applied for a seizure and search warrant, and the judge of the district court issued the instant warrant as requested by the police.

(b) In the instant warrant, the Defendant’s younger brother, Non-Indicted Person 3, is specified and stated as the suspect of the crime; a. Jeollabuk-do, Jeonju-si address omitted, b. the body of the suspect Non-Indicted Person 3 and the property possessed, owned, or held by the suspect are specified and stated as the places, persons, or things to be searched and inspected; and smartphones, etc., digital devices and storage media owned, possessed, held, managed, or used by the suspect Non-Indicted Person 3 are specified and stated as the items to be seized.

(c) When the police arrived at the Defendant’s residence to execute the instant warrant, the Defendant was absent because he had gone to work, and the police heard from Non-Indicted Person 1 and Non-Indicted Person 3 that the person who committed the instant charged facts was not Non-Indicted Person 3 but the Defendant.

(d) Accordingly, the police presented the instant warrant to Non-Indicted Person 1 and searched the above residence pursuant to the instant warrant and seized the instant mobile phone, etc. owned by the Defendant. At that site, the police prepared a seizure record for each of the seized items, and in the seizure circumstances section, they wrote: Although Non-Indicted Person 3, residing at the Facebook access IP installation location, was identified as the suspect, upon on-site visit, the older brother, the Defendant, was residing there together in a separately divided household status, and after hearing the statements of the mother and Non-Indicted Person 3, it was confirmed that the actual suspect was the Defendant. However, because he was at work and absent at the time of execution of the warrant, the instant warrant was executed with the participation of the mother, Non-Indicted Person 1.

(3) Examining the above facts together with the following circumstances in light of the legal principles discussed above, the seizure of the Defendant’s mobile phone, etc. by executing the instant warrant issued against a person other than the Defendant as the suspect was unlawful.

(a) In light of the spirit of due process and the warrant principle that the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act seek to realize, the words used by a judge when issuing a seizure and search warrant to specify the items to be seized must be strictly construed and must not be expansively or analogically construed to the disadvantage of the person subject to seizure, etc. see Supreme Court Decision 2008DO763, decided 2009. 3. 12., etc.

(b) The police applied for the instant warrant in order to seize items owned or possessed by Non-Indicted Person 3, by identifying Non-Indicted Person 3 as the suspect in this case, and the judge issued the instant warrant to permit seizure of items owned or possessed by Non-Indicted Person 3 in accordance with the purpose of that application. Therefore, according to the wording of the instant warrant, the person subject to the seizure and search is Non-Indicted Person 3, and the items to be seized are limited to those owned, possessed, held, managed, or used by Non-Indicted Person 3.

(c) Even if the police heard at the seizure and search site from another person that the true offender in this case was the Defendant, they cannot seize items owned by the Defendant contrary to the wording stated in the instant warrant. Even if there may be a recognized difference between coercive measures against property and coercive measures against persons in terms such as the degree of substantiation of the criminal facts, once a warrant has been issued identifying the suspect and the person subject to seizure, it cannot be regarded as lawful and valid to execute the warrant by construing another person as the person subject to seizure.

(4) Nevertheless, the court below, for the reasons stated in its holding, determined that the execution of the instant warrant was lawful; thus, the court below erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the unlawfulness of seizure procedures pursuant to a warrant issued against a person other than the Defendant as the suspect.

(5) However, among the instant mobile phone, etc. seized by executing the instant warrant, the file discovered in the E310K mobile phone cannot be regarded as relating to a crime connected with the suspected facts stated in the instant warrant, and thus lacks admissibility of evidence; and because no evidence that could be used as evidence of a crime was discovered in the remainder, the court below did not use as evidence of guilt the evidence obtained from the instant mobile phone, etc. that were unlawfully seized as above.

Accordingly, since the above error by the court below did not affect the outcome of the judgment, the Defendant’s argument in this part of the grounds for final appeal cannot be accepted.

3. Judgment concerning seizure by voluntary submission

A. The seizure and search by an investigative agency of electronic information such as e-mails stored in a suspect’s information processing device, such as a computer, against an internet service user who is the suspect is permitted by the interpretation of the Criminal Procedure Act as a coercive measure in rem against the owner or possessor of the electronic information. Even where the electronic information to be seized and searched is not contained in an information processing device, such as a computer, at the search location stated in the seizure and search warrant, but is stored in a storage medium such as a remote server managed by a third party, connected to the information processing device through an information and communications network, if the investigative agency, pursuant to a warrant issued in lieu of the access authority to the suspect’s email account, enters the suspect’s email account ID and password lawfully obtained by using the information processing device, such as a computer, at the search location stated in the warrant, thereby accessing the remote storage medium in the ordinary manner by which the suspect would access it and downloading or displaying on the screen of the information processing device at the search location the suspect’s email-related electronic information stored there, this also concerns electronic information belonging to or possessed by the suspect, and therefore the seizure and search of that electronic information need not be viewed differently see Supreme Court Decision 2017DO9747, decided 2017. 11. 29. If, when voluntarily submitting a mobile phone, the suspect voluntarily provided the investigative agency with the ID and password for accessing cloud storage, etc., with the intent to submit to the investigative agency electronic information stored not in the mobile phone but in remote locations such as the cloud, managed by a third party, then the electronic information stored in the cloud, etc. may be regarded as having been voluntarily submitted.

B. Judgment

The court below determined, for the reasons stated in its holding, that the Defendant, based on his voluntary intent, submitted the Samsung mobile phone Galaxy Note8 in his possession to the investigative agency, and voluntarily submitted to the investigative agency the SDCard stored files, Naver Cloud files, and Galaxy Note gallery files connected to the Galaxy Note8.

In light of the legal principles discussed above, the court below’s above determination is proper, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal, in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the unlawfulness of seizure procedures by voluntary submission, the admissibility of evidence voluntarily submitted, or the specification of the source of evidence, nor is there any error exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience.

4. Conclusion

Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudged as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}
