Regarding the grounds of appeal challenging 증거능력\\n\\n1) Admissibility of the 전자정보 stored in the two PCs in the lecturer break room of OO University hereinafter referred to as the PCs at issue\\n\\na) Relevant legal principles\\n\\n(1) When an information storage medium containing 전자정보 is voluntarily submitted, the 기준 for determining the scope of 압수 of electronic information and relevance\\n\\nIn light of the 중요성 of electronic information stored in an information storage medium from the perspective of 적법절차, the warrant requirement, and the 비례원칙 that the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act seek to realize, as well as the protection of 사생활의 비밀과 자유, 정보자기결정권, and 재산권, a declaration of intent by a person voluntarily submitting an information storage medium to 지정 the electronic information contained therein or to 한정 the scope of submission must be 엄격하게 construed, and it is not permissible for an investigative agency to 함부로 추단 the unidentified submitter’s intent. Therefore, where an investigative agency can readily 확인 the submitter’s intent but, without doing so, voluntarily receives an information storage medium containing both 전자정보 related to a specific criminal suspicion and unrelated electronic information, it cannot be treated as though all electronic information stored in that medium was voluntarily submitted and seized.\\n\\nWhere an investigative agency seeking to seize electronic information receives an information storage medium and the electronic information stored therein by the method of 임의제출, if due to reasons such as failing to properly confirm the submitter’s intent regarding the specific scope of submission the object and scope of seizure are unclear or cannot be ascertained, only the electronic information related to the criminal suspicion that motivated the seizure and having at least minimal value capable of proving it shall be subject to 압수. Here, related electronic information may include not only the criminal suspicion itself or conduct directly related to an offense based on the same basic 사실관계, but also information usable as 간접증거 or 정황증거 to prove the motive and background of the offense, the means and method, the time and place, and the like. However, such 관련성 is recognized only where, taken 종합적으로 in light of the content of the criminal suspicion, the object of the investigation, the course of the investigation, the process of voluntary submission, and the like, there exists a 구체적·개별적 연관관계; mere similarity or the fact that the offense is of the same kind is not enough (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2016DO348, decided November 18, 2021).\\n\\n(2) Guarantee of the right to participate in searching, copying, and printing electronic information\\n\\nWhere an investigative agency that has voluntarily received an information storage medium or a copy thereof containing both seized and non-seized electronic information transfers the medium to the prosecutor’s office or the like and searches, copies, and prints it, in such a series of processes it must in principle comply with the warrant requirement and 적법절차 by guaranteeing the opportunity to participate to the party subject to seizure/search under Articles 219 and 121 of the Criminal Procedure Act hereinafter referred to as the person subject to seizure or his or her defense counsel, by preparing and delivering a 압수목록 specifying the file details of the seized electronic information, and by taking appropriate measures to prevent arbitrary copying of unrelated electronic information. If such measures were not taken, then unless there are 특별한 사정 such as where the person subject to seizure expressly indicated an intent not to participate or where, in light of the purpose and course of the voluntary submission or the nature and content of the procedure violating act, it cannot be deemed that the purpose of guaranteeing participation was substantially infringed, the seizure/search cannot be regarded as lawful, and this is not changed by the fact that the investigative agency copied or printed only related electronic information from the medium or its copy.\\n\\nFurthermore, where a third party such as a victim voluntarily submits without a warrant an information storage medium belonging to or under the control of the suspect, it is difficult to deem that the suspect, who is the person substantially subject to seizure, consented to the investigative agency’s unrestricted search of all electronic information therein; moreover, even when the suspect himself or herself voluntarily submits the information, in view also of the fact that the suspect’s right to participate must be guaranteed, unless there are special circumstances, appropriate measures must be taken under Articles 219, 121, and 129 of the Criminal Procedure Act to guarantee the suspect’s procedural rights, such as guaranteeing the right to participate and delivering a list of seized electronic information see the above en banc decision in 2016DO348, etc.\\n\\nIn this way, in addition to the person subject to seizure who voluntarily submitted the information storage medium, the information storage medium belonging to or under the control of the suspect, as to which the right to participate must also be guaranteed to a suspect who is not the submitter, refers to a case where the suspect at the time of seizure/search or until a time temporally proximate thereto actually dominated and managed the medium, possessed and exercised exclusive authority to manage and dispose of all electronic information stored therein, and did not otherwise transfer or waive it to a third party according to his or her own intent, and thereby may be evaluated as the person substantially subject to seizure with respect to the electronic information stored in that medium. Whether this applies must be determined not by a legal or ex post facto judgment based on civil-law attribution of rights, but on the basis of the externally and objectively recognizable factual condition at the time of seizure/search. Apart from such externally and objectively dominant and managerial conditions concerning the medium, persons who merely had prior involvement in the use of the medium or the creation/use of individual electronic information, or persons identified as the data subject by electronic information created in that process, are not to be treated as actual parties subjected to seizure/search.\\n\\nb) Facts found\\n\\nThe reasons of the lower court judgment and the evidence lawfully admitted show the following facts.\\n\\n(1) By around September 10, 2019, the prosecution had conducted investigative measures including execution of search-and-seizure warrants for the Defendant’s professor’s research room at OO University and for ◇◇◇ High School, with criminal suspicion facts including forgery of a private document concerning a commendation certificate in the name of the President of OO University dated September 7, 2012 against the Defendant the facts charged in Seoul Central District Court Case No. 2019GOHAP738, uttering of a forged private document arising from Person 1’s submission of the above commendation certificate in the application process to the Graduate School of Medicine of △△ University and □□ University, obstruction of the performance of official duties by deception concerning the admissions screening work of the Graduate School of Medicine of □□ University arising from the above commendation certificate and other false career entries, and other offenses related to Person 1’s fraudulent application to the medical graduate school.\\n\\n(2) Person 2 had served as an assistant to the ☆☆ College of OO University from March 1, 2019, and had been responsible for taking over and managing the lecturer break room at OO University and the items therein from his or her predecessor. The PCs at issue were stored in the lecturer break room without any separate marking as to ownership or legal relations.\\n\\n(3) The basic purport of Person 2’s statement regarding the ownership and management status of the PCs at issue was that, having been told by his or her predecessor that they were items left behind by retirees, so return them to the school authorities or handle them as appropriate, he or she understood them in that way. Furthermore, according to Person 2’s statement, if there were a professor who wished to use the PCs at issue, he or she intended to provide them.\\n\\n(4) The Defendant’s side also argued, at the first hearing date in the first instance, that the Defendant had never used the PCs at issue and that they had been used only as shared PCs at OO University; although their arguments changed several times up to the lower court, their basic position was that the PCs at issue had been used as shared PCs at OO University, then taken by the Defendant to his or her residence, etc. for use for a certain period, and then returned to OO University around December 2016 so that they could again be used as shared PCs at the OO University English camp and the like. This is consistent with the state at the time of the search and seizure in this case, in which the objective and actual dominion, custody, and attribution of the authority to manage and dispose of the PCs at issue were with OO University.\\n\\n(5) While cooperating in the investigation by guiding the prosecutorial investigators through the interior of the ☆☆ College building at OO University on September 10, 2019 based on the cooperation instructions of OO University, Person 2, at the request of the prosecutorial investigator, enabled the prosecutorial investigator to operate one of the PCs at issue and to inspect the electronic information stored therein. In the course of the prosecutorial investigator’s search of the electronic information stored in that PC in Person 2’s presence, a folder related to Person 3 was discovered, and while the search continued, a situation occurred in which the PC emitted a pop sound and powered off. Thereupon, the prosecutorial investigator asked Person 2 and Person 4, the Director of the Administrative Support Office who oversaw the management of OO University’s property, whether they could discontinue the search at the scene and submit the PCs at issue to the prosecution.\\n\\n(6) In response, Person 2 and Person 4 voluntarily submitted the PCs at issue in response to the prosecutorial investigator’s request, and in that process they entered their personal details, signed, and affixed their seals/thumbprints on the Consent to Voluntary Submission form, which stated that they were voluntarily submitting the PCs at issue and listed the PCs at issue in the section for voluntarily submitted items.\\n\\n(7) At that time, the prosecutorial investigator asked Person 2 and Person 4 whether they wished to attend the imaging and search of the PCs at issue, extraction of electronic information, and the like, but Person 2 and Person 4 replied that they would not attend. Thereafter, Person 2 and Person 4 entered their personal details, signed, and affixed their seals/thumbprints in the section for the person subject to seizure voluntary submitter of the Confirmation of Whether to Attend the Submission and Imaging etc. of an Information Storage Medium form hereinafter referred to as the Confirmation of Whether to Attend, which stated in substance that they would not attend the hard copy imaging of the voluntarily submitted medium, search and copying printing of electronic information, and the like.\\n\\n(8) The prosecutorial investigator received the above Consent to Voluntary Submission and Confirmation of Whether to Attend from Person 2 and Person 4, delivered to them a Seizure Inventory Receipt concerning the PCs at issue, and then took the PCs at issue to the Supreme Prosecutors’ Office. In that process, the prosecutorial investigator did not additionally reconfirm with Person 2 and Person 4 their intent regarding the specific scope of submission of the electronic information stored in the PCs at issue.\\n\\n(9) Thereafter, the prosecution carried out imaging and forensic work on the PCs at issue to extract electronic information, and as a result, evidence was discovered indicating that the forgery of the private document concerning the commendation certificate in the name of the President of OO University had been carried out around June 16, 2013 using one of the PCs at issue.\\n\\n(10) Accordingly, on November 27, 2019, in Seoul Central District Court Case No. 2019GOHAP738, the prosecution filed a motion for amendment of the indictment, changing the existing charged facts that the Defendant forged a commendation certificate in the name of the President of OO University by arbitrarily affixing the President’s official seal of OO University on September 7, 2012 at OO University to the effect that the Defendant forged a commendation certificate in the name of the President of OO University in electronic file form using a PC at his or her residence on June 16, 2013. However, upon being denied leave on the ground that the identity of the charged facts was not recognized, the prosecution additionally indicted the Defendant on December 17, 2019 in Seoul Central District Court Case No. 2019GOHAP1050 on charged facts identical to those in the motion for amendment of the indictment.\\n\\n(11) On February 11, 2020, the prosecution delivered to Person 2 and Person 4 a list specifying the file details of the electronic information extracted from and seized from the PCs at issue.\\n\\n(12) The electronic information stored in the PCs at issue was used as evidence of the offenses related to Person 1’s fraudulent application to the medical graduate school among the facts charged in this case, including forgery of a private document dated June 16, 2013 the facts charged in Seoul Central District Court Case No. 2019GOHAP1050.\\n\\nc) Holding\\n\\n(1) Voluntary submission of the PCs at issue\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles, examination of the above facts found shows that, as of September 10, 2019, the PCs at issue were not being used exclusively by a specific person for a specific purpose, but were being kept in the lecturer break room for nearly three years on the premise that OO University personnel would use them as shared PCs at OO University or otherwise dispose of them at their discretion, and the assistant responsible for the management and custody of the PCs at issue at the ☆☆ College of OO University, Person 2, was carrying out the custody and management duties concerning the PCs at issue. It is therefore recognized that Person 2, the assistant in charge of the custody and management duties at the time, and Person 4, the Director of the Administrative Support Office overseeing the management of OO University’s property, submitted the PCs at issue to the prosecution according to a voluntary intent reflecting OO University’s position.\\n\\n(2) Necessity and relevance of the seizure of electronic information stored in the PCs at issue\\n\\n(a) In light of the foregoing legal principles, the lower court erred in presuming that, in the case of a voluntary submission of an information storage medium and the electronic information stored therein, the object of seizure is not limited to the extent that necessity and relevance are recognized, and in concluding that, even though the investigative agency did not confirm with Person 2 and Person 4 their intent regarding the specific scope of submission of the electronic information stored in the PCs at issue, all of the PCs at issue and all electronic information stored therein could be regarded as having been voluntarily submitted. The PCs at issue were an information storage medium in which electronic information related to the criminal suspicion concerning the Defendant and electronic information unrelated thereto were commingled, and in such a case, it is in principle impermissible to arbitrarily infer the unidentified submitter’s intent and treat all electronic information stored in the PCs as having been voluntarily submitted and seized.\\n\\n(b) Where, as such, the object and scope of seizure of electronic information according to the voluntary submitter’s intent cannot be clearly ascertained, only electronic information related to the criminal suspicion that motivated the seizure pursuant to the voluntary submission and having at least minimal value capable of proving it should be deemed subject to seizure.\\n\\nAt the time of the voluntary submission of the PCs at issue, the Defendant was already under investigation for the offense of uttering a forged private document to the effect that a forged commendation certificate in the name of the President of OO University had been submitted in the application process to the Graduate School of Medicine of △△ University and □□ University by Person 1, as well as for obstruction of the performance of official duties by deception concerning the admissions screening work of the Graduate School of Medicine of □□ University arising from the above commendation certificate and other false career entries.\\n\\nAccordingly, electronic information created by using the PCs at issue in the process of Person 1’s fraudulent application to the medical graduate school, such as the Defendant’s use of one of the PCs at issue on June 16, 2013 to forge the above commendation certificate, can be regarded as evidence having a concrete and individual nexus to proving the motive and background, means and method, and the like, of the offense concerning the above criminal suspicion, and even comprehensively considering the object and course of this investigation and the process of voluntary submission, it is sufficient to recognize necessity and relevance.\\n\\n(c) Ultimately, among the electronic information stored in the PCs at issue, the portions used as evidence of the offenses related to Person 1’s fraudulent application to the medical graduate school among the facts charged in this case have both necessity and relevance for seizure pursuant to voluntary submission; thus, the lower court’s legal error as noted above does not affect the result of the judgment.\\n\\n(3) Guarantee of the right to participate in the process of search and extraction of the electronic information stored in the PCs at issue\\n\\n(a) In light of the foregoing legal principles, the lower court erred in stating, in substance, that when an information storage medium and the electronic information stored therein are voluntarily submitted and seized, there is in principle no room to recognize the right to participate on the part of the person subject to seizure or the suspect during the process of searching the electronic information.\\n\\nThe PCs at issue were an information storage medium in which electronic information related to the criminal suspicion concerning the Defendant and electronic information unrelated thereto were commingled, and after the prosecution voluntarily received them from Person 2 and Person 4 and seized them, the prosecution moved them to the National Digital Forensics Center of the Supreme Prosecutors’ Office and, in the process of searching and extracting the electronic information stored therein, had, in principle, to guarantee the opportunity to participate to OO University, the person subject to seizure.\\n\\n(b) However, as seen in the facts found above, in light of the course of the search and extraction of the electronic information related to the criminal suspicion from the PCs at issue, it is recognized that the prosecution confirmed the intent to participate and afforded an opportunity to Person 2 and Person 4, who were the persons subject to seizure, but that the persons subject to seizure waived that opportunity. Therefore, it cannot be said that there was a defect in the seizure/search procedure for the electronic information extracted from the PCs at issue in that the right to participate of the persons subject to seizure was not guaranteed.\\n\\nFurthermore, in light of the purpose of guaranteeing the opportunity for the persons subject to seizure to participate as one of the appropriate measures to prevent distortion of electronic information in an information storage medium subject to seizure/search or arbitrary copying of unrelated electronic information see Supreme Court Order 2009MO1190, dated May 26, 2011, Supreme Court en banc Order 2011MO1839, dated July 16, 2015, etc., examining the entire process of the seizure/search in this case, the reasons asserted by the Defendant alone, such as that no additional measure such as detailed notification of the criminal suspicion facts was taken with respect to Person 2 at the time of seizure pursuant to voluntary submission of the PCs at issue, cannot establish that the purpose of guaranteeing procedural participation to the persons subject to seizure was substantially infringed.\\n\\n(c) Also, examining the above facts found on the basis of the foregoing legal principles, when viewed according to the objectively and externally recognizable factual condition at the time of the seizure/search pursuant to voluntary submission of the PCs at issue, it cannot be recognized that the PCs at issue or the electronic information stored therein belonged to or were under the Defendant’s ownership or control. Rather, in light of objective circumstances such as OO University’s actual domination and management of the PCs at issue by keeping them in the lecturer break room for nearly three years from around December 2016 while also seeming to be able to use them as shared PCs or take other measures such as discretionary disposal, it is recognized that OO University was, at that time, in a state of actually possessing and exercising comprehensive authority to manage and dispose of all electronic information stored in the PCs at issue.\\n\\nEven considering all the circumstances asserted by the Defendant, such as that the Defendant had, before around December 2016, taken the PCs at issue to the Defendant’s residence, etc. and used them exclusively, or that after around December 2016 the lecturer break room where the PCs at issue were stored was near the Defendant’s professor’s research room, it cannot be said that the Defendant’s actual domination and management of the PCs at issue and the authority to manage and dispose of all electronic information stored therein continued until the time of the seizure/search in this case. Accordingly, this case does not fall within a situation in which the Defendant can be evaluated as the person substantially subject to seizure/search in relation to the seizure/search in this case.\\n\\nTherefore, even under the legal principles set forth in the above Supreme Court en banc Decision 2016DO348, the seizure/search of the electronic information stored in the PCs at issue does not fall within a case in which the suspect’s right to participate must be guaranteed.\\n\\n(d) Meanwhile, the Defendant also argues that, during the seizure/search process of the electronic information stored in the PCs at issue, the Defendant’s side should have been guaranteed the right to participate on the ground that the Defendant’s side was the data subject of the electronic information. As noted above, in order for a suspect to assert a right to participate in the course of searching electronic information in an information storage medium voluntarily submitted without the suspect’s involvement, the premise is the suspect’s actual domination and control over the information storage medium and possession of exclusive authority to manage and dispose of all electronic information therein. Therefore, this argument cannot be accepted, as it is not intended to recognize the right to participate even to those who merely participated in the creation/use, etc. of individual electronic information, or to persons who are the data subjects identified by the electronic information created in that process, irrespective of such domination and control.\\n\\n(e) Ultimately, the right to participate was guaranteed to the persons subject to seizure in the course of the search and extraction of the electronic information stored in the PCs at issue, and the case does not fall within a situation where the Defendant’s side also had to be guaranteed a right to participate; accordingly, the lower court’s error in this part also does not affect the result of the judgment.\\n\\n(4) Admissibility of the electronic information extracted from the PCs at issue\\n\\nThe lower court, for the reasons stated in its judgment, held that the prosecution’s voluntary receipt and seizure of the PCs at issue from OO University, the possessor and custodian of those PCs, did not constitute an unlawful investigation after indictment, that it could not be said that the admissibility of the electronic information extracted from the PCs at issue was recognized only if the Defendant’s side consented thereto, and that the electronic information extracted from the PCs at issue could be used as evidence because the identity and integrity between that electronic information, the documents printed therefrom, and the originals were proven.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the foregoing legal principles and the facts found above, although there are some inappropriate parts in the lower court’s statement of reasons, the conclusion of the lower court recognizing the admissibility of the evidence extracted from the PCs at issue is proper, and there is no error affecting the judgment, such as misapprehension of legal principles concerning compulsory investigation after indictment, the necessity of consent of the data subject in the seizure/search of voluntarily submitted items by a third party’s consent, the status and voluntariness of the custodian in seizure of voluntarily submitted items, the scope of the provisions mutatis mutandis of Article 219 of the Criminal Procedure Act in the seizure of voluntarily submitted items from an information storage medium, identity and integrity with the original, and the warrant requirement, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2) Admissibility of the results of execution of the search-and-seizure warrants for tracing financial accounts\\n\\na) The lower court, for the reasons stated in its judgment, held that, in executing the search-and-seizure warrants for tracing financial accounts, the prosecution’s series of execution methods sending, through the Criminal Justice Information Network, requests for provision of financial transaction information, copies of the warrants, and copies of the investigators’ identification cards to several financial institutions by electronic fax, receiving financial transaction data by e-mail or fax from the financial institutions, analyzing the received financial transaction data, then finally preparing a list of selected data related to the case, and thereafter directly visiting the financial institutions to present the original warrants, storing the selected data in a storage medium, while also delivering a seizure inventory and preparing a seizure protocol did not violate the seizure/search procedures prescribed by the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act, and that the financial transaction data collected and submitted as evidence by such method in this case were admissible.\\n\\nb) However, as a matter of principle, investigative agencies’ seizure and search must be based on a search-and-seizure warrant issued by a judge, and the original warrant must be presented to the person receiving the disposition see Supreme Court Decision 2015DO10648, decided September 7, 2017; Supreme Court Decision 2018DO2841, decided March 14, 2019. Accordingly, even in executing a search-and-seizure warrant for tracing financial accounts, if the investigative agency did not present the original warrant in advance to the financial institution before receiving financial transaction data from it, such method cannot in principle be regarded as a lawful method of execution.\\n\\nHowever, where, as a result of the investigative agency’s request to the financial institution for provision of financial transaction information under Article 4(2) of the Act on Real Name Financial Transactions and Guarantee of Secrecy hereinafter referred to as the Financial Real Name Act, accompanied by a copy of the warrant, the financial transaction data received in reply from the financial institution fall within the objects and scope of execution of the warrant; and where the entire process of requesting provision and receiving the data by facsimile transmission or electronic transmission is based on the financial institution’s voluntary willingness to cooperate; and where, after going through the procedure of selecting from among the data those financial transactions related to the criminal suspicion facts, the original warrant is finally presented and the seizure procedure is executed for the selected data; and where the process is carried out in the manner prescribed by the Financial Real Name Act and there are no circumstances suggesting that it was otherwise conducted with the intent to circumvent due process and the warrant requirement only in such a case may it exceptionally be regarded as a lawful method of execution of the warrant, on the basis that the entire series of procedures can be evaluated as presenting the original warrant in a timely manner based on one warrant and seizing/searching on that basis.\\n\\nc) In light of such legal principles, examining the process of execution of each of the search-and-seizure warrants for tracing financial accounts in this case, even if the original warrant was not presented in advance to the financial institution before the investigative agency received financial transaction data from it, this case falls within a situation where the subsequent series of procedures after going through the selection process for data related to the criminal suspicion facts, ultimately presenting the original warrant and directly seizing the selected data can, viewed as a whole, be evaluated as presenting the original warrant in a timely manner based on one warrant and seizing/searching within the original objects and scope of execution of the warrant on that basis. Nor are there circumstances sufficient to recognize that the investigative agency executed the warrant in the above manner with the intent to circumvent due process and the warrant requirement.\\n\\nAccordingly, the lower court’s conclusion that the admissibility of the financial transaction data secured in the execution process of the search-and-seizure warrants for tracing financial accounts in this case is recognized is proper, and there is no error affecting the judgment, such as misapprehension of legal principles concerning the method of presenting the warrant and the lawfulness of the seizure/search procedure, the admissibility of the seized items and secondary evidence in this part, or insufficient judicial examination, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3) 120,000 physical shares of [Company Name 1 omitted]\\n\\nThe lower court, for the reasons stated in its judgment, held that the search-and-seizure warrant concerning 120,000 physical shares of [Company Name 1 omitted] was lawfully presented to the person subject to seizure, and that admissibility of evidence was recognized because the necessity of seizure and relevance to the criminal suspicion facts were also recognized.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the evidence lawfully admitted, the lower court’s determination contains no error, such as misapprehension of legal principles concerning the admissibility of evidence of this seized item and secondary evidence, or insufficient judicial examination, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n4) Admissibility of the audio recording file of a telephone conversation kept by [Company Name 2 omitted]\\n\\nThe lower court, for the reasons stated in its judgment, held that the necessity of seizure and the relevance to the criminal suspicion facts were recognized with respect to the audio recording file of the telephone conversation kept by [Company Name 2 omitted], and thus the evidence was admissible.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the evidence lawfully admitted, the lower court’s determination contains no error, such as misapprehension of legal principles concerning the admissibility of evidence of this seized item and secondary evidence, or insufficient judicial examination, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nB. Regarding the grounds of appeal concerning the offenses related to Person 1’s fraudulent application to the medical graduate school\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in its judgment, the lower court found that the Defendant forged the commendation certificate in the name of the President of OO University as alleged in the facts charged in this part obstruction of business, obstruction of performance of official duties by deception, uttering of a forged official document concerning the experiential activity confirmation issued in the name of the head of the ◎◎◎◎ Research Institute of ▽▽ University, uttering of a forged official document as an alternative charge concerning the internship confirmation issued in the name of the head of the ▷▷▷▷▷ Center of ◁ University at △△ University, forgery of a private document dated June 16, 2013, and uttering of a forged private document, and that all other supporting documents were also false; that submitting them in the application process to the Graduate School of Medicine of △△ University and □□ University by Person 1, or entering them in the career history, constituted deception for the offenses of obstruction of business and obstruction of performance of official duties by deception; that the Defendant’s intent and the conspiracy with Person 1, etc. were recognized in that process; and that this constituted an act obstructing the admissions screening work of each medical graduate school and could not be regarded as merely due to inadequate review by the persons in charge. On that basis, the lower court found this part of the charges guilty.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the evidence lawfully admitted, the lower court’s determination contains no error affecting the judgment, such as exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, misapprehension of legal principles concerning the establishment of co-principal liability, the deception and intent elements of obstruction of business and obstruction of performance of official duties by deception, or danger of obstruction, or omission of judgment or insufficient judicial examination, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nC. Regarding the grounds of appeal concerning fraud and violation of the former Subsidy Management Act the Act before amendment by Act No. 13931 on January 28, 2016 hereinafter referred to as the former Subsidy Act\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in its judgment, the lower court held that the special grant money stated in the facts charged in this part constituted a subsidy under the former Subsidy Act, and that the Defendant fraudulently applied for and received research assistant allowances, thereby finding that this constituted a deceptive act for the offense of fraud. On that basis, the lower court found this part of the charges guilty.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the evidence lawfully admitted, the lower court’s determination contains no error affecting the judgment, such as exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or misapprehension of legal principles concerning the interpretation of Article 2(1) and Article 9 of the former Subsidy Act, Article 4(1) Appended Table 1 of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act, or deception in the offense of fraud, or insufficient judicial examination, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nD. Regarding the grounds of appeal concerning the part violating the Capital Markets and Financial Investment Services Act hereinafter referred to as the Capital Markets Act due to the use of undisclosed material information excluding the part acquitted on grounds\\n\\nThe lower court, for the reasons stated in its judgment, held that, as alleged in the facts charged in this part, the Defendant purchased shares of [Company Name 1 omitted] using undisclosed material information. On that basis, the lower court found this part of the charges guilty.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the evidence lawfully admitted, the lower court’s determination contains no error affecting the judgment, such as exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or misapprehension of legal principles concerning the establishment of the act of using undisclosed material information, the presumption of innocence, insufficient judicial examination, or lack of reasons, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nE. {"[2022DO7453]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.

1. Determination on the argument that the legal doctrine concerning the participation right in the voluntary submission procedure for a digital storage medium was misunderstood

a. Relevant 법리

1) The importance of 전자정보 stored in a digital storage medium derives, along with 적법절차, 영장주의, and 비례의 원칙, from the perspective of privacy, the secrecy and freedom of private life, and 정보에 대한 자기결정권.

Where a law-enforcement agency that has received on a voluntary basis a digital storage medium, or a duplicate thereof, in which seized and non-seized electronic information are intermingled, transports the medium to the office and searches, copies, and prints it, the agency must, in that series of processes, guarantee participation to the party subject to seizure and search under Articles 219 and 121 of the Criminal Procedure Act, or to defense counsel, prepare and deliver a seizure inventory specifying the file details of the seized electronic information, and take appropriate measures to prevent arbitrary copying of unrelated information, thereby complying with the warrant requirement and due process. If such measures were not taken, then, unless there are special circumstances such as an express intention not to participate, or such that, in light of the purport and course of the voluntary submission or the nature and content of the process in which the violation occurred, it cannot be said that the purpose of guaranteeing participation was substantially infringed, the seizure and search cannot be assessed as lawful. Nor does it matter even if the agency copied and printed only electronic information related to the suspected facts.

Where a victim or other third party voluntarily submits a digital storage medium belonging to or under the control of the suspect, it is difficult to regard the suspect as having consented to unrestricted search of all electronic information, and even when compared with the case where the suspect himself or herself makes the voluntary submission, in which participation rights must be guaranteed, unless special circumstances exist, proper measures to ensure procedural rights such as participation and delivery of an inventory must be taken. See 2016DO348 etc.

2) The phrase digital storage medium belonging to or under the control of the suspect means a case in which the suspect, at the time of seizure and search or at a temporally close point thereto, actually dominates and controls the medium while retaining and exercising exclusive authority to manage and dispose of all electronic information stored in it, and has not otherwise transferred or abandoned it to a third party according to his or her own will, so that the suspect can be evaluated as a substantive party to the seizure and search as to all electronic information stored in the medium. Whether this applies shall be determined not on the basis of civil-law attribution, but on the basis of the outwardly and objectively recognizable factual condition at the time of seizure and search. Apart from such outward and objective state of domination and control, it is not the case that the suspect or another third party must be treated as a substantive party merely because of past use or involvement, or because they are the data subject identified by electronic information created in that process. See 2021DO11170 etc.

b. Facts found

According to the reasons of the lower-court judgment and the evidence duly admitted, the following facts can be found.

1) The law-enforcement agency, starting with search and seizure conducted around 2019. 8. 27. at (Name 2 omitted) University, (Name 3 omitted) office, and (Name 1 omitted) academy, etc. in connection with suspicions of admissions and academic irregularities involving the children of Non-Indicted Persons 1 and 2, suspicions of improprieties in private equity fund investments, suspicions of irregularities at the (Name 1 omitted) academy, and the like, began a full-scale investigation into the various allegations.

2) In preparation for the investigation such as search and seizure, Non-Indicted Person 1, in order to conceal computers storing electronic information related to the suspected facts, around 2019. 8. 31., handed over to Non-Indicted Person 3 three digital storage media used at their residence, namely one HDD detached from a computer in the study, one HDD and one SSD detached from the computer of his son Non-Indicted Person 4, and instructed him to hide them until the investigation was over. Non-Indicted Person 3 concealed the instant hard disk drive in places such as a personal locker at a gym in Seoul Yangcheon-gu.

3) The instant hard disk drive stored evidence that Non-Indicted Person 1 intended to conceal, namely internship certificates used in his children’s university and graduate school admissions and text messages of Non-Indicted Person 4, the Defendant, and other related persons.

4) Around 2019. 9. 10. the law-enforcement agency took Non-Indicted Person 3 into custody as a suspect on charges of concealment of evidence. Non-Indicted Person 3 voluntarily submitted the instant hard disk drive on 2019. 9. 11.

5) In the process of the voluntary submission of the instant hard disk drive and the search, copying, and printing of the electronic information stored therein, the law-enforcement agency guaranteed the participation right by confirming with Non-Indicted Person 3 and his defense counsel whether they wished to participate and by affording them the opportunity to participate, but Non-Indicted Person 3’s side indicated an intention not to participate. The law-enforcement agency did not confirm such intention with Non-Indicted Persons 1 etc. nor afford them an opportunity to participate.

c. Determination

Taking into account the legal principles examined above and the following circumstances discernible from the facts found, it cannot be said that participation rights had to be guaranteed also to Non-Indicted Persons 1 etc. who were not the persons making the voluntary submission, in addition to Non-Indicted Person 3 who voluntarily submitted the instant hard disk drive as a suspect in the offense of concealment of evidence. In the same purport, the lower court’s determination recognizing the admissibility of the electronic information stored in the instant hard disk drive is justified and can be accepted.

1) Non-Indicted Person 3, as a suspect in the offense of concealment of evidence, voluntarily submitted the instant hard disk drive during the investigation against him. The hard disk drive and the electronic information stored therein are evidence not only concerning the suspected facts of Non-Indicted Persons 1 etc., who are the principal offenders, but also the direct object of the concealment act, and thus constitute evidence concerning Non-Indicted Person 3’s concealment suspicion. Accordingly, Non-Indicted Person 3 is a person with a substantive interest in the instant hard disk drive and the electronic information stored therein. Throughout the entire process, including the voluntary submission itself and the searching, copying, and printing of the electronic information related to the concealment suspicion, Non-Indicted Person 3 has an interest in participation.

2) As the investigation into himself and Non-Indicted Persons 2 etc. became full-scale, Non-Indicted Person 1 delivered the instant hard disk drive to Non-Indicted Person 3 while instructing him to hide it. Non-Indicted Person 3 voluntarily concealed the hard disk drive in a place known only to himself so that it would not be discovered. Thereafter, when Non-Indicted Person 3 was taken into custody as a suspect on concealment of evidence, he disclosed the concealment to the law-enforcement agency and voluntarily submitted the hard disk drive. In light of the circumstances surrounding the concealment and voluntary submission, and the extent of involvement of Non-Indicted Person 3 and Non-Indicted Persons 1 etc., it may be said that the person who actually possessed the hard disk drive at the time of seizure and search or at a close time thereto was Non-Indicted Person 3. Further, insofar as Non-Indicted Person 3 actually possessed the hard disk drive around that time by the foregoing circumstances, it may be regarded, absent other special circumstances, that he was also in a position to de facto retain and exercise the authority to manage and dispose of the stored electronic information.

3) Non-Indicted Person 1 was not the suspect in the offense of concealment of evidence, which was the criminal facts giving rise to the voluntary submission, and moreover, he delivered the instant hard disk drive to Non-Indicted Person 3, requesting vaguely that it be hidden until the investigation into himself is over, with the purpose of concealing the very existence of the instant hard disk drive. This can be regarded as an expression of an intention, under the purpose of concealing and severing the outward connection between himself and the instant hard disk drive and the electronic information stored therein, to abandon or wholly transfer to Non-Indicted Person 3 the exclusive right of domination and control over the instant hard disk drive until the indefinite time of completion of the investigation, if necessary for achieving that purpose. As a result, Non-Indicted Person 3 came to be in a state where he could de facto retain and exercise actual domination over the instant hard disk drive and exclusive authority to manage and dispose of all electronic information stored therein, and he actually exercised that authority by concealing the hard disk drive at a place of his own choosing and thereafter voluntarily submitting it to the law-enforcement agency.

2. Determination of the remaining grounds for final appeal

The lower court maintained the first-instance judgment, which found the facts charged in this case guilty for the reasons stated in the opinion. Examining the reasons of the lower-court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the evidence duly admitted, there is no error affecting the judgment in that the lower court either exceeded the limits of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, without fully conducting the necessary examination, or misunderstood the legal principles concerning relevance between seized items and the facts charged, abuse of prosecutorial authority, the presumption of innocence and the principle of trial based on evidence concerning the falsity of the instant certificate, deception and risk of result in the crime of obstruction of business, intent and co-principal liability, and the admissibility of derivative evidence, etc.

3. Conclusion

Therefore, the final appeal is dismissed, and judgment is rendered as stated in the main text. In this judgment, except for the dissenting opinion of Supreme Court Justices Min Yu-sook, Lee Heung-gu, and Oh Kyung-mi, the views of the participating Justices were unanimous, and there are the concurring opinions of Supreme Court Justices Ahn Cheol-sang, Noh Tae-ak, and Cheon Dae-yeop on the majority opinion, as well as the concurring opinion of Supreme Court Justice Oh Kyung-mi on the dissenting opinion.

4. Dissenting opinion of Supreme Court Justices Min Yu-sook, Lee Heung-gu, and Oh Kyung-mi

a. Summary of the dissenting opinion

1) The majority opinion held that Non-Indicted Person 3, who voluntarily submitted the instant hard disk drive, had a substantive interest in the electronic information stored therein as a suspect in the offense of concealment of evidence, and could de facto retain and exercise the authority to manage and dispose of that electronic information by actually possessing it; therefore, it was sufficient that participation rights were guaranteed to him in the seizure and search procedure, and since Non-Indicted Persons 1 etc., who handed over the instant hard disk drive to Non-Indicted Person 3 to conceal evidence concerning their own suspected facts, had abandoned or transferred the exclusive authority to manage and dispose of it, they did not correspond to the substantive persons subject to seizure who were the objects of the guarantee of participation rights.

2) However, we cannot agree. The majority opinion understands the substantive person subject to seizure, the subject to whom participation right is guaranteed, narrowly with a focus on the suspect in the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search, and this does not accord with the purport and direction of the precedents. In addition, according to the majority opinion, by disregarding the constitutional demand to realize due process and the warrant requirement in the coercive disposition of the law-enforcement agency concerning electronic information, which is increasingly important to individuals and businesses in modern society, it allows an anti-constitutional result in which the fundamental rights concerning the secrecy and freedom of private life of the electronic-information manager and disposer, who is the substantive person subject to seizure, are infringed.

3) In the above 2016DO348 en banc decision and 2021DO11170 etc., the Supreme Court stated that the substantive person subject to seizure, who is the subject to whom participation rights are guaranteed in the seizure and search of electronic information, is a person who actually dominates and controls the digital storage medium concerned, retains and exercises exclusive authority to manage and dispose of all electronic information in that medium, and can be evaluated as a person who is a substantive party to the seizure and search thereof. According to the legal principles and purport of such precedents, where, in addition to the actual possessor and custodian of the digital storage medium, there separately exists an owner/manager, and there is a risk that his or her privacy, freedom, information self-determination, property rights, etc. may be infringed by the coercive disposition, that owner/manager must be regarded as the substantive person subject to seizure who is the object of the guarantee of participation rights. At this time, it is not required that the substantive person subject to seizure be the suspect in the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search.

4) Therefore, where a person who concealed evidence received instruction from the principal offender to conceal evidence and voluntarily submitted to the law-enforcement agency, in the status of a suspect, the digital storage medium belonging to or under the control of the principal offender that the evidence concealer had possessed and kept, and where the principal offender can be assessed as having a substantive interest not to have his privacy and freedom, etc. infringed during the search, copying, and printing of the electronic information stored in that medium, participation rights must also be guaranteed to the principal offender, who has such substantive interest together with the evidence concealer as both the voluntary submitter and the suspect.

On that point, we differ from the majority opinion. The detailed grounds are as follows.

b. The purport of guaranteeing participation rights in the seizure and search of electronic information and the concretization of the participation right

The participation-right doctrine in the seizure and search of electronic information in precedent evolved toward protecting the person who actually suffers infringement of fundamental rights by the coercive disposition, namely the substantive party to the seizure and search disposition, centering on the person subject to seizure who became the direct object of the State’s coercive disposition.

1) The Supreme Court first set forth, in its decision of 2011. 5. 26. 2009MO1190, the legal doctrine guaranteeing the participation right to the person subject to seizure or that person’s defense counsel in the seizure and search of the digital storage medium located in the office of the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union, which was the object of the coercive disposition. Subsequently, through the en banc decision of 2015. 7. 16. 2011MO1839, the Supreme Court reaffirmed, in the seizure and search of Kyungdong Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd., the legal doctrine of guaranteeing participation rights centered on the person subject to seizure, who is the object of the coercive disposition, and declared that, where there is procedural illegality excluding the person subject to seizure’s participation right, the admissibility of evidence is, in principle, excluded.

In the above Supreme Court decisions 2009MO1190 and 2011MO1839 en banc, the Supreme Court emphasized that, although the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union and Kyungdong Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. were not in the status of suspects, they were in the status of persons subject to seizure who had a substantive interest not to have their right to informational self-determination, property rights, etc. infringed by the seizure and search of the law-enforcement agency, and recognized them as the subjects to whom participation rights belong. Thereafter, in various cases where the person subject to seizure and the suspect were the same person, the Supreme Court recognized the participation right in the person subject to seizure who was the object of the seizure and search disposition regarding the digital storage medium, and finally, through the 2016DO348 en banc decision, held that where a coercive disposition is made against a digital storage medium owned and controlled by the suspect by making a third party the person subject to seizure when the person subject to seizure and the suspect are not the same person, appropriate measures must be taken, such as guaranteeing the participation right to the suspect who is the substantive person subject to seizure and delivering an inventory of the seized electronic information, thereby expanding the subject to whom the participation right is guaranteed to the substantive person subject to seizure. In 2016MO587, while the law-enforcement agency conducted a seizure and search of the KakaoTalk conversation contents etc. of the service user stored on the server of Kakao Corp. by making Kakao Corp. the person subject to seizure, the Supreme Court recognized the status of the service user as the substantive person subject to seizure. Meanwhile, in 2021DO11170, it was held that where a third party voluntarily submitted to the law-enforcement agency a digital storage medium used by the suspect, if it can be seen that the authority to manage and dispose of it had been transferred to the third party, it is sufficient that the opportunity to participate was afforded to the third party who is not the suspect.

2) Thus, the fact that the Supreme Court established the concept of participation rights centering on the person subject to seizure in the procedure for seizure and search of electronic information, and extended the subject to whom such rights belong to the substantive person subject to seizure, is the result of responding to the constitutional demand that, because in large-capacity computer or server information-processing systems, smartphones, and other digital storage media widely used in the work of corporations or individuals today, electronic information about private daily life or corporate management unrelated to criminal suspicion is extensively intermingled with electronic information concerning the suspected facts subject to seizure, procedural measures are urgently needed to prevent the law-enforcement agency conducting coercive dispositions such as seizure and search from searching, copying, and printing unrelated information as well, in order to protect the legal interests concerning privacy and freedom of private life, information self-determination, property rights, etc. of individuals and businesses.

In this purport, the Supreme Court declared that, when a third party voluntarily submits a digital storage medium owned and controlled by the suspect, the object of seizure should be construed more narrowly to relevant information, because the digital storage medium stores everything concerning personality-related legal interests such as secrecy and freedom of private life and information self-determination, and considering that, even though the subject of the voluntary submission is merely a possessor or custodian other than the owner, if seizure and search are permitted without any restriction, there is a risk that the suspect’s personality-related legal interests will be substantially infringed, in cases where the submission act is likely to substantially infringe the owner’s privacy and other personality-related legal interests, special consideration for the legal interests of the owner who did not consent to the voluntary submission is required, together with the necessity of seizure and search pursuant to the voluntary submission. See 2016DO348 en banc decision and 2019DO7342 etc.

c. The meaning of the substantive person subject to seizure, who is the subject to whom the participation right belongs, and the criteria for determining it

The substantive person subject to seizure who becomes the subject to whom the participation right belongs in the seizure and search of electronic information should be understood as a person who, until the time of seizure and search, actually dominates and manages the relevant digital storage medium while retaining and exercising exclusive authority to manage and dispose of all electronic information in the medium, and who has personality-related legal interests, such as the secrecy and freedom of private life, that exclude the law-enforcement agency’s search and printing of unrelated information intermingled with the lawful seizure target.

1) Participation right of the person subject to seizure, who is the object of coercive disposition

It is sufficient that the subject to whom the participation right belongs is the actual possessor and custodian of the digital storage medium that became the object of the coercive disposition and the manager and disposer of the stored electronic information, that is, the real counterparty to the coercive disposition; it is not necessary that such person be the suspect in the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search.

The Constitution of Korea provides that no one shall be subjected to seizure or search except by due process of law, and that when arresting, detaining, seizing, or searching, a warrant issued by a judge upon the request of a prosecutor in accordance with due process of law shall be presented, thereby declaring the principles of due process and warrant requirement. In order to concretely realize these principles, the Criminal Procedure Act has detailed provisions limiting the seizure and search procedure of the law-enforcement agency, such as the method of issuance of a seizure and search warrant, presentation of the warrant in the execution procedure, participation of the party and prior notice to the person with participation rights, and participation of the person in charge. The Supreme Court, focusing on the particularity of seizure and search of digital storage media in which relevant information and irrelevant information are intermingled, sought to firmly uphold the normative force of the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act by effectively curbing unlawful searching and collecting of irrelevant information. In light of the provisions of Article 12 of the Constitution concerning due process and the principle of warrant requirement, together with the fundamental purport of the various procedural provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act, the Supreme Court established the doctrine that the person subject to seizure and defense counsel may participate in the seizure and search procedure of electronic information and extended the scope of such guarantee to the substantive person subject to seizure.

The Supreme Court, even before the enactment of Article 243-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which provides for defense counsel’s participation right, in the suspect interrogation procedure under the former Criminal Procedure Act, where there was no express provision concerning the defense counsel’s right to participate, recognized the defense counsel’s right to participate in the suspect interrogation procedure by analogically applying the provisions concerning the right of detention-bound defendants or suspects to meet and communicate, based on the constitutional principle of due process. Recognizing the person subject to seizure’s participation right in the seizure and search procedure of electronic information and extending it to the substantive person subject to seizure is an extension of the Supreme Court’s stance to date of interpreting the Criminal Procedure Act in conformity with the Constitution so as to protect the fundamental human rights of the subject of the State’s coercive disposition from infringement.

The constitutional freedom of residence and the secrecy and freedom of private life are guaranteed to everyone, and the object of the warrant requirement is not limited to suspects; therefore, the substantive person subject to seizure, as the subject to whom the participation right is attributed, is not required to be in the status of a suspect in the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search. Just as in a typical seizure and search of a residence or office, the substantive owner or manager of the premises that became the object of the coercive disposition is protected by privacy and freedom, in the seizure and search procedure of electronic information, the owner/manager of the digital storage medium must receive procedural guarantees such as participation rights in accordance with the warrant requirement. This is because, as the owner/manager of the digital storage medium, there is no reason to endure a State agency investigating the criminal suspicion of a third party broadly searching, copying, and printing unrelated information from his or her digital storage medium merely because he or she is not the suspect. Permitting this would have the same result as permitting a general warrant.

According to the precedents’ attitude regarding the purpose and scope of recognition of participation rights, in determining the subject to whom the participation right belongs, it is not very important who submitted the relevant digital storage medium to the law-enforcement agency or whether that person is in the status of a suspect. This is because, without needing to distinguish between the case where the manager/disposer of the electronic information directly submits the digital storage medium to the law-enforcement agency and the case where a third party such as a victim possesses or keeps it for some reason and then submits it to the law-enforcement agency, the necessity of guaranteeing participation rights to the person subject to seizure or the substantive person subject to seizure, who is the manager/disposer of the electronic information, in order to substantially protect his or her secrecy and freedom of private life and other personality-related legal interests, is the same.

The 2016DO348 en banc decision recognized the suspect’s participation right in the case where a victim or other third party unlawfully took a digital storage medium belonging to or under the control of the suspect and voluntarily submitted it, because the suspect, as the owner/manager of the digital storage medium and manager/disposer of the electronic information, occupies the status of the substantive object of the coercive disposition, that is, the status of a person subject to seizure. The manager/disposer of irrelevant information existing within the digital storage medium has an interest, as a substantive party to the seizure and search, in blocking the infringement of personality-related legal interests arising from the coercive disposition even if that person is not the suspect. Conversely, even if one is a suspect, if one is not the manager/disposer, one does not have such an interest.

The Supreme Court, only in a case where the law-enforcement agency received voluntary submission from a lodging business operator of a disguised camera secretly installed in a guest room for the purpose of illegal filming so as to photograph nudity or sexual acts, and did not afford the suspect who had secretly installed it an opportunity to participate, held that, due to the function and attributes of the relevant digital storage medium, in cases where, from the perspective of the owner’s secrecy and freedom of private life and other personality-related legal interests, there is almost no room for electronic information subject to lawful seizure through voluntary submission and electronic information not subject to it to be intermingled and, in substance, most of the electronic information stored is that which is subject to seizure, the evidence should not be denied merely because the person subject to seizure other than the possessor/custodian was not guaranteed an opportunity to participate and no inventory of seized electronic information was prepared and delivered. See 2019DO7342. In the case of a digital storage medium storing only relevant information, there is in substance no risk of arbitrary searching and copying of irrelevant information, so there is no concern that the purport of guaranteeing participation rights will be undermined. The above decision confirmed that, in such a case, even the suspect, who is the manager/disposer of the electronic information, is not a subject to whom participation rights are guaranteed, thereby showing that the basis of the attribution of participation rights lies not in the status of suspect but in the status of being subject to coercive disposition such as seizure and search and thereby suffering substantial infringement of privacy and other personality-related legal interests.

In this way, in our criminal justice system and investigative practice, the person subject to seizure’s participation right guaranteed in the seizure and search procedure of electronic information has become a practical yet essential procedural right and institution that can constitutionally control the coercive disposition of the law-enforcement agency. By granting the person subjected to coercive disposition the opportunity to directly confirm on site the manner in which the seizure is executed and to raise objections, it is possible to effectively deter the searching and collecting of unrelated information contrary to the warrant requirement. For the participation right to function substantially in accordance with its purpose, it is necessary to grant the participation right to the subject to whom the legal interests, such as secrecy and freedom of private life, that may be infringed by the search, copying, and printing of unrelated information belong.

The majority opinion, based on the fact that the instant hard disk drive and the electronic information stored therein are evidence concerning Non-Indicted Person 3’s concealment suspicion, held that Non-Indicted Person 3 corresponds to a substantive interest holder in the hard disk drive and the electronic information stored therein and has an interest in participation throughout the search, copying, and printing process, and that, since participation rights were guaranteed to Non-Indicted Person 3, the seizure and search procedure was lawful even though the owner Non-Indicted Persons 1 etc. did not participate. However, this runs counter to the precedents concerning the basis for and object of the guarantee of participation rights and is improper. As examined above, the precedents declared the guarantee of participation rights in order to limit the object of seizure to electronic information concerning the suspected facts and to prevent arbitrary copying of electronic information that is unrelated thereto; accordingly, the interest in participation under the precedents lies in the protection of interests concerning unrelated evidence. The above 2019DO7342 decision also did not regard only having an interest in electronic information related to the facts charged, i.e. relevant information, as an interest in participation.

The majority opinion, while emphasizing the importance of electronic information stored in a digital storage medium in modern society and the protection of privacy, the right to informational self-determination, etc. along with the due process and warrant requirement that the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act seek to realize, adopts the contradictory stance of interpreting very narrowly the meaning of the substantive person subject to seizure, who is the subject guaranteed the participation right, centering on the suspect in the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search. Thereby, the majority opinion has substantially nullified the achievements made by the precedents so far in responding to the constitutional demand that due process and warrant requirement be realized by declaring the participation-right doctrine in the coercive disposition of the law-enforcement agency concerning electronic information and expanding the scope of the subjects to whom it belongs. As a result, in the seizure and search procedure of electronic information, the door to the procedural right called the participation right, which the Supreme Court opened for the guarantee of fundamental rights of the person subject to seizure or the substantive person subject to seizure, has been half-closed again. It is no appropriate measure to realize the principle of relevance in the seizure and search of a digital storage medium to say that it is sufficient to guarantee participation rights only to the suspect, who is the direct and formal party to the coercive disposition, even though that person has no special interest in preventing arbitrary searching of unrelated information, and that there is no need to guarantee participation rights even to the owner/manager of the digital storage medium; this is tantamount to abandoning the protection of due process and the warrant requirement against infringement of personality-related legal interests concerning unrelated information that may arise for the owner/manager of the digital storage medium.

2) Guarantee of participation rights where the formal person subject to seizure and the substantive person subject to seizure are separate

Where, in addition to the actual possessor and custodian of the digital storage medium, who is the direct object of the law-enforcement agency’s coercive disposition and the formal person subject to seizure, the owner/manager exists separately, it is necessary to regard the latter as the substantive person subject to seizure and guarantee participation rights to him or her as well.

With the development of technology, as the portability and mobility of digital storage media increased, it has become common for an owner/manager to exist separately from the actual possessor and custodian of the digital storage medium. First, there are cases where the digital storage medium leaves the owner/manager’s possession and comes to be in the possession or custody of a third party regardless of the owner/manager’s will. This includes cases where the owner/manager loses the digital storage medium, or where it becomes the object of a criminal act such as theft or embezzlement of lost property, or where a third party takes the medium arbitrarily without the consent of the owner/manager. On the other hand, there are also cases where the digital storage medium comes to be in the possession or custody of a third party based on a possessory-mediated relationship formed according to the owner/manager’s will. This would include cases where the owner/manager requests a specialist repair shop to repair the digital storage medium or deposits it with a bank’s safe deposit box, cases where a child temporarily borrows and uses a parent’s mobile phone, or cases where the owner/manager entrusts his or her digital storage medium to a family member or acquaintance living separately for safekeeping. A case where the principal offender, intending to conceal evidence concerning the suspected facts, hands over a digital storage medium that he or she owned and controlled to an evidence concealer may also fall under the latter category in that it is based on a possessory-mediated relationship formed according to the owner/manager principal offender’s will.

The 2016DO348 en banc decision recognized the suspect’s participation right in the former situation, where a victim or other third party took, without the suspect’s knowledge, a digital storage medium belonging to or under the control of the suspect from the crime scene and voluntarily submitted it to the law-enforcement agency, that is, the case in which the digital storage medium left the owner/manager’s possession regardless of his or her will. This doctrine must likewise apply to the latter situation, where a third party possessed or kept the digital storage medium on the basis of a possessory-mediated relationship formed according to the owner/manager’s will and coercive disposition is made against the third party. When determining whether the subject falls within the object of the participation-right guarantee, there is no reason to treat differently the case where the separation of the owner/manager and actual possessor/custodian of the digital storage medium occurred according to the owner/manager’s will and the case where it did not. In both cases, they are the same in that the manager/disposer of the electronic information is the subject to whom personality-related legal interests, which may be infringed by the law-enforcement agency’s arbitrary copying of unrelated information, belong.

3) Criteria for determining the substantive person subject to seizure

Whether one corresponds to the substantive person subject to seizure as the subject to whom the participation right belongs must be determined on the basis of the factual state outwardly and objectively recognizable at the time of seizure and search, such as who actually dominated and managed the relevant digital storage medium until the time of seizure and search or a temporally close point thereto, and whether, based on the objective circumstances surrounding the progress of the investigation and the loss of possession or possessory mediation concerning the medium, the law-enforcement agency could recognize that an owner/manager existed separately from the possessor/custodian of the medium. Internal, subjective circumstances between related persons that the law-enforcement agency could not recognize at the time of seizure and search, or a legal and retrospective judgment concerning the attribution of rights under civil law, are not to be considered. In addition, even a person who actually dominated and managed the medium is excluded from the subject to whom the participation right belongs if he or she transferred it to a third party according to his or her own will or abandoned the right of domination and control over it. See 2021DO11170.

When, as above, the substantive person subject to seizure is determined based on the objectively and outwardly recognizable factual state at the time of seizure and search, there is little risk of causing confusion and side effects in investigative practice, such as being unable to identify the person with the participation right or unreasonably expanding the scope of the guarantee to many persons. This is because, unless there are special circumstances suggesting the existence of a separate manager/disposer, it is acceptable to regard the actual possessor/custodian of the digital storage medium at the time of seizure and search as the manager/disposer of the electronic information, and it is sufficient to regard a person as the substantive person subject to seizure only when there are special circumstances from which the law-enforcement agency can, based on the objectively and outwardly recognizable factual state, acknowledge that a person who exclusively holds authority to manage and dispose of the electronic information exists separately from the actual possessor/custodian. For example, this includes cases where, from an objective and outward perspective, a customer’s digital storage medium kept in a bank safe deposit box or a client’s computer temporarily kept by a computer repair company that has been entrusted with repair is plainly separated, by its very nature, from the actual possessor/custodian and the exclusive manager/disposer of the electronic information, or where the law-enforcement agency can recognize, through the statement of the actual possessor/custodian or the progress of the investigation, that a separate exclusive manager/disposer exists.

The majority opinion stated that, in light of the circumstances surrounding the concealment and voluntary submission of the instant hard disk drive, the person who actually possessed the instant hard disk drive at the time of seizure and search or at a time close thereto was Non-Indicted Person 3, and thus, absent other special circumstances, the person in a position to de facto retain and exercise the authority to manage and dispose of the electronic information stored in the instant hard disk drive was also Non-Indicted Person 3; however, this is not proper. In this case, in light of the progress of the respective investigative procedures concerning Non-Indicted Person 1 etc., the principal offenders, and Non-Indicted Person 3, the evidence concealer, as well as the content of the statements made by Non-Indicted Person 3 to the prosecutor at the time he voluntarily submitted the instant hard disk drive, and other factual circumstances objectively and outwardly recognizable to the law-enforcement agency, the agency could recognize, at the time it accepted the voluntary submission, that, in addition to Non-Indicted Person 3, who was the actual possessor/custodian of the instant hard disk drive, there existed Non-Indicted Person 1 etc., who were the exclusive managers/disposers of the electronic information.
