In particular, the fact that the law-enforcement agency, while investigating the suspect facts against the principal offender, took as a suspect for the offense of concealment of evidence the person who was concealing the digital storage medium belonging to or under the control of the principal offender and accepted the concealed item by voluntary submission, by itself means that, at the time of voluntary submission, the agency was aware of the existence of the principal offender, who is an element of the offense of concealment of evidence, and that the concealed item belonged to or was under the control of the principal offender.

d. Scope of the guarantee of participation rights in the case of the principal offender and the evidence concealer

1) The legal doctrine of guaranteeing participation rights should likewise apply to cases where the principal offender instructs the concealment of evidence by handing over to the evidence concealer a digital storage medium in which electronic information constituting evidence concerning the suspected facts is stored, and the evidence concealer keeps and conceals it and then submits it to the law-enforcement agency in the form of seizure or voluntary submission. In such a case, the principal offender, as the owner/manager of the digital storage medium that is in a typical possessory-mediated relationship vis-à-vis the evidence concealer, who is the actual possessor/custodian of the concealed item, corresponds to the substantive person subject to seizure, who has an interest in protecting rights such as the secrecy and freedom of private life by preventing the searching and collecting of unrelated information in the course of seizure and search. Even if the evidence concealer voluntarily submitted it to the law-enforcement agency in the status of a suspect for concealment of evidence, the substantive person subject to seizure is the principal offender, and participation rights should also be guaranteed to him or her. Because the evidence concealer, who is not the subject to whom the personality-related legal interests concerning unrelated information within the concealed digital storage medium belong, has no incentive to actually exercise participation rights even if such rights are guaranteed, the purpose of guaranteeing participation rights for the sake of the warrant requirement cannot be realized merely by excluding the principal offender and guaranteeing participation rights only to the evidence concealer. Nor can it be prevented, in the seizure and search procedure of the concealed digital storage medium, that unrelated information concerning the principal offender’s private life is broadly and indiscriminately collected by the law-enforcement agency. In this case as well, Non-Indicted Person 3, the evidence concealer, waived the exercise of his participation right.

2) Where the principal offender, by handing over to the evidence concealer a digital storage medium in which electronic information constituting evidence concerning his or her own suspected facts is stored, instructed concealment, unless there are other special circumstances that would justify recognizing that he or she definitively and completely abandoned the authority to manage and dispose of that electronic information, it cannot be concluded solely from the fact that actual and direct possession of the medium was transferred to the evidence concealer by such handover that the principal offender transferred or abandoned the authority to manage and dispose of the electronic information or that the interest in the participation right, which enables protection of personality-related legal interests such as the secrecy and freedom of private life by excluding the law-enforcement agency’s search of unrelated information intermingled in the medium, has disappeared.

Considering the characteristics of digital storage media and electronic information, the purpose of their concealment, the circumstances of the concealment of evidence, whether the concealed evidence is to be returned, and the true intentions of the parties, it is natural and consistent with experience rules to interpret that the principal offender merely entrusted the storage to the evidence concealer on a temporary basis through concealment of the medium until the risk of exposure or discovery of relevant information disappeared, and that, once that risk disappeared, the principal offender intended to regain actual dominion over the medium, including the electronic information that is unrelated evidence. Owing to the characteristics of the possessory-mediated relationship formed between the principal offender and the evidence concealer concerning the concealment of a medium in which relevant information and unrelated information are intermingled, the principal offender should be understood as having concealed the medium with the intention not only of evading criminal responsibility but also of preserving and keeping the unrelated information, which has personal and personality-related value, and of receiving it back at an appropriate time in the future, in a situation where it is technically difficult to sift out and discard or destroy only the relevant information inside the medium.

3) The majority opinion viewed that Non-Indicted Person 1, the principal offender, expressed an intention to waive or wholly transfer the exclusive right of domination and control over the instant hard disk drive to Non-Indicted Person 3 until the indefinite time of completion of the investigation, by handing over the hard disk drive to Non-Indicted Person 3, requesting that it be hidden until the investigation into himself is over, with the purpose of concealing the very existence of the hard disk drive, which is evidence concerning the principal-offense suspicion, and thereby under the purpose of concealing and severing the outward connection between himself and the hard disk drive etc. However, the majority opinion exceeds the bounds of reasonable interpretation of intent in the structure of the principal offender and evidence concealer, which is a typical possessory-mediated relationship, and is not proper.

The majority opinion also errs in equating this with cases where one instructs concealment of tangible objects that are themselves evidence concerning the suspected crime, such as a weapon used in a murder offense or narcotics or syringes provided for a drug-related offense, overlooking the specificity and importance of the intermingling of unrelated evidence in a digital storage medium with respect to the guarantee of participation rights. If the context of personality-related legal interests in the coercive disposition such as seizure and search of a digital storage medium intermingled with relevant and unrelated evidence had originally been the same as in the case of the above weapon, narcotics, or other evidence objects, there would have been no need for the precedents to establish the doctrine of guaranteeing participation rights to the person subject to seizure in the seizure and search procedure of electronic information.

The majority opinion is also confusing the issue of interpreting intent concerning domination and control over the electronic information that is the concealed item between the principal offender and the evidence concealer in this case, or the issue of identifying the subject to whom the participation right belongs, with the assessment of illegality, culpability, or the existence of criminal responsibility for the act of Non-Indicted Person 1 in infringing the judicial function concerning the investigation of the principal offense through instigation of concealment of evidence. If there were no act of instigation of concealment of evidence by the principal offender, that is, if the principal offender had concealed the digital storage medium by handing it over to a third party unaware of the concealment intent while concealing such intent, would the majority opinion really take the same view and exclude the principal offender’s participation right? If the conclusion regarding the existence or nonexistence of the principal offender’s participation right differs in the two cases, this can only be seen as confusing the assessment of punishability of concealment instigation and the issue of identifying the subject to whom participation rights belong.

4) In this case, the majority opinion, where the law-enforcement agency, while investigating the principal-offense facts against the principal offender, voluntarily received from the evidence concealer the digital storage medium belonging to or under the control of the principal offender that he or she had concealed, overlooked the fact that the investigative procedure against the evidence concealer is, in substance, conducted as part of the investigative procedure against the principal offender, and, without exploring the legal issue of who is the substantive person subject to seizure as the subject to whom participation rights belong in the possessory-mediated relationship of the principal offender and evidence concealer structure, handled the matter as an issue of interpreting whether the principal offender had transferred or abandoned the authority to manage and dispose of the medium to the evidence concealer. That is not the proper attitude a Supreme Court, a bulwark for the protection of human rights, should take.

e. Determination concerning this case

1) Based on the following circumstances, judged from the factual state outwardly and objectively recognizable at the time of seizure and search pursuant to the voluntary submission of the instant hard disk drive, it is difficult to see that, until the time of Non-Indicted Person 3’s voluntary submission and at a temporally close point thereto, Non-Indicted Person 1 etc., who were the principal offenders, actually dominated and managed the hard disk drive on the basis of actual possession or of a possessory-mediated relationship through Non-Indicted Person 3, while retaining and exercising exclusive authority to manage and dispose of the electronic information stored therein as the subject to whom legal interests belong, and that they had lost neither the authority to manage and dispose of it nor ownership or control. Accordingly, it is proper to regard Non-Indicted Person 1 etc. as the substantive persons subject to seizure with respect to that electronic information.

2) In the series of processes such as searching and extracting the electronic information stored therein after seizing the instant hard disk drive by voluntary submission from Non-Indicted Person 3 during the investigation of the principal-offense facts against Non-Indicted Person 1, the law-enforcement agency must guarantee an opportunity to participate to Non-Indicted Person 1 etc., who are the substantive persons subject to seizure of the instant hard disk drive and the electronic information, in addition to Non-Indicted Person 3, who is the person subject to seizure. However, in such a series of processes, the law-enforcement agency did not guarantee participation rights to Non-Indicted Person 1 etc., who are the substantive persons subject to seizure, in addition to Non-Indicted Person 3.

Accordingly, the electronic information in the instant hard disk drive seized by the law-enforcement agency constitutes illegally obtained evidence and cannot be used as evidence of guilt. It is also difficult to find any special circumstances to recognize an exception thereto. The statements of the related persons collected by the law-enforcement agency on the basis of that illegally obtained evidence also constitute derivative evidence based on illegally obtained evidence and likewise cannot be used as evidence to establish guilt.

3) In this case, there is room to view that, excluding evidence without admissibility, it is difficult to say that the remaining evidence alone proved the facts charged beyond a reasonable doubt. Nevertheless, the lower court maintained the first-instance judgment, which found the facts charged guilty for the reasons stated in the opinion. Such a determination contains errors affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning participation rights in the seizure of voluntarily submitted items and the exclusionary rule for illegally obtained evidence, and by failing to conduct the necessary examination.

For the foregoing reasons, I state that I cannot agree with the majority opinion.

5. Concurring opinion of Supreme Court Justices Ahn Cheol-sang, Noh Tae-ak, and Cheon Dae-yeop on the majority opinion

With respect to the subject of participation rights for securing procedural legality in the seizure and search process of electronic information, in light of the holdings and purport of a series of precedents that guaranteed participation rights to the suspect when the suspect, rather than the formal person subject to seizure, corresponds to the substantive person subject to seizure, the scope of seizure and search resulting from Non-Indicted Person 3’s voluntary submission of the instant hard disk drive is limited to evidence related to the criminal facts that motivated it, namely the crime of concealment of evidence. Therefore, procedural legality is clearly established by guaranteeing participation rights to Non-Indicted Person 3, who is both the suspect in the relevant criminal facts and the actual dominator and manager of the digital storage medium that is the relevant evidence, and it does not appear necessary to provide further argumentation in this regard. Below, we supplement the grounds of the majority opinion only to the extent necessary to prevent misunderstanding of the majority opinion’s purport among the matters pointed out in the dissenting opinion.

a. The purport of the precedents concerning participation rights

The substantive person subject to seizure concept in the precedents is a kind of instrumental concept devised to overcome the gap between statutory wording and the basic ideas centered on the constitutional principle of due process and warrant requirement in the phase of guaranteeing participation rights concerning seizure and search of electronic information, which traditional seizure and search doctrine premised on tangible objects did not anticipate. The purport contained in the series of precedents concerning participation rights is that, in seizure and search of a digital storage medium in which it is difficult to know the subject to whom a multitude and wide variety of individual pieces of stored information belong, the matter should in principle be regulated centering on the person subject to seizure, who is the manager/disposer of all electronic information, but where the person subject to seizure has no substantive interest whatsoever in the criminal facts suspected and the seized items, there is no reason to participate in the seizure and search procedure; on the other hand, in order to prevent the possibility that indiscriminate seizure and search execution may occur without anyone’s participation by excluding a suspect who has a substantive interest on the ground that he or she is not the person subject to seizure, the problem is resolved through the concept of the substantive person subject to seizure.

In light of this stance of the precedents, where the evidence concealer voluntarily submits, with respect to the criminal facts of concealment of evidence, the digital storage medium that is the object of concealment, even if the medium belongs to the principal offender, it is sufficient to grant participation rights to the evidence concealer, who is the suspect in and the cause of the voluntary submission seizure and search, and who also corresponds to the person subject to seizure, and there is no need further to regard the principal offender as the substantive person subject to seizure and recognize participation rights for him or her as well. In this case, because the suspect, who is the evidence concealer, voluntarily submits a digital storage medium in his or her possession or custody that is recognized as related to the investigation into his or her own criminal facts, the evidence concealer has direct, substantive, and legal interests as both suspect and person subject to seizure in the seizure and search flowing therefrom. The 2016DO348 en banc decision, in recognizing participation rights for a suspect who is not the formal person subject to seizure as the substantive person subject to seizure, addressed a different plane of discussion from the evidence concealer’s voluntary submission case, because in that case the person subject to seizure, who was the formal voluntary submitter, was merely a victim of the criminal facts and the purpose of guaranteeing the opportunity to participate to that person alone could not substantially realize the purpose of the participation-right guarantee.

In short, where the suspect in the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search not only is related to the facts suspected but also has direct, substantive, and legal interests by dominating and managing the digital storage medium and electronic evidence that are the objects of the seizure and search, if participation rights are guaranteed to that suspect, who simultaneously occupies the status of interested person and person subject to seizure, the procedural legality concerning the participation right can be viewed as thereby satisfied and completed. Unless there are other special circumstances, there is no need to separately posit the substantive person subject to seizure in such a case.

Turning to this case, the instant hard disk drive was voluntarily submitted to the law-enforcement agency by Non-Indicted Person 3, the evidence concealer, while he was dominating and managing it after receiving it from Non-Indicted Person 1, and, in relation to the concealment of evidence that constituted his own criminal facts, Non-Indicted Person 3 has direct, substantive, and legal interests in the hard disk drive, which is the evidence. Accordingly, insofar as the seizure and search procedure for the instant hard disk drive was conducted with the participation of Non-Indicted Person 3, who is the rightful interested party, the procedural legality of that procedure is, in principle, satisfied by affording Non-Indicted Person 3 the opportunity to participate. Further, the dissenting opinion, which would allow an anti-constitutional result infringing the legal interests concerning secrecy and freedom of private life, etc. by not even granting participation rights to Non-Indicted Person 1 etc., who handed over the hard disk drive for the purpose of destroying evidence, is difficult to accept.

b. Recognition of participation rights based on the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search

Recognition of the participation right, including the concept of the substantive person subject to seizure, should in principle be based on the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search. The scope and limits of guaranteeing participation rights should be determined through a balancing of the purpose sought to be achieved through the procedure and the interests infringed thereby, taking into account the characteristics of the investigative procedure. This is because the purport of the participation right is to minimize infringement of the legal interests of the person subject to seizure in the course of a real property-based coercive disposition, while at the same time the ideal of criminal justice, discovering the substantive truth through prompt and effective investigation, must also be harmoniously realized to the extent that such legal interests are not essentially infringed.

The dissenting opinion’s purport is that participation rights in the seizure and search procedure of electronic information should be understood separately from the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search. However, criminal facts are both the ultimate object and purpose to be elucidated through coercive investigation and the basis and cause of the issuance of a warrant and the seizure and search, and the electronic information that is searched, copied, and printed in the process of executing the warrant is also the direct object related to the relevant facts. Therefore, the criminal facts concerned are the most important consideration in the process of searching, copying, and printing relevant electronic information, and it is neither natural nor in accord with the purport of participation rights to disregard precisely the most important element in the relevant criminal procedure when recognizing that procedural right. The precedents concerning this have attempted to rationally interpret, in light of actual and concrete circumstances, the provisions on seizure and search centered on tangible objects, which do not adequately reflect the characteristics of electronic information and its storage medium; however, the dissenting opinion overemphasizes certain phrases from the precedents or understands them superficially, and in the end develops an argument that does not fit the wording of the Criminal Procedure Act and is also detached from the ideal of criminal justice, so it is difficult to accept. This is because the question of whether seizure and search of electronic information related to criminal facts and the guarantee of participation rights are centered on the digital storage medium and its manager/controller, versus the question of whether they are understood separately from the criminal facts, are entirely different matters.

Furthermore, understanding participation rights on the premise of the criminal facts is also consistent with the warrant-execution practice, where promptness, expedition, timeliness, and secrecy are important, because it enables concise and clear identification of the subject of the participation right. The above 2021DO11170 decision, premised on the 2016DO348 en banc decision that where a third party voluntarily submitted a suspect’s digital storage medium in relation to the suspect’s criminal facts, participation rights should be guaranteed to the suspect, who is the substantive person subject to seizure, held that whether the digital storage medium falls within the category for which participation rights are recognized for the suspect should be determined based on the objectively and outwardly recognizable factual state. This is also to harmoniously realize the ideals of criminal justice, protection of fundamental rights and discovery of substantive truth, by reasonably setting the scope of participation rights in light of the on-site nature of seizure and search, etc. The dissenting opinion’s approach, which determines participation rights solely on the basis of the possibility of infringement of legal interests concerning unrelated information in the process of searching, copying, and printing electronic information, ignores the essence of participation rights derived from coercive investigation procedures concerning the facts charged and presupposes that the law-enforcement agency’s seizure and search is, as a rule or in general, exploratory and thus unlawful. Although the concern it raises is understandable, this is a matter to be resolved through the rational interpretation of the relevant legal doctrines, including the participation right, as well as through the application of strict rules of evidence; it is not possible, on that basis, to construct a general doctrine premised on such an exceptional situation.

c. Transfer of the authority to manage and dispose and the existence of the participation right

Where a third party voluntarily submits a digital storage medium belonging to or under the control of the suspect, in order for the suspect to be evaluated as the substantive party to the seizure and search of all electronic information stored in that medium and to receive participation rights, the suspect must, until the time of seizure and search or a temporally close point thereto, have actually dominated and managed the relevant digital storage medium while retaining and exercising the exclusive authority to manage and dispose of all electronic information in that medium, and must not otherwise have transferred or abandoned it to a third party according to his or her will. Meanwhile, as precedent has clearly stated, the authority to manage and dispose here is for the purpose of setting a reasonable scope of protection for participation rights by harmonizing protection of fundamental rights and the ideal of discovery of substantive truth in the seizure and search procedure of electronic information, and is not for the purpose of determining private-law rights and relationships from a legal and retrospective perspective according to the attribution of rights under civil law. See 2021DO11170.

In light of such legal principles, the reason Non-Indicted Persons 1 etc. are not regarded as the substantive persons subject to seizure and thus participation rights are not recognized in the process of voluntary submission and seizure of the instant hard disk drive and the stored electronic information is self-evident. Since Non-Indicted Person 1 handed the instant hard disk drive to Non-Indicted Person 3 and instructed concealment of evidence, and Non-Indicted Person 3 concealed it, it is clear that Non-Indicted Persons 1 etc. thereby lost actual domination and management of the instant hard disk drive; furthermore, the authority to manage and dispose of all stored electronic information was transferred to Non-Indicted Person 3, and in fact Non-Indicted Person 3, by concealing the hard disk drive in a place known only to him, even placed the entire digital storage medium and built-in electronic information in a situation where he could, according to his own judgment, manage and dispose of them at will so that they would not be exposed to the law-enforcement agency. Accordingly, at least for Non-Indicted Persons 1 etc., it must be regarded that they had already reached a state where they could no longer retain and exercise the exclusive authority to manage and dispose.

Moreover, the fact that the principal offender not only conceals the evidence himself or herself but also instructs the evidence concealer, who is the principal offender in form, and thereby causes the state of concealment of evidence, exceeds the scope of legitimate defense rights. Even in light of the fact that the principal offender intentionally created a state in which evidence had departed from its position while infringing the judicial function of the State, it is normatively consistent to regard that the participation right, which is a procedural right in criminal proceedings, or the authority to manage and dispose underlying it, is no longer reserved to the principal offender as a result of such infringement of the State’s judicial function. This also accords with the ideal of criminal justice, which seeks to harmonize discovery of the substantive truth and the principle of due process and thereby realize justice. As noted above, with respect to the criminal facts that caused the voluntary submission in this case or the instant hard disk drive, which is the evidence in question, Non-Indicted Person 3 corresponds to a person having direct, substantive, and legal interests; therefore, by guaranteeing Non-Indicted Person 3 the opportunity to participate in the seizure and search process concerning the instant hard disk drive, the procedural legality thereof can, in principle, be recognized, and this is all the more so because there are no special circumstances that would otherwise require viewing that multiple separate participation-right holders exist.

This is not an evaluation of the illegality of Non-Indicted Person 1’s act of instigating concealment of evidence, but rather an evaluation grounded in the purport of precedent following the loss of Non-Indicted Persons 1 etc.’s exclusive authority to manage and dispose of the instant hard disk drive, so the dissenting opinion’s criticism on this point is incorrect. The dissenting opinion’s argument that a different conclusion can be reached on the basis of civil-law doctrines such as possessory-mediated relationships is likewise difficult to accept for the same reason.

d. Other circumstances

The other grounds advanced by the dissenting opinion likewise cannot be adopted as general legal doctrine or as the conclusion of this case and the subsumption doctrine of precedent.

One point to add in this regard is that the majority opinion does not differ from the dissenting opinion even as to the direction of guaranteeing participation rights in seizure and search procedures proposed by the dissenting opinion. Compared with the legislative examples or trial practice of major foreign jurisdictions, our doctrine concerning participation rights in seizure and search procedures is still in the process of formation. Its orientation lies in realizing, in the seizure and search of electronic information, the constitutional principles of warrant requirement and due process while preventing infringement of fundamental rights such as the secrecy and freedom of private life and the right to informational self-determination, but the essence of coercive investigation procedures is, in any event, to function so as to secure procedural legality and legitimacy in the seizure and search process concerning specific criminal facts suspected. In addition, since it must not be substantially detached from the ideal of criminal justice, discovering the substantive truth through prompt and effective investigation, it is necessary to approach carefully so as not to lose direction, but while striking a balance among conflicting values, also not to deviate from concrete propriety and common-sense conclusions. In that respect, I would like to make clear that, at least in this case, it is only that the dissenting opinion cannot be adopted; the majority opinion does not negate all of the arguments or purport developed by the dissenting opinion.

6. Concurring opinion of Supreme Court Justice Oh Kyung-mi on the dissenting opinion

The situation in which the smartphone you lost recently by leaving it in a taxi is illegally distributed and used in a voice phishing crime and then seized by the law-enforcement agency can happen at any time. The same is true of the situation where your child, who had briefly borrowed and used your smartphone, is caught engaging in illegal filming on the subway and voluntarily submits it to the law-enforcement agency. If the law-enforcement agency learns that you are the owner/manager of the smartphone and that your personal information is stored in it, is the procedural legality concerning participation rights satisfied and completed by recognizing participation rights only for the voice-phishing offender or your child, who are the persons subject to seizure and suspects with direct, substantive, and legal interests based on the criminal facts in the course of the search and extraction process? The concurring opinion of Justices Ahn Cheol-sang, Noh Tae-ak, and Cheon Dae-yeop on the majority opinion answers yes. In such a situation, can one accept that the law-enforcement agency searches and extracts your personal information from your smartphone without your knowledge? Was the participation right in the seizure and search of electronic information recognized by precedent such a flimsy and formal right? The dissenting opinion says no. That is precisely the issue in this case.

a. Concerning the assertion that participation rights must be recognized based on the criminal facts

1) The majority concurring opinion’s assertion that the subject of participation rights must be recognized centering on the criminal facts amounts, in the end, to recognizing participation rights based on suspect status. Such an assertion not only contravenes the explicit stance and flow of the precedents concerning the purport of guaranteeing participation rights, but also contradicts the majority concurring opinion’s own reasoning.

The precedents have repeatedly and explicitly stated that the practical significance and purport of participation rights lie in protecting the person subject to seizure, who is placed at risk of indiscriminate searching and collecting of information unrelated to the suspected facts that caused the seizure and search, in the opportunity for lawful coercive disposition concerning relevant information. The need to be protected from such risks is unrelated to whether the person subject to seizure is a suspect. Rather, from the standpoint of balancing interests, a person subject to seizure who is not a suspect would likely find it even more difficult to accept having to endure disclosure of private life for the investigation of another person unrelated to himself or herself. The above 2019DO7342 decision clearly stated that, even where a suspect who had secretly installed a disguised camera for the purpose of illegal filming corresponds to the substantive person subject to seizure as the manager/disposer of the electronic information, there is no need to recognize participation rights, thereby making clear that if there is no risk of infringement of the person subject to seizure’s legal interests concerning unrelated information, there is no practical benefit in guaranteeing participation rights. By contrast, the majority concurring opinion’s argument that participation rights should be attributed centering on the criminal facts or suspect status can, in effect, be seen as conflicting with the above precedents’ legal doctrine.

Moreover, the majority concurring opinion also stated that the purport of the precedents concerning participation rights is to regulate, in principle, seizure and search of a digital storage medium centering on the person subject to seizure, who is the manager/disposer of all electronic information, but to use the concept of the substantive person subject to seizure instrumentally in order to solve the problem of no participation-right holder where the person subject to seizure has no substantive interest in the criminal facts and the seized items. Even so, the majority concurring opinion’s argument that the subject of participation rights should be recognized centering on the criminal facts lacks consistency.

2) The majority concurring opinion uses direct, substantive, and legal interest in the criminal facts or seized items as an important indicator for recognizing participation rights, but such an interest is unrelated to the purport of the precedents in which participation rights were recognized or to their protected sphere, so it is not logical to use it as an indicator for the attribution of participation rights.

Although the exact purport of direct, substantive, and legal interest in the criminal facts or seized items is not clear, it appears roughly to mean the interest of a suspect in avoiding exposure of evidence concerning his or her own criminal facts to the law-enforcement agency in order to evade criminal liability, that is, the suspect’s defense-right-related interest concerning relevant evidence. If so, this is not directly related to the purport of participation-right guarantees explicitly declared by the precedents. What exists to protect such an interest is the traditionally recognized principle of due process and the warrant requirement itself. It is precisely that, unless there is a warrant lawfully issued by a judge through the specification and substantiation of the suspect’s criminal suspicion, the suspect’s defense-right-related interest concerning relevant evidence is not infringed. Once a warrant has been lawfully issued, both the suspect and any third party must endure the coercive disposition of relevant evidence, which is evidence within the line drawn by the warrant, i.e. within the principle of relevance. This is the active aspect of the warrant requirement vis-à-vis the law-enforcement agency. In this area, participation rights do not have special significance.

Participation rights function in the passive aspect of the warrant requirement vis-à-vis the law-enforcement agency. That is, they are the power to restrain and deny effect when the law-enforcement agency’s coercive disposition extends to irrelevant evidence, i.e. evidence outside the line drawn by the warrant, the principle of relevance. Participation rights protect, in this area, the interests of the subject of the coercive disposition in respect of irrelevant evidence outside the above line.

In the end, the direct, substantive, and legal interest referred to by the majority concurring opinion is not much different from the relevance that determines the scope of the warrant’s effect, and, at least as to recognition of participation rights, it has no meaning beyond being the benchmark for distinguishing relevant evidence from irrelevant evidence. The sphere protected by participation rights according to precedent is the sphere of irrelevant evidence, and it does not overlap at all with the sphere in which a direct, substantive, and legal interest in the criminal facts or seized items is recognized.

b. Concerning the criticism of detachment from the criminal facts

The majority concurring opinion points out that the dissenting opinion understood participation rights separately from the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search, but this is a misunderstanding of the dissenting opinion and is an assertion that cannot logically stand. Participation rights form one pillar of the warrant requirement and, by their nature, cannot be discussed detached from the criminal facts.

Even under the dissenting opinion, the criminal facts substantially affect the setting of the scope or limits of participation rights. In order to set the scope of the guarantee of participation rights, a distinction between relevant information and irrelevant information must first be made, and this is based on the criminal facts. In other words, the line of the principle of relevance, which functions in the passive aspect of the warrant requirement vis-à-vis the law-enforcement agency, is set based on the criminal facts. The area outside that line is the area of participation rights. In the end, the concept of the substantive person subject to seizure according to the dissenting opinion is by no means understood detached from the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search; rather, it is a concept associated with irrelevant evidence premised on the criminal facts.

c. Implications for investigative practice for protecting fundamental rights suited to a highly advanced information society

A smartphone spends all day with its owner/manager in daily life and stores his or her personal information in detail. Corporations cannot conduct business activities without large-capacity computers, servers, and the exchange and storage of information through the internet. Furthermore, due to the increase in portability and mobility, it often happens that digital storage media leave the possession of the owner/manager, either according to his or her will or regardless of it, and come to be in the possession or custody of another person. In the seizure and search process of the law-enforcement agency, one frequently encounters situations in which a suspect conceals or discards his or her mobile phone or computer etc. The dissenting opinion assumes a relation of dispossession or a possessory-mediated relationship etc. as the situation in which participation-right issues arise. It is not unusual for the owner/manager of a digital storage medium and the law-enforcement agency to stand in opposition within such a relationship.

With the dramatic development of information technology, the problematic situations surrounding digital storage media will become even more complex in the future, and the proposition that the coercive disposition of the law-enforcement agency concerning such matters must be constitutionally controlled so that investigative practice develops in a direction that guarantees fundamental rights has become self-evident. The Supreme Court should present, as a guarantee of the procedural right demanded by such a proposition, the standards for seizure and search procedures of electronic information that can both respond to the constitutional demand by guaranteeing procedural rights and satisfy the ideals of criminal justice through discovery of the substantive truth. The dissenting opinion, reflecting the factors considered by precedent in developing the participation-right doctrine, typifies situations of seizure and search of electronic information and establishes a unified standard capable of protecting the interests of the substantive person subject to seizure based on the principle of warrant requirement. This can serve as a guideline for investigative practice to develop in response to the advancement of the information society while efficiently fulfilling the role of discovering the substantive truth and also meeting the demand for protection of fundamental rights.

d. The relationship between expansion of participation-right guarantees and the ideal of discovering substantive truth

The criticism that, if the dissenting opinion is followed, confusion and burden will be imposed on investigative practice and another ideal of criminal justice, discovery of the substantive truth, may regress, is not correct. The scope of the guarantee of participation rights has already expanded to the substantive person subject to seizure by virtue of the legal doctrine of the 2016DO348 en banc decision. This doctrine is evaluated as having achieved a balance and harmony between the ideal of criminal justice that, in the seizure and search procedure of electronic information, the warrant requirement must be effectuated so as to guarantee the fundamental rights of the person subject to seizure concerning irrelevant information, and the other ideal of discovering substantive truth. It is true that law-enforcement agencies have come to bear a greater burden than before in determining the scope of participation-right guarantees, but such a circumstance cannot be described as a regression of the criminal justice ideal of discovering substantive truth. Criticizing the dissenting opinion, which sets the scope of the participation-right guarantee on the basis of the above legal doctrine, as causing a retreat in the discovery of substantive truth is no different from criticizing the 2016DO348 en banc decision on the same grounds.

The seizure and search practice of electronic information is being carried out in the form of imaging the digital storage medium on site, taking it out, and then searching and printing relevant information externally in a separate procedure. Since finding and seizing the tangible object of a digital storage medium at the scene is not greatly different from coercive investigation of traditional tangible objects, there is no additional restraint imposed on warrant-execution practice by expanding participation rights. The part where additional burden arises is in the imaging procedure and the procedure in which relevant information is separately searched and printed externally. However, because this part of the procedure is separately performed after the law-enforcement agency has securely secured the digital storage medium and the electronic information therein based on on-site presence and secrecy, etc., it is difficult to say that the expansion of participation rights creates additional obstacles to the on-site nature, speed, timeliness, and secrecy of the investigative procedure or burdens it to the degree that it would regress the criminal justice ideal of discovering substantive truth. Rather, the majority concurring opinion, by invoking the efficiency of investigative procedure and discovery of substantive truth, is causing the principle of warrant requirement and due process, which are demanded for the protection of the fundamental rights of individuals and businesses in a highly developed information society, to regress.

e. Participation-right issues arising from concealment of digital storage media etc.

When the law-enforcement agency investigating the principal offender’s facts suspected of crime traces the whereabouts of the principal offender’s concealed digital storage medium and ultimately secures it from a third party who concealed evidence, is the principal offender not guaranteed participation rights in the search and printing process? Is it not a distortion of the fundamental purpose of the participation-right doctrine established by precedent to apply it so formally that it is sufficient to guarantee participation rights only to the third party, the evidence concealer? In such a situation, is there any device that ensures constitutional control over the execution of the warrant other than guaranteeing the principal offender’s participation rights? Is there any difference, for purposes of guaranteeing participation rights, between seizing a digital storage medium directly from the suspect and seizing it from a third party who received it from the suspect and concealed it? Are the intent to conceal evidence or the suspect status as a suspect for the crime of concealment of evidence on the part of the third party who concealed the digital storage medium an essential element in determining whether participation rights should be guaranteed to the principal offender? In all of these cases, should the principal offender, as the owner/manager of the digital storage medium, not still be regarded as having the interest in participation through exclusion of irrelevant information as the exclusive manager/disposer of the electronic information? From the perspective of participation rights, are the investigative procedure against the principal offender and the investigative procedure against the evidence concealer truly and substantively completely independent separate procedures, or is the latter substantially subsumed as part of the former? Since the principal offender and the evidence concealer each occupy the status of suspect while simultaneously and overlap-wise occupying the status of a third party with respect to the other party’s criminal suspicion, can each not become a subject to whom participation rights belong?

The structure of the principal offender and the evidence concealer contains a variety of issues for debate in determining the subject to whom participation rights belong. Focusing on these many special features, the dissenting opinion is the result of an effort to find answers to the above questions and, based on the precedents concerning the guarantee of participation rights, to determine the essence of participation rights and the core indicia of the subject to whom they belong. Based on the discussion developed by the dissenting opinion, I hope that this will provide an opportunity for active additional discussion on the scope and direction of participation-right guarantees in seizure and search procedures concerning digital storage media in an increasingly advanced information society.

For the foregoing reasons, I supplement the dissenting opinion."}

{"[2010HEONGA82]": "[Appendix] 관련 Provisions

Former Act on the Attachment, etc. of Electronic Devices for 위치추적 of Specific Criminal Offenders (as amended by Act No. 10257 on April 15, 2010, and before amendment by Act No. 11558 on December 18, 2012)

Article 1 (Purpose) The purpose of this Act is to protect the people from 특정범죄 by taking the additional measure of attaching to the body an electronic device that can track the offender’s movements and determine his or her location, for the prevention of 재범 and for their 재사회화 through the correction of their conduct.

Article 2 (Definitions) The definitions of terms used in this Act are as follows:
4. “Location-tracking electronic device (hereinafter referred to as electronic device)” means a series of mechanical equipment, as determined by Presidential Decree, that identifies location or detects a movement route by using the principle of emitting and tracking electromagnetic waves.

Article 4 (Scope of Application) When an attachment order is sentenced against a person under 19 years of age, an electronic device under this Act may not be attached until the person reaches 19 years of age.

Article 5 (Petition for an Attachment Order) ① A prosecutor may file with the court a petition for an order to attach an electronic device (hereinafter referred to as an attachment order) against a person who falls under any of the following subparagraphs and is deemed likely to commit a sexual violence offense again.
1. Where a person who has been sentenced to an actual term of imprisonment with labor for a sexual violence offense commits a sexual violence offense within 10 years after the execution thereof has been completed or exempted
2. Where a person who has previously been attached with an electronic device under this Act for a sexual violence offense again commits a sexual violence offense
3. Where a person has committed a sexual violence offense two or more times (including cases where a final and conclusive judgment of conviction has been rendered) and thus a habitual pattern is recognized
4. Where a sexual violence offense is committed against a person under 16 years of age
④ A petition for an attachment order under paragraphs 1 through 3 shall be filed by the time the appellate proceedings of a specific crime case in which an indictment has been instituted are concluded.
⑤ When the court deems it necessary to sentence an attachment order as a result of hearing a specific crime case in which an indictment has been instituted, it may require the prosecutor to file a petition for an attachment order.
⑥ No petition for an attachment order may be filed if 15 years have elapsed from the institution of an indictment without a final judgment in a specific crime case under paragraphs 1 through 3.

Article 6 (Investigation) ① When deemed necessary in order to file a petition for an attachment order, a prosecutor may request the head of the probation office (including its branch office; hereinafter the same shall apply) having jurisdiction over the residence of the suspect or the location of the prosecutor’s office to which the suspect belongs (including its branch office; hereinafter the same shall apply) to investigate matters necessary regarding the suspect, such as the motive for the crime, the relationship with the victim, mental state, and the risk of recidivism.
④ In filing a petition for an attachment order, the prosecutor shall, if necessary, refer to the results of a psychiatric evaluation of the suspect or other expert diagnosis.

Article 9 (Judgment on Attachment Order, etc.) ① When the court deems a petition for an attachment order to be well-founded, it shall sentence an attachment order by judgment, setting the attachment period within the following periods. Provided, however, that where a specific crime is committed against a person under 13 years of age, the lower limit of the attachment period shall be twice the lower limit of the attachment period under the following subparagraphs.
1. Specific crimes for which the upper limit of the statutory punishment is death or life imprisonment: not less than 10 years and not more than 30 years
2. Specific crimes for which the lower limit of the term of imprisonment among the statutory punishments is fixed-term imprisonment of not less than 3 years (excluding specific crimes falling under subparagraph 1): not less than 3 years and not more than 20 years
3. Specific crimes for which the lower limit of the term of imprisonment among the statutory punishments is fixed-term imprisonment of less than 3 years (excluding specific crimes falling under subparagraph 1 or 2): not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years
③ A person sentenced to an attachment order shall be subject to probation under the Act on Probation, etc. during the attachment period.
④ The court shall dismiss a petition for an attachment order by judgment when it falls under any of the following subparagraphs:
1. When the petition for an attachment order is deemed to be without merit
2. When a judgment or decision of acquittal (excluding cases where medical treatment and custody is sentenced on the ground of mental incapacity), extinguishment of prosecution, or dismissal of prosecution is rendered in a specific crime case
3. When a fine is imposed in a specific crime case
4. When a suspended sentence or suspension of execution is imposed in a specific crime case (excluding cases where attachment of an electronic device is ordered pursuant to Article 28(1))
⑤ A judgment in a case involving a petition for an attachment order shall be rendered simultaneously with the judgment in the specific crime case.
⑦ The pronouncement of an attachment order shall not be considered favorably in sentencing for the specific crime case.

Article 9-2 (Compliance Requirements) ① When sentencing an attachment order pursuant to Article 9(1), the court may, within the scope of the attachment period, set a compliance period and impose one or more of the following compliance requirements. Provided, however, that the compliance requirement under subparagraph 4 shall have its period set within the scope of 500 hours.
1. Restriction on going out during nighttime or at specific times
2. Prohibition of entry into specific areas or places
2-2. Restriction on residential areas
3. Prohibition of approach to specific persons, such as victims
4. Completion of a specific crime treatment program
5. Other matters necessary for the prevention of recidivism and the correction of conduct of a person sentenced to an attachment order

Article 14-2 (Extension, etc. of Attachment Period) ① If a person subject to attachment falls under any of the following subparagraphs, the court may, upon a petition by a prosecutor filed at the request of the head of the probation office, extend the attachment period within the limit of 1 year or make a decision to add or modify the compliance requirements under Article 9-2(1).
1. Where a compliance requirement under Article 32 of the Act on Probation, etc. has been violated without justifiable grounds
2. Where the report has not been made in violation of Article 14(2) without justifiable grounds
3. Where, in violation of Article 14(3), the person moved residence, traveled within the country, or departed from the country without permission, or obtained permission by false means, without justifiable grounds
② Even where there is a change in circumstances other than those prescribed in the subparagraphs of paragraph 1, the court may, if it deems there to be reasonable grounds, make a decision to add, modify, or delete the compliance requirements under Article 9-2(1) upon a petition by a prosecutor filed at the request of the head of the probation office.

Article 16 (Preservation, Use, Destruction, etc. of Received Data) ① The head of the probation office shall receive the electromagnetic waves emitted from the electronic device of a person subject to attachment and preserve the data therefrom (hereinafter referred to as received data).
② The received data may not be inspected, queried, or disclosed except in the following cases:
1. Where used as investigation or trial materials concerning a suspicion of a specific crime committed by the person subject to attachment
2. Where used by a probation officer for the purpose of guidance and assistance
3. Where used for the review of the provisional suspension of an attachment order and its revocation by the Probation Review Committee under Article 5 of the Act on Probation, etc. (hereinafter referred to as the Review Committee)
④ When a prosecutor or judicial police officer inspects or queries the received data, they shall present a warrant of seizure and search issued by a judge.
⑤ The head of the probation office shall destroy the received data when it falls under any of the following subparagraphs:
1. Where the sentence imposed together with the attachment order becomes extinguished under Article 81 of the Criminal Act
2. Where the sentence imposed together with the attachment order loses its effect due to pardon
3. Where five years have elapsed since the person whose attachment of the electronic device has ended has completed the attachment of the electronic device without having been subjected to a sentence of suspension of qualifications or to attachment of an electronic device under this Act
⑥ Necessary matters concerning the preservation, use, destruction, etc. of received data shall be prescribed by Presidential Decree.

Article 17 (Application for Provisional Suspension of Attachment Order, etc.) ① The head of the probation office, the person subject to attachment, and his or her legal representative may apply to the Review Committee having jurisdiction over the relevant probation office for provisional suspension of the attachment order.
② The application under paragraph 1 shall be made after 3 months have elapsed from the date on which execution of the attachment order commenced. If the application is dismissed, a new application may be made after 3 months have elapsed from the date of dismissal.

Article 19 (Revocation of Provisional Suspension, etc.) ① The head of the probation office may apply to the Review Committee for revocation of provisional suspension when a person whose attachment order has been provisionally suspended is deemed to pose a risk of recidivism, such as by committing a specific crime or failing to comply with reports on residence changes. In such case, when the Review Committee deems that the risk of recidivism of the person whose provisional suspension has been granted is significant, it shall revoke the provisional suspension.
② A person whose provisional suspension is revoked pursuant to paragraph 1 shall attach the electronic device during the remaining attachment period. In such case, the period of provisional suspension shall not be included in the attachment period.

Article 36 (Penalties) ① Where a person in charge of electronic device attachment duties, without justifiable grounds, releases or damages the electronic device of a person subject to attachment, he or she shall be punished by fixed-term imprisonment with labor for not less than 1 year.
② Where a person in charge of electronic device attachment duties receives, demands, or promises money, valuables, or other benefits and commits the offense under paragraph 1, he or she shall be punished by fixed-term imprisonment with labor for not less than 2 years.
③ Where a person who manages received data violates Article 16(2), he or she shall be punished by fixed-term imprisonment with labor for not less than 1 year.

Article 38 (Penalties) Where a person subject to attachment violates Article 14 (including cases where it applies mutatis mutandis pursuant to Articles 27 and 31) and, during the attachment period of the electronic device, arbitrarily detaches or damages the electronic device from the body, interferes with radio waves, tampers with the received data, or otherwise impairs its utility, he or she shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 7 years or by a fine not exceeding 20 million won.

Article 39 (Penalties) ① Where a person subject to attachment violates the compliance requirement under Article 9-2(1) subparagraph 3 or 4 without justifiable grounds, he or she shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 3 years or by a fine not exceeding 10 million won.
② Where a person subject to attachment violates the compliance requirement under Article 9-2(1) subparagraph 1, subparagraph 2, subparagraph 2-2, or subparagraph 5 without justifiable grounds, he or she shall be punished by a fine not exceeding 10 million won.

Supplementary Provisions to the Act on the Attachment, etc. of Electronic Devices for Location Tracking of Specific Criminal Offenders (Act No. 9112 of June 13, 2008, as amended by Act No. 10257 of April 15, 2010)
① Omitted
② The procedures for an attachment order against a person scheduled for release under paragraph 1 shall be as follows:
1. The head of a prison, detention house, treatment and custody facility, or protective custody facility (hereinafter referred to as custodial facility) shall notify the prosecutor of the local district public prosecutors’ office having jurisdiction over the location of the custodial facility and the head of the probation office of the personal details, correctional performance, and other necessary matters no later than 6 months before the execution of the term of imprisonment, etc. for the person scheduled for release is completed.
2. The prosecutor may request the head of the probation office having jurisdiction over the location of the prosecutor’s office to which he or she belongs or over the residence of the person scheduled for release to conduct an investigation under Article 6 concerning the person scheduled for release under paragraph 1.

4. The prosecutor shall file a petition for an attachment order with the court no later than 3 months before the execution of the term of imprisonment, etc. for the person scheduled for release is completed, with respect to a person among those scheduled for release who meets the requirements for petitioning an attachment order under paragraph 1.
5. When the court deems a petition for an attachment order under subparagraph 4 to be well-founded, it shall issue an attachment order by decision no later than 1 month before the execution of the term of imprisonment, etc. for the person scheduled for release is completed.
6. An appeal against a decision under subparagraph 5 shall not have the effect of suspending execution of the attachment order.
③ The procedures for an attachment order against a person nearing release and a released person under paragraph 1 shall be as follows:
1. The head of a custodial facility shall notify the prosecutor of the local district public prosecutors’ office having jurisdiction over the location of the custodial facility and the head of the probation office of the personal details, correctional performance, and other necessary matters for persons nearing release and released persons within 1 month from the date this Act enters into force.
2. The prosecutor may request the head of the probation office having jurisdiction over the location of the prosecutor’s office to which he or she belongs or over the residence of persons nearing release and released persons to conduct an investigation under Article 6 concerning persons nearing release and released persons.
3. The head of the probation office shall submit the investigation report under Article 6(3) concerning persons nearing release and released persons within 2 months from the date of receipt of the request.
4. The prosecutor shall file a petition for an attachment order with the court within 1 year from the date this Act enters into force with respect to a person among those nearing release or released persons who meets the requirements for petitioning an attachment order under paragraph 1. Provided, however, that if a person nearing release or a released person flees, the period shall be 3 years.
5. When necessary for the investigation under subparagraph 2 or the petition under subparagraph 4, the prosecutor or the head of the probation office may require the released person to appear and hear his or her statement.
6. When a released person fails, without justifiable grounds, to comply with a request to appear under subparagraph 5, or is likely not to comply, the prosecutor may petition the judge of the competent district court to issue a warrant for apprehension and apprehend the released person, and the head of the probation office may apply to the prosecutor of the competent local public prosecutors’ office, obtain a warrant for apprehension issued by the judge of the competent district court upon the prosecutor’s petition, and apprehend the released person.
7. When the prosecutor or the head of the probation office apprehends a released person pursuant to subparagraph 6, he or she shall complete the necessary investigation within 48 hours from the time of apprehension, and shall immediately release the released person when the investigation is completed.
8. When the court deems a petition for an attachment order under subparagraph 4 to be well-founded, it shall issue an attachment order by decision within 2 months from the date of the petition.
9. The head of the probation office may summon the released person for the execution of the decision under subparagraph 8.
10. If the released person fails to comply with the summons under subparagraph 9, the head of the probation office may apply to the prosecutor, obtain a writ of execution of the attachment order, and apprehend the released person.
11. An appeal against a decision under subparagraph 8 shall not have the effect of suspending execution of the attachment order.
