{"[2015HEONMA1204]": "1. 사건개요
A. Suspect 윤○현 was arrested pursuant to an arrest warrant at around 19:00 on 2015. 10. 5., and a detention warrant was sought. The Claimant, an attorney, was entrusted by the family of the above suspect and, after inquiring by telephone at around 17:00 on 2015. 10. 6. to the Respondent prosecutor of the XX District Prosecutors’ Office who was investigating the case (hereinafter referred to as the “Respondent Prosecutor”) whether a counsel visitation was possible, visited prosecutor’s office room No. XX at the XX District Prosecutors’ Office at around 19:00 on the same day, carrying a visitation application, and applied to the Respondent Prosecutor for a counsel visitation.
B. The Respondent correctional officer of the XX Detention Center who was in charge of escorting the above suspect (hereinafter referred to as the “Respondent Correctional Officer”) received custody of the above suspect from the Respondent Prosecutor’s office at around 17:00 on the same day and kept him waiting in the detention room within the Prosecutors’ Office, and then, at around 19:10 on the same day, upon receiving a request from the Respondent Prosecutor to summon the suspect for night questioning, brought the above suspect into the prosecutor’s office.
C. The Respondent Prosecutor informed the Respondent Correctional Officer that the Claimant had made an application for visitation, and the Respondent Correctional Officer, after inquiring with the official in charge of counsel visitation at the XX Detention Center regarding the procedures for handling it, informed the Claimant that, pursuant to Article 58(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and Treatment of Prisoners, counsel visitation could not be permitted because the working hours under the Regulations on the Service of National Public Officials (“09:00 to 18:00”) had elapsed.
D. Thereafter, the Respondent Prosecutor took no further action regarding the Claimant’s application for visitation, and the Claimant remained in the prosecutor’s office but ultimately left without having visited the above suspect. After the Claimant left, the Respondent Prosecutor continued questioning the above suspect, and the Claimant was not retained as counsel for the above suspect.
E. The Claimant filed the present constitutional complaint on 2015. 12. 28., alleging that the acts of the Respondents in denying the application for counsel visitation, and Article 58(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and Treatment of Prisoners, which the Respondent Correctional Officer relied upon as the legal basis therefor, infringed his fundamental rights.

2. Subject Matter of Adjudication
The subject matter of this case is whether ① the acts of the Respondents in failing to take measures to permit visitation between the Claimant and suspect 윤○현 at prosecutor’s office room No. XX of the XX District Prosecutors’ Office at around 19:00 on 2015. 10. 6. and ② Article 58(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and Treatment of Prisoners, the “Visitation Hours Provision in this case,” infringe the Claimant’s fundamental rights. Here, the “Act on the Execution of Sentences and Treatment of Prisoners” shall be referred to as the “Execution of Sentences Act.”

[Provision Subject to Adjudication]
Enforcement Decree of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and Treatment of Prisoners
Article 58 (Visitation) (1) Visitation by a prisoner shall take place every day, excluding public holidays and days designated by the Minister of Justice, within working hours pursuant to Article 9 of the Regulations on the Service of National Public Officials.

[Related Provisions]
Criminal Procedure Act
Article 34 (Visitation, Communication, and Medical Treatment with Defendant or Suspect) A defense counsel or a person who intends to become defense counsel may visit a defendant or suspect who is under physical restraint and may exchange documents or articles with him or her, and may have a physician provide treatment.
Article 243-2 (Participation of Defense Counsel, etc.) (1) A prosecutor or judicial police officer shall, upon application by a suspect or his or her defense counsel, legal representative, spouse, lineal relative, brother, or sister, allow defense counsel to visit the suspect or allow defense counsel to participate in the interrogation of the suspect unless there is a justifiable ground.

Act on the Execution of Sentences and Treatment of Prisoners
Article 3 (Scope of Application) This Act applies to the premises of correctional institutions and to other places where correctional officers are guarding prisoners and where the control of correctional officers is required.

Regulations on the Service of National Public Officials
Article 9 (Working Hours, etc.) (1) The weekly working hours of public officials shall be 40 hours excluding lunch time, and Saturdays shall, in principle, be days off.
(2) The daily working hours of public officials shall be from 9:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., and lunch time shall be from 12:00 noon to 1:00 p.m.

3. The Claimant’s Arguments
A. The Claimant was unable to visit suspect 윤○현 due to the Respondents’ denial of visitation in this case, and as a result, lost the opportunity to assist the above suspect, and direct disadvantage was caused to the exercise of the above suspect’s right of defense. Accordingly, the denial of visitation in this case infringed not only the above suspect’s right of access and communication with counsel, but also the Claimant’s constitutional fundamental right of access and communication with counsel.
B. Since a detention warrant is sought within 48 hours after a suspect is arrested, the right of a suspect to immediately receive assistance from counsel must be guaranteed during that period as well. Considering that the period immediately before the warrant review hearing is the time when counsel assistance is most needed, the Visitation Hours Provision in this case, which limits counsel visitation hours to public officials’ working hours, violates the principle of prohibition against excessive restriction and infringes the Claimant’s right of access and communication with counsel.
Moreover, where an arrested suspect is housed in a police detention cell, counsel visitation is permitted even outside the working hours under the relevant rules, so because an unreasonable discrimination arises depending on whether the suspect is confined in a detention center or housed in a detention cell, the Visitation Hours Provision in this case infringes the Claimant’s right to equality.

4. The Visitation and Communication System between Suspects/Defendants and Defense Counsel
A. Constitutional Basis
The main text of Article 12(4) of the Constitution provides that any person who is arrested or detained shall have the right to prompt assistance of counsel. Even in the case of a suspect who is not detained, the right to the assistance of counsel is recognized under the constitutional principles of a rule-of-law state and due process. In this manner, a suspect or defendant, that is, 피의자 등, is recognized as having the right to the assistance of counsel regardless of whether he or she is arrested or detained.
In order for a suspect, etc. to sufficiently exercise the right of defense, he or she must be able to consult sufficiently on all factual and legal issues through visitation and communication with defense counsel or a person who intends to become defense counsel, hereinafter defense counsel, etc. The Criminal Procedure Act and the Execution of Sentences Act concretize that constitutional right, and Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act expressly provides that a person who intends to become defense counsel also has the right to visit and communicate with a suspect, etc.

B. Meaning of “Under Physical Restraint” and “Person Who Intends to Become Defense Counsel”
(1) Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act covers not only a suspect detained under a detention warrant but also a suspect arrested under an arrest warrant or by emergency arrest or as a person caught in flagrante delicto, and it presupposes any form of deprivation of physical liberty.
(2) The phrase “person who intends to become defense counsel” includes not only a person who has been requested to be appointed as defense counsel but has not yet filed a notice of appointment, but also a person who seeks to act as defense counsel on his or her own. If such visitation and communication were allowed only when the suspect expressly indicates an intention to receive counsel assistance, the existence of the right could be practically determined by investigative authorities, which would be problematic. The Supreme Court has also held in 2013DO16162 decided on 2017. 3. 9. that even where a person objectively has a possibility of becoming defense counsel, he or she may not be restricted from visiting a defendant or suspect under physical restraint merely because he or she is not yet formally defense counsel.

C. Subject Authorized to Determine Whether to Permit Visitation
The Execution of Sentences Act aims to promote correction and rehabilitation of convicted prisoners and their sound return to society, and matters concerning treatment of prisoners are vested in the authority of prison or detention center heads. Where a prisoner applies for visitation, if the place is one where correctional officers are guarding and controlling the prisoner, the prison or detention center warden, or the delegated correctional officer, in principle decides whether to permit it.
However, Article 243-2(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides a special rule for visitation requests made during interrogation of a suspect, requiring the prosecutor or judicial police officer to decide whether to permit defense counsel visitation. Since Article 34 does not distinguish between defense counsel and a person who intends to become defense counsel, the same rule should apply to such a person as well.

5. Determination on Whether the Requirements for Adjudication Are Satisfied
A. Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case
(1) Existence of the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case
A constitutional complaint presupposes an exercise or non-exercise of public power that caused infringement of fundamental rights. Here, the Respondent Prosecutor merely informed the correctional officer that the Claimant had applied for visitation, and after the correctional officer denied visitation, the Respondent Prosecutor did not take any further measure, such as allowing visitation in the prosecutor’s office or in a separately prepared counsel visitation room. Such inaction is substantially equivalent to denying the Claimant’s application for visitation, so the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case exists as an exercise of public power subject to constitutional complaint.
(2) Whether the possibility of infringement of fundamental rights is recognized
Because the Claimant was not appointed as defense counsel for suspect 윤○현, only whether the right of visitation and communication of a person who intends to become defense counsel was infringed is at issue. A constitutional complaint is lawful only if the allegedly infringed right is not merely a statutory right but also a constitutional fundamental right.
The Constitutional Court in 2000HEONMA474 and 2016HEONMA503 recognized the core part of the right to assistance of counsel as a constitutional fundamental right, reasoning that the right of a suspect or defendant to receive assistance from counsel is concretely realized through the mutual relationship with defense counsel and that if defense counsel’s core assisting function is not protected, the right becomes hollow.
1) Under Article 27(4) of the Constitution, the principle of presumption of innocence is declared. Detention may be used only when especially unavoidable, but it is susceptible to abuse. Therefore, Article 12(4) of the Constitution guarantees the right of a person under physical restraint to receive the assistance of counsel as a fundamental right. The same reason applies to arrested suspects as well.
2) Article 12(4) clearly states that a person has the right to prompt assistance of counsel upon arrest or detention, showing that the right exists even before counsel is appointed. The right of a suspect who has not yet appointed counsel to receive assistance is concretized through the appointment of counsel, and the right to appoint counsel is the starting point and most basic component of that right. Accordingly, the visitation and communication right with a person who intends to become defense counsel for purposes of appointment must also be protected as a constitutional fundamental right.
3) In order to appoint counsel, trust must be formed between the suspect and the person who intends to become defense counsel, and sufficient consultation through visitation and communication is required. If this right is not guaranteed, the suspect’s ability to obtain sufficient assistance through appointment of counsel becomes meaningless. Thus, the right of visitation and communication of a person who intends to become defense counsel is a core part of the suspect’s assistance right and stands in a mutual complementary relationship with it.
4) Therefore, the right of visitation and communication of a person who intends to become defense counsel must also be guaranteed as a constitutional fundamental right in order to practically secure the suspect’s right to receive assistance. The present petition also satisfies the possibility of infringement of fundamental rights.
(3) Whether an exception to the principle of subsidiarity is recognized
A constitutional complaint must generally be filed only after exhausting other legal remedies. However, where the claimant failed to use a prior remedy because of a justifiable mistake, or where it is objectively uncertain whether the prior procedure is available or likely to provide relief, an exception to subsidiarity is recognized.
Here, the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case is subject to quasi-appeal under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act as a disposition concerning detention or a disposition concerning a defense counsel’s participation, etc. Nevertheless, the Claimant filed this constitutional complaint without first filing a quasi-appeal.
The Supreme Court has held that a quasi-appeal requires a legal interest, and where such interest has been lost due to the lapse of time or other circumstances, the petition becomes unlawful for lack of interest. But specific criteria are not clearly provided. Since the denial in this case ended on the day of the incident, it is objectively uncertain whether a court would dismiss a quasi-appeal for lack of legal interest or proceed to the merits. Therefore it is difficult to expect the Claimant to have exhausted the prior remedy procedure.
Accordingly, this part of the petition should be recognized as lawful as an exception to subsidiarity.
(4) Sub-conclusion
The petition concerning the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case targets an exercise of public power, the possibility of infringement of fundamental rights is recognized, and the exception to subsidiarity is also recognized. Therefore, it is lawful.

B. The Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation in this case
Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act limits the subject matter of constitutional complaint to acts of public power. According to the record, at the time of the Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation, the Respondent Prosecutor had handed over physical custody of suspect 윤○현 to the Respondent Correctional Officer so that he could have dinner and rest, but a night interrogation was still scheduled, so the interrogation was ongoing. The Claimant also applied to the Respondent Prosecutor for counsel visitation.
As seen above, during interrogation of a suspect, the prosecutor or judicial police officer must decide whether to permit defense counsel visitation. Therefore, the correctional officer who escorted the suspect to the investigative agency does not have authority to permit or restrict such visitation. The Operational Guidelines on the Management of Prisoners in force at the time dealt with cases where the warden or delegated officer decides whether to permit visitation, and thus cannot be applied to this case.
Ultimately, because the Respondent Correctional Officer had no authority to decide whether to permit visitation between the Claimant and suspect 윤○현, the Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation in this case does not constitute an exercise of public power subject to constitutional complaint.

C. The Visitation Hours Provision in this case
The Constitutional Court Act allows constitutional complaint only when the complainant’s own fundamental rights have been directly and presently infringed by public power. If the challenged public power has no effect on the legal status of the complainant, there is no possibility of infringement in the first place, and the complaint is not permitted.
The Visitation Hours Provision in this case applies to visitation requests where the warden of a prison or detention center decides whether to permit them, but it does not apply to visitation requests made during interrogation of a suspect, where the prosecutor or judicial police officer decides whether to permit them. In practice, the police and prosecutors impose no time restrictions on such visitation requests. Since the Claimant’s visitation request was made to the Respondent Prosecutor while interrogation was ongoing, this provision does not apply, and the Respondent Prosecutor did not deny the request on that basis. Accordingly, this part of the petition lacks self-relatedness.

6. Determination on Whether the Prosecutor’s Denial of Visitation in this Case Infringed Fundamental Rights
A. Whether the Claimant’s right of access and communication was restricted
The Claimant applied to the Respondent Prosecutor for visitation and remained in the prosecutor’s office, but due to the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case he ultimately could not visit suspect 윤○현 and left. Thus, it is reasonable to view that denial as restricting the Claimant’s right of access and communication with the above suspect.
Although the suspect later met another attorney twice and that attorney appeared at the pre-detention interrogation hearing, those facts do not control this case. Even if the suspect did not expressly indicate an intention to visit and communicate with a person who intends to become defense counsel, visitation must be permitted where such person is objectively recognized as a possible defense counsel. Moreover, the Claimant had been entrusted by the suspect’s family and intended to visit the suspect, so at the time of the request there was sufficient possibility that the Claimant would become defense counsel. The person claiming infringement here is the Claimant, not the suspect. Therefore those later facts are not determinative.

B. Whether the Claimant’s visitation application was exercised within the scope of the right of access and communication
The right of access and communication of defense counsel, etc. must be exercised within the limits that do not infringe the original purpose of physical restraint. Attempts to visit a suspect beyond what can realistically be guaranteed in the concrete temporal and spatial circumstances are not proper exercises of that right.
Here, because the suspect was scheduled to continue night interrogation that same day, it appears that visitation and communication could have been permitted in the prosecutor’s office or in a separately prepared counsel visitation room before the interrogation. In light of the concrete temporal and spatial circumstances, there are no specific circumstances showing that the Claimant attempted to abuse the right beyond the realistic limits or beyond the original purpose of the physical restraint system.
Accordingly, the Claimant’s visitation request must be deemed to have been exercised within the scope of the right guaranteed to a person who intends to become defense counsel.

C. Whether it was based on the Constitution or statutes
(1) When actual visitation occurs between a person under arrest or detention and defense counsel, free visitation, meaning a visitation in which confidentiality is fully guaranteed and the parties may converse freely without restriction or interference, is not subject to restriction on any pretext. But that does not mean that visitation itself can never be limited at all. The right to assistance of counsel and the associated visitation and communication right may be restricted by law when necessary for national security, order, or public welfare, and the same applies to a person who intends to become defense counsel.
(2) The Respondent Prosecutor temporarily handed the suspect over to the correctional officer so that he could have dinner and rest, but because a night interrogation was planned, the investigation was still continuing. Although the right may be restricted by law, neither the Constitution nor the Criminal Procedure Act contains a provision allowing restriction or refusal where there is a visitation request by defense counsel, etc. during interrogation of a suspect. This is to ensure that the suspect’s own visitation right is protected to the maximum extent.
The Visitation Hours Provision in this case limits visitation to working hours under the Regulations on the Service of National Public Officials, but it applies only where the warden decides whether to permit visitation, and not where the prosecutor or judicial police officer decides during interrogation. Thus the request cannot be denied or restricted on that basis.
Accordingly, the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case was made without the basis of the Constitution or statutes.
D. Sub-conclusion
Ultimately, the Claimant’s visitation request concerning suspect 윤○현 was within the scope of the right of access and communication guaranteed to a person who intends to become defense counsel, and the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case was without constitutional or statutory basis. Therefore, it infringed the Claimant’s right of access and communication.

7. Conclusion
Accordingly, the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case should be found unconstitutional and revoked, but since the denial has already ended, a declaratory finding of unconstitutionality is made to prevent repetition of the same or similar infringement. The petition regarding the Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation in this case and the Visitation Hours Provision in this case is unlawful in its entirety and shall be dismissed. The concurrence of the remaining participating Justices was reached, except for the dissenting opinion by Justices Cho Yong-ho, Lee Eun-ae, and Lee Jong-seok regarding the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case as stated below.

8. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Cho Yong-ho, Lee Eun-ae, and Lee Jong-seok on the Prosecutor’s Denial of Visitation in this Case
We are of the view that the constitutional complaint concerning the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case is also unlawful and should be dismissed.

A. Possibility of Infringement of Fundamental Rights
(1) A constitutional complaint under Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act may be filed only by a person whose fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution have been infringed by public power. Therefore, a complaint alleging infringement of a right based merely on statute is unlawful.
(2) In Constitutional Court 2012HEONMA610 decided on 2015. 7. 30., three Justices stated in a separate opinion that the right to assistance of counsel means sufficiently and substantively guaranteeing the activities of defense counsel for the arrested person, and that special rights such as visitation and communication, records inspection and copy, and participation in procedures are all statutory means for protecting that right. The reason such rights are granted to defense counsel is to faithfully guarantee the arrested person’s right to assistance of counsel, not to protect defense counsel’s own fundamental rights. From that perspective, the right of a person who intends to become defense counsel is merely a statutory right concretely formed by individual statutes as an indirect and incidental effect of recognizing the arrested person’s right to assistance of counsel as a fundamental right.
Accordingly, it cannot be viewed as an independent fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution.
(3) The majority opinion relies on Constitutional Court 2000HEONMA474 and 2016HEONMA503, but even if the core part of defense counsel’s right to assist a suspect must be protected as a constitutional fundamental right, there is no need to elevate the visitation and communication right of a person who intends to become defense counsel to the level of a constitutional fundamental right. The main purpose of such visitation may be the person’s own retention activities, and the disadvantage suffered when visitation is denied is only indirect, factual, and economic. Even if the meaning of person who intends to become defense counsel includes a person who has not yet filed a notice of appointment but seeks to act as counsel on his or her own, the right of visitation and communication of such a person is a right recognized before the stage of assistance and regardless of the suspect’s will. Therefore, it cannot be said to stand in a mutual complementary relationship with the suspect’s right to assistance.
(4) Ultimately, the right of visitation and communication of a person who intends to become defense counsel cannot be regarded as a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution, so the Claimant’s petition lacks the possibility of infringement of fundamental rights.

B. Subsidiarity
(1) Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act allows a quasi-appeal against a prosecutor’s or judicial police officer’s disposition concerning detention, seizure, return of seized articles, or defense counsel participation. An investigative agency’s denial of visitation between a suspect and defense counsel, etc. falls under such a disposition, and a person who intends to become defense counsel may also challenge it through quasi-appeal. The Constitutional Court has held that where such a remedy exists, filing a constitutional complaint without using it is unlawful for failure to exhaust other legal remedies.
(2) The Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case is also a disposition subject to quasi-appeal. Nevertheless, the Claimant filed the present constitutional complaint without seeking revocation or alteration through the quasi-appeal procedure.
The majority opinion said that because the denial ended on the day of the incident, it is objectively uncertain whether a quasi-appeal would be heard on the merits, so exhaustion of the prior remedy cannot be expected. However, after the denial, the Claimant could not visit the suspect or participate in the interrogation and was not retained as defense counsel, and a detention warrant was issued and the suspect was prosecuted while in custody. There is no circumstance suggesting that a court would find legal interest lacking if a quasi-appeal were filed. The Supreme Court has decided on the merits even where defense counsel participation was denied during interrogation and the interrogation had ended, and the same should apply here.
Accordingly, even if the denial has ended, the Claimant can challenge it by quasi-appeal under Article 417, so the constitutional complaint fails the subsidiarity requirement.

C. Conclusion
The right of visitation and communication of a person who intends to become defense counsel cannot be said to be a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution, and the Claimant did not go through the quasi-appeal procedure under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act. Therefore, the constitutional complaint concerning the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case is unlawful and must be dismissed."}

A. 2020HEONGA1

2. Subject Matter of Review

The subject matter of this case is whether Article 63(1) of the Immigration Control Act as amended by Act No. 12421 on 2014. 3. 18. violates the Constitution. The provision subject to review and the relevant provisions are as follows.

[Provision Subject to Review]

Immigration Control Act as amended by Act No. 12421 on 2014. 3. 18.

Article 63 (보호 and Release from 보호 of a Person Subject to a Deportation Order) (1) The head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may detain in a detention facility a person subject to a deportation order until such person can be repatriated when immediate repatriation outside the Republic of Korea is impossible for reasons such as the absence of a passport or lack of transportation.

[Relevant Provisions]

Immigration Control Act as amended by Act No. 10282 on 2010. 5. 14.

11. The term 보호 means enforcement activity by which an immigration control official takes and confines a person who has reasonable grounds to be suspected of falling under a person subject to deportation under any item of Article 46(1) in an alien detention room, alien detention center, or any other place designated by the Minister of Justice, for the purpose of deporting such person.

Immigration Control Act as amended by Act No. 12421 on 2014. 3. 18.

3. A person whose ground for denial of entry, falling under any item of Article 11(1), is discovered or arises after entry

8. A person who has violated Article 17(1) or (2), Article 18, Article 20, Article 23, Article 24, or Article 25

Article 63 (보호 and Release from 보호 of a Person Subject to a Deportation Order) (2) Where the period of 보호 under paragraph (1) exceeds 3 months, the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office shall obtain prior approval from the Minister of Justice every 3 months.
