(2) Where the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office revokes the temporary release from 보호 pursuant to paragraph (1), he or she may issue a revocation document of temporary release from 보호 and forfeit all or part of the security deposit to the National Treasury.

Immigration Control Act as amended by Act No. 15492 on 2018. 3. 20.

Article 65 (Temporary Release from 보호) (1) The head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may, ex officio or upon request of the detainee, including his or her surety or legal representative, etc., temporarily release the detainee from 보호 by requiring the deposit of a security deposit not exceeding 20 million won and attaching restrictions on residence or other necessary conditions, after considering the detainee’s circumstances, reasons for request for release, assets, and other matters.

3. Grounds for the Referring Court’s Request for Constitutional Review

A. The provision subject to review does not set an upper limit on the detention period, thereby rendering the detainee unable to predict at all when he or she will be released, which itself causes serious mental pressure. Permitting detention without a time limit merely for the administrative purpose of facilitating execution of a deportation order emphasizes only administrative convenience and uniformity, and thus violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and infringes the detainee’s freedom of the person.

B. Detention under the Immigration Control Act restricts freedom of the person as it is equivalent to arrest or detention in criminal procedure. Therefore, it should be subject to strict warrant principle; yet the provision subject to review allows the physical restraint of an alien subject to a deportation order without a court warrant, and thus violates the warrant principle.

C. In light of the fact that no third independent and neutral institution or judicial body is involved at all in the stage of commencement or extension of 보호; that the detainee may file an objection against the detention order with the Minister of Justice, and detention may be extended only with the Minister of Justice’s approval, but the Minister of Justice is merely the supervisory authority over the administrative agency that issues and executes detention orders, so it cannot be said that ex post remedies or control procedures by an external neutral and objective institution are secured; and that there is no provision in the Immigration Control Act requiring that the person concerned be given an opportunity to present opinions before issuance of a detention order under the provision subject to review, the provision subject to review violates the principle of due process.

4. Judgment

A. Alien detention system under the Immigration Control Act

(1) Detention under the Immigration Control Act means enforcement activity by which an immigration control official takes and confines a person who has reasonable grounds to be suspected of falling under a person subject to deportation under Article 46(1) of the Immigration Control Act in an alien detention room, alien detention center, or any other place designated by the Minister of Justice, for the purpose of deporting such person. Detention under the Immigration Control Act includes detention for the determination of a person subject to deportation prescribed in Article 51 and detention for the execution of a deportation order prescribed in the provision subject to review.

(2) According to the provision subject to review, the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may detain an alien subject to a deportation order, hereinafter referred to as a person subject to deportation, in an alien detention room, alien detention center, or any other place designated by the Minister of Justice, hereinafter referred to as a detention facility, until such person can be repatriated when immediate repatriation outside the Republic of Korea is impossible for reasons such as the absence of a passport or lack of transportation. Detention under the provision subject to review is intended to secure the execution of a deportation order where a deportation order has been issued upon determining that an alien falls under a person subject to deportation, but immediate execution is impossible, and is distinguished from detention under Article 51 of the Immigration Control Act, which secures the physical presence of an alien in order to examine whether the alien falls under a person subject to deportation.

The provision subject to review states that detention is permissible until such person can be repatriated, and thus, in the wording of the statute, imposes no limitation on the detention period; instead, where the period of detention exceeds 3 months, prior approval from the Minister of Justice must be obtained every 3 months, and if such approval is not obtained, detention must be released. In addition, a person detained in a detention facility pursuant to the provision subject to review may file an objection with the Minister of Justice, and the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may, ex officio or upon request of the detainee, temporarily release the detainee from detention by requiring the deposit of a security deposit not exceeding 20 million won and attaching restrictions on residence or other necessary conditions, after considering the detainee’s circumstances, reasons for request for release, assets, and other matters.

B. Issues and Standard of Review

(1) Detention under the provision subject to review is a compulsory measure by which a person subject to deportation is taken and confined in a detention facility in order to secure execution of a deportation order when immediate execution of the deportation order is impossible, and thus restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person. Therefore, the issue in this case is whether the provision subject to review infringes freedom of the person by violating the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction, which is the limiting principle on restriction of fundamental rights, and the principle of due process under Article 12 of the Constitution.

(2) Immigration control administration is state administration that promotes the national interest and security by appropriately controlling and adjusting the entry and exit of nationals and foreigners and the stay of foreigners. Among matters relating to immigration control, matters concerning the entry and domestic stay of foreigners are necessary for performing the functions of a sovereign state and lie within the domain of broad policy discretion, and detention under the provision subject to review, which is carried out to secure execution of a deportation order, may be regarded as part of immigration control administration.

However, freedom of the person under Article 12(1) of the Constitution is the most fundamental minimum freedom necessary to realize human dignity and value, and serves as the premise for the guarantee of all fundamental rights. By its nature, it is a human right, and whether it is recognized does not vary depending on whether one has lawful status of stay in the country. Therefore, a strict standard of review must be applied to whether the provision subject to review infringes freedom of the person.

C. Constitutional Opinion of Justices Yoon Nam-seok, Lee Seok-tae, Kim Gi-yeong, Moon Hyeong-bae, and Lee Mi-seon

(1) Whether the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction is violated

(a) Legitimacy of purpose and appropriateness of means

The legislative purpose of the provision subject to review is to appropriately control and adjust the entry, exit, and stay of foreigners, thereby promoting national security and order, by taking and confining persons subject to deportation in a detention facility until they can be repatriated outside the Republic of Korea so that deportation orders may be executed easily and efficiently. Such legislative purpose is legitimate, and taking and confining persons subject to deportation in a detention facility until they can be repatriated outside the Republic of Korea is an effective means of securing execution of a deportation order; thus, appropriateness of means is also recognized.

(b) Minimum infringement and balance of interests

However, the provision subject to review fails to satisfy the minimum infringement requirement and the balance of interests requirement for the following reasons.

1) Detention under the provision subject to review is a compulsory measure temporarily and provisionally taken to secure execution when a deportation order cannot be executed immediately upon issuance. Yet the provision subject to review merely provides that a person subject to deportation may be detained until such person can be repatriated outside the Republic of Korea, and does not set an upper limit on the detention period, thereby making indefinite detention possible.

Detention by which a person subject to deportation is temporarily and provisionally confined in a specific place for the purpose of executing a deportation order can, by its very nature, be deemed justified only when the person is confined within a reasonable period necessary for the execution of the deportation order. However, according to the provision subject to review, for example, where the detainee has applied for refugee status recognition under the Refugee Act or has filed an objection to a decision of non-recognition of refugee status, etc., so that the deportation order cannot be executed until the related procedures are completed, or where the detainee has filed an action for cancellation, etc. against the deportation order or civil or criminal disputes are pending, making execution of the deportation order practically difficult, the detention period may be extended indefinitely depending on the progress of those procedures. In addition, the provision subject to review permits continued detention without any limitation on the period until repatriation becomes possible even where repatriation is impossible because entry is denied by another country. Long-term or indefinite detention of a person subject to deportation even where the deportation order cannot be executed within a considerable period exceeds the limits of a temporary and provisional compulsory measure and seriously restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person. Furthermore, detention without an upper limit on duration causes serious mental pressure in itself, regardless of the actual length of detention, because the detainee cannot predict at all when he or she will be released.

Detention under the provision subject to review has a substantive limitation in purpose, in that it may not be ordered for any purpose other than securing execution of a deportation order; and it has a temporal limitation in that it may be temporary only for the minimum period necessary until repatriation is possible and the period of detention may not be extended for other purposes. Although the average detention period until an actual person subject to deportation is repatriated is only a little over 10 days, and cases in which long-term detention exceeding one year becomes an issue are only few, such limitations naturally derive from the nature of detention as a temporary and provisional measure. Therefore, notwithstanding the above interpretive limitations, the provision subject to review, which does not set an upper limit on detention period, still leaves the problems arising from the absence of such an upper limit unresolved, in that long-term or indefinite detention is possible, and even where execution of the deportation order is impossible for reasons not attributable to the detainee, the person may still be detained for a long period until actual repatriation if immediate repatriation is impossible.

Meanwhile, there may be cases where there is no objective reason making repatriation impossible, but the detainee does not cooperate with repatriation, making it impossible to execute the deportation order promptly; however, non-cooperation with repatriation alone cannot justify indefinite detention. If execution of the deportation order is delayed due to the detainee’s refusal to cooperate, that refusal may be taken as a reason for extending the detention period; however, as the immigration authorities in charge of repatriation must faithfully carry out repatriation work by removing obstacles delaying repatriation, they cannot keep detaining the person until repatriation is realized merely because the detainee does not cooperate with repatriation.

2) Therefore, even if the appropriate upper limit on the detention period is left aside, at the very least the law must clearly specify that upper limit so as to prevent harm arising from unreasonable prolongation or uncertainty of the detention period. Permitting detention without a time limit merely for the administrative purpose of efficient execution of a deportation order emphasizes only administrative convenience and uniformity, and excessively restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person. It is difficult to regard foreigners who were not able to choose voluntary departure for various reasons or who were unable to depart voluntarily and therefore were apprehended and detained as having, in effect, a freedom to depart, so the infringement of fundamental rights due to the absence of an upper limit on detention period cannot be deemed mitigated on the ground that a person subject to deportation is free to depart at any time and thus escape from being a detainee.

Looking to international standards and foreign legislation, many countries set an upper limit on the period when detaining a person subject to a deportation order. The EU Returns Directive requires Member States to prescribe in domestic law an absolute maximum period of detention in order to curb unnecessary long-term detention and respect the basic human rights of foreigners subject to deportation; it strengthens control over prolonged detention by providing that the initial detention period may not exceed 6 months and may be extended exceptionally, but the extension period shall be at most 12 months. Accordingly, EU Member States have enacted domestic laws establishing detention requirements and procedures that are equal to or stricter than the standards set forth in the above directive and have set upper limits on detention periods. For example, France provides by law that detention may be ordered up to a maximum of 90 days only where effective custody is difficult for a foreigner whose repatriation is reasonably possible and other measures to ensure effective execution are insufficient. Germany provides by law that detention for deportation may be ordered up to 6 months, but even upon extension may not exceed a maximum of 12 months. Taiwan and South Africa also limit by statute the detention period for persons subject to deportation to a maximum of 100 days or 120 days, respectively. The reason why international standards and other legislative examples set upper limits on detention periods is that detention with no fixed duration may cause serious human rights violations.

The period required until repatriation in the actual process of executing a deportation order may vary depending on whether the person subject to deportation cooperates and on the circumstances of the Republic of Korea or the receiving country. One may argue from this point that the provision subject to review necessarily had no upper limit on the detention period; however, considering that detention under the provision subject to review is a temporary and provisional measure taken for the purpose of executing a deportation order and that many countries set upper limits on detention periods for persons subject to deportation, it cannot be said that it is impossible to set a reasonable upper limit on the detention period necessary to execute a deportation order.

3) If an upper limit is set on the detention period, and repatriation is delayed so that the period exceeds that upper limit, detention of the person subject to deportation must be released. In such a case, it may be argued that the person subject to deportation who has been released may go into hiding or be exposed to crime. However, this is merely a vague and potential possibility that has not yet materialized, or a concern that exaggerates some situations; thus, based only on such vague assumptions, it is difficult to justify measures that seriously restrict freedom of the person, such as detention without any upper limit on duration. One cannot conclude that a foreigner who committed a crime in the Republic of Korea will abscond or commit crimes again if released from detention. Moreover, among persons subject to deportation there may be not only foreigners who committed crimes and were sentenced to punishment, but also foreigners who merely violated administrative regulations concerning entry or stay. Treating all such persons as potential fugitives or potential criminals and detaining them without any time limit is an excessive measure.

There may be concern that if an upper limit is imposed on the detention period, the detainee could exceed that upper limit through a cancellation action against the deportation order or by applying for refugee status recognition, etc.; however, such cases can be minimized through institutional improvements such as having the courts give priority and focus to such cases, expediting refugee status examination and decisions, or preventing abuse of refugee status applications.

Furthermore, securing execution of a deportation order is possible through various means other than detention under the provision subject to review. For example, execution of a deportation order may be secured through means substituting for detention, such as restricting the residence of a person subject to deportation until departure requirements are met or requiring periodic reporting of residence, designating a guarantor or requiring payment of an appropriate security deposit, or continuously observing or supervising the person subject to deportation through supervisors, etc. Therefore, in order to secure execution of a deportation order, it is not inevitable to adopt a method that excessively restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person, such as detention without an upper limit on duration.

4) Meanwhile, the current procedures and operation of the Immigration Control Act are insufficient, by themselves, to properly control the detention period and thereby mitigate excessive restrictions on freedom of the person.

First, the detainee may request temporary release from detention from the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office under the Immigration Control Act, and the head may temporarily release the detainee from detention ex officio. However, unless there are circumstances such that the detainee has won a cancellation action against the deportation order, etc., whether to grant temporary release from detention is entirely within the discretion of the head, etc., and it is highly likely to be carried out for administrative convenience rather than through a substantive review of the necessity of detention. According to the result of the fact inquiry dated 2021. 7. 1. to the Minister of Justice in Case 2020HEONGA1 and the reference materials submitted by the Minister of Justice on 2022. 9. 5., while the average number of cases of temporary release from detention during the five years from 2013 to 2017 was 120 per year and the average number during the three years from 2018 to 2020 was 131 per year, temporary release from detention in 2021 surged to 461 cases. The sharp increase in requests and grants appears to have been due to difficulties in infection control within detention facilities caused by COVID-19, and administrative convenience appears to have been the main reason. Article 63(4) of the Immigration Control Act provides that the head may release a person from detention where it becomes manifest that the person subject to deportation cannot be repatriated for reasons such as denial of entry from another country, but this too is entirely within the discretion of the head. In light of these points, it is difficult to regard the temporary release from detention system as functioning as a device that can supplement the problem of having no upper limit on the detention period.

In addition, the Immigration Control Act provides for objections to detention orders and a system of prior approval by the Minister of Justice for extensions of detention periods; however, these are merely procedures conducted by the Minister of Justice, who is the supervisory authority over the administrative agency issuing and executing detention orders, and thus cannot be considered effective enough to supplement the problem of not setting an upper limit on the detention period. In particular, according to the reference materials submitted by the Minister of Justice on 2021. 7. 21. and 2022. 9. 5., the rate of disapproval of extensions was 4.9% in 2017, 6.7% in 2018, 6.4% in 2019, 4.0% in 2020, and 9.4% in 2021, with an average disapproval rate of only 6.28% over the past five years, making it impossible not to question the effectiveness of the extension approval system.

5) Taking the above circumstances together, although means exist for securing execution of a deportation order other than indefinite detention in a detention facility, the provision subject to review allows the detainee to be detained without any upper limit on duration, which exceeds the minimum necessary to achieve the legislative purpose and excessively restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person. Even if the public interest the provision subject to review seeks to achieve is important, the degree of restriction on the detainee’s freedom of the person resulting from detention without any upper limit on duration is too great; therefore, the provision subject to review fails to satisfy the requirements of minimum infringement and balance of interests.

(c) Conclusion

The provision subject to review infringes the detainee’s freedom of the person in violation of the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.

(2) Whether the principle of due process is violated

(a) Article 12(1) of the Constitution declares the principle of due process by providing that no person shall be punished, placed under preventive restrictions, or subjected to forced labor, except by virtue of law and due process. The principle of due process is not limited to criminal procedure but applies to all state action generally. Therefore, the constitutional principle of due process must also be observed in detention under the provision subject to review. The provision subject to review, however, raises the following issues from the perspective of the constitutional principle of due process.

(b) When freedom of the person is restricted by coercive measures in administrative procedure, controlling such measures by a neutral institution independent from the executing agency is an important component of the principle of due process. The concrete form and level of such control should be determined by considering all factors, such as the purpose of the coercive measure, the public interest sought to be achieved thereby, and the degree to which freedom of the person is restricted by the coercive measure. Considering that detention under the provision subject to review seeks to secure execution of a deportation order and restricts freedom of the person to the extent of deprivation, such that it can be regarded as equivalent to arrest or detention in criminal procedure, an institution independent from and neutral to the immigration control official, who is the executing agency, must be able to review and control the validity of detention at the stage of commencement or extension of detention under the principle of due process.

Under the Immigration Control Act, the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office examines and decides whether to deport and issues the deportation order and the detention order for execution of deportation, while immigration control officials execute the detention order and the deportation order. Thus, formally, the person who issues the detention order and the person who executes it are separate. However, the head who makes the detention decision is not an independent third institution, but merely a superior within the same executing agency to which the immigration control officials belong, and in substance the detention decision-making body and the executing body cannot be said to be separated. Moreover, Article 63(2) of the Immigration Control Act separates the body approving extension of detention by requiring the head to obtain prior approval from the Minister of Justice every 3 months where the detention period exceeds 3 months; however, the Minister of Justice is merely the supervisory authority over the administrative agency issuing and executing detention orders, and it cannot be said that review by an external neutral and objective institution is thereby secured.

As such, under the current Immigration Control Act, no independent neutral institution at all is involved at the stage of commencement or extension of detention, and in such a situation it cannot be guaranteed that review of the necessity of detention, etc. will be properly performed. The reality that, once a deportation order exists, a detention order is almost automatically issued, and that when an application is made by the head, the Minister of Justice’s approval for extension is granted almost without exception, attests to this point.

Meanwhile, the detainee may file an objection with the Minister of Justice against the detention order, but as noted above, the Minister of Justice is merely the supervisory authority over the administrative agency issuing and executing detention orders, so this cannot be regarded as securing a review system by an external neutral and objective institution. Even considering that there was not a single case in which an objection to a detention order was granted during the eight years from 2013 to 2020, it is difficult to see the Minister of Justice’s review as having substantive significance as a control procedure to ensure the legality of detention. In addition, although the detainee may file an administrative action against the deportation order, detention order, or a decision dismissing an objection to the detention order, and may request a stay of execution of the detention order in the course thereof, such general and ex post judicial control alone cannot be regarded as sufficiently protecting the detainee in the absence of any prior control by a fair and neutral institution at the stage of commencement or extension of detention.

(c) Since providing the parties with an opportunity to submit opinions and materials is an important procedural requirement derived from the principle of due process, such opportunity must also be guaranteed to the detainee when detention is imposed under the provision subject to review.

However, the Immigration Control Act does not contain any provision requiring that the person concerned be given an opportunity to submit opinions before a detention order is issued pursuant to the provision subject to review. The Administrative Procedures Act provides that when an administrative agency imposes obligations on a party or issues a disposition restricting rights and interests, the agency must give the party, etc. an opportunity to submit opinions, while excluding dispositions concerning the entry and departure of foreigners from the scope of the Administrative Procedures Act. Therefore, under the current law, the detainee is not being given an opportunity to make statements or submit opinions favorable to him or her in the detention order procedure.

A detention order presupposes a deportation order, and a deportation order is issued based on an investigation into a foreigner suspected of falling under a person subject to deportation, the so-called suspect. Since the investigation of a suspect requires that his or her statements be recorded in a written statement and, where there is a request for addition or correction to the contents, such request must also be recorded in the statement, the suspect may be regarded as being given an opportunity to state his or her opinions in the deportation order procedure. However, the detainee must be able to state opinions regarding the necessity of detention or the risk of flight in the detention order procedure, and the opportunity to state opinions in the deportation order procedure cannot exclude the opportunity to state opinions in the separate and independent detention order procedure. Meanwhile, at the stage of objection to a detention order, the Minister of Justice is merely authorized at his or her discretion to hear statements of the parties concerned if necessary, and prior approval by the Minister of Justice for extension of detention merely provides that the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office must demonstrate the necessity of extending the detention period; thus, no procedural opportunity exists under the law for the detainee to submit opinions or materials to the Minister of Justice.

(d) Taken together, the provision subject to review violates the constitutional principle of due process because there is no control procedure by a fair and neutral institution at the stage of commencement or extension of detention and because the person concerned is not guaranteed an opportunity to submit opinions.

(3) Necessity of a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution and temporary application

As examined above, the provision subject to review violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and the principle of due process and thereby infringes the detainee’s freedom of the person; therefore, as a matter of principle, a simple declaration of unconstitutionality would be appropriate for the provision subject to review.

However, the unconstitutionality of the provision subject to review lies in the fact that it does not set an upper limit on the detention period, thereby allowing long-term or indefinite detention, and in the fact that no control by a fair and neutral institution is exercised at the stage of commencement or extension of detention and no opportunity to submit opinions is afforded to the person concerned. In such a situation, if a simple declaration of unconstitutionality were rendered with respect to the provision subject to review, the legal basis for detention for execution of a deportation order would disappear, making it impossible to secure the physical presence of persons subject to deportation and thereby creating an intolerable legal vacuum. Moreover, the legislature has legislative discretion over the formation of procedures, such as how to set an upper limit on the detention period, how to structure a body to review the validity of physical restraint at the stage of commencement or extension of detention, and in what form to guarantee an opportunity to submit opinions.

Accordingly, a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution shall be rendered with respect to the provision subject to review, and its continued application shall be ordered until the legislature enacts remedial legislation. Since the legislature has an obligation to enact remedial legislation as soon as possible, such legislation must be enacted by no later than 2025. 5. 31., and if no remedial legislation is enacted by then, the provision subject to review shall lose effect from 2025. 6. 1.

D. Constitutional Opinion of Justice Lee Seon-ae

I concur with the conclusion of the constitutional opinion of Justices Yoon Nam-seok, Lee Seok-tae, Kim Gi-yeong, Moon Hyeong-bae, and Lee Mi-seon to the effect that the provision subject to review violates the Constitution and that a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution should be rendered. However, regarding the reasons therefor, I have already participated in and argued in the dissenting opinion in Constitutional Court 2018. 2. 22. 2017HEONGA29, and I therefore cite that reasoning below and leave my dissenting opinion in this case. The reasoning leading to a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution is the same as the constitutional opinion of Justices Yoon Nam-seok, Lee Seok-tae, Kim Gi-yeong, Moon Hyeong-bae, and Lee Mi-seon.

(1) Whether the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction is violated

(a) Legitimacy of purpose and appropriateness of means

The provision subject to review is intended to promote national security by appropriately controlling and adjusting the entry, exit, and stay of foreigners through facilitating execution against persons subject to deportation orders, and thus its legislative purpose is legitimate. In addition, detaining a person subject to a deportation order in a detention facility until departure requirements are met so as to secure physical custody is an effective means for prompt and efficient execution of a deportation order, so appropriateness of means is also recognized.

(b) Minimum infringement and balance of interests

1) The subject of detention under the provision subject to review is a person subject to a deportation order under the Immigration Control Act. Since such persons are foreigners who have already committed unlawful acts during their stay in the country, such as illegal stay, illegal employment, or criminal acts, it cannot be said that there is no possibility of flight or potential risk, and it is acknowledged that detention and management are necessary to secure their physical presence until they are repatriated to their home country.

However, the provision subject to review does not set an upper limit on the detention period, thereby making indefinite detention possible until the person subject to a deportation order can be repatriated outside the Republic of Korea. Detention without a fixed upper limit causes serious mental pressure in itself, regardless of the actual length of detention, because it makes the detainee unable to predict at all when he or she will be released. Therefore, leaving aside the question of what the appropriate upper limit on the detention period should be, it is necessary at least to specify such upper limit in the law so that the detainee can predict the maximum period during which he or she may be detained, and allowing detention without any time limit merely for the administrative purpose of facilitating execution of a deportation order emphasizes only administrative convenience and uniformity, constituting in itself an excessive restriction on the detainee’s freedom of the person.

Looking at international standards and foreign legislation, the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention states that an upper limit on detention must be prescribed by law and that detention must not be indefinite. Germany provides that detention for deportation may be ordered for up to 6 months, and if a longer period is expected to be required, it may be extended up to a maximum of 12 months; the EU Returns Directive similarly provides the same. The reason why international standards and other legislative examples prescribe a maximum detention period is likewise that detention with no fixed duration may cause serious human rights violations.

The Supreme Court stated that the detention order under Article 63(1) of the Immigration Control Act is a temporary compulsion with a substantive limitation, in that it may be issued only for the purpose of securing execution of a deportation order and, even once lawfully issued, detention may be provisionally maintained only for the minimum period necessary until repatriation is possible, and the detention period may not be extended for other purposes. However, even if so held, the possibility of long-term or indefinite detention does not disappear, and because that decision merely described the limits inherent in the nature of detention and did not set an upper limit on the detention period, it cannot be regarded as functioning as an appropriate and substantive control over the detention period. For example, where the detainee files a cancellation action against the deportation order or applies for refugee status recognition, the detention period may be prolonged indefinitely depending on the progress of the procedures, and the length of detention is determined solely by how quickly the administrative agency and the judiciary process the relevant procedures. In such a case, prolonged detention may result for reasons not attributable to the detainee.

2) Since the time required for repatriation varies depending on each country’s circumstances and the progress of procedures, it may not be possible to know in advance when the detainee can be repatriated. Therefore, there may be a view that allowing detention until repatriation becomes possible without limiting the detention period is inevitable for achieving the legislative purpose of the provision subject to review. However, considering that many countries set upper limits on the detention period for persons subject to deportation, it cannot be said that setting a reasonable upper limit on the detention period is impossible.

If the provision subject to review prescribes an upper limit on the detention period, and repatriation is delayed so that the upper limit is exceeded, the person subject to deportation must be released; in such a case, it may be argued that released persons subject to deportation may go into hiding or commit crimes. However, this is merely a vague and potential possibility that has not yet materialized, and there is insufficient empirical basis to support it. Thus, based only on such vague assumptions, it is difficult to justify measures that seriously restrict freedom of the person, such as detention without any upper limit on duration. One cannot conclude that a foreigner who has committed a crime in the Republic of Korea will abscond or commit crimes again if released from detention. Moreover, among persons subject to deportation there may be not only foreigners who have committed crimes and been sentenced to punishment, but also foreigners who have merely violated administrative regulations concerning entry or stay. Detaining all such persons without any time limit on the premise that they are potential fugitives or potential criminals is an excessive measure.

As for cases where the detainee files a cancellation action against the deportation order or applies for refugee status recognition, etc., institutional improvements such as having the courts give priority and focus to such cases and expediting refugee status examination and decisions can minimize instances in which the detention period exceeds the upper limit. Even if detention is released after exceeding the upper limit, it appears possible to prevent flight or additional unlawful acts to a considerable extent through measures such as restricting their residence until departure requirements are met or requiring periodic reporting of residence, designating a guarantor or requiring the payment of an appropriate security deposit, and continuously observing and supervising them through supervisors, etc. Therefore, it is doubtful that, in order to achieve the legislative purpose of the provision subject to review, one must necessarily adopt a method that excessively restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person, such as detention without any upper limit on duration.

3) It is difficult to regard foreigners who were apprehended and detained because they did not choose voluntary departure for various reasons or because voluntary departure was impossible as having, in effect, a freedom to depart, so the infringement of fundamental rights due to the absence of an upper limit on detention period cannot be deemed mitigated on the ground that persons subject to deportation have the freedom to depart at any time and thus escape from being detainees.

The detainee may request temporary release from detention from the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office, hereinafter referred to as the head, etc.; however, unless there are circumstances such as a successful cancellation action against the deportation order, etc., whether to grant temporary release from detention is entirely within the discretion of the head, etc., so the temporary release from detention system cannot be regarded as substantially functioning as a device that can supplement the problem of long-term detention. Other ex post remedies such as objections to deportation orders and detention orders likewise cannot be regarded as effective, as will be discussed below.

4) In this way, although the public interest the provision subject to review seeks to achieve is significant and detention of persons subject to deportation is necessary to achieve that public interest, even taking this into account, the degree to which the detainee’s freedom of the person is restricted by detention without any upper limit on duration is excessively large; accordingly, the provision subject to review fails to satisfy the requirements of minimum infringement and balance of interests.

(c) Conclusion

The provision subject to review infringes the detainee’s freedom of the person in violation of the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.

(2) Whether the principle of due process is violated

Article 12(1) of the Constitution provides that no person shall be punished, placed under preventive restrictions, or subjected to forced labor, except by law and due process, thereby setting forth the principle of due process. Since the principle of due process applies not only to criminal procedure but to all state action, it must also be observed in the execution of deportation orders and detention orders carried out as part of immigration control administration.

(a) Since alien detention under the Immigration Control Act is equivalent to arrest or detention in criminal procedure and deprives a foreigner of freedom of the person, there must be, even if not the strict warrant principle of a prosecutor’s request and a judge’s issuance, at least a device by which a person in an objective and neutral position other than an immigration control official can review the validity of such physical restraint. However, the current alien detention system under the Immigration Control Act is contrasted with detention in criminal procedure, where the commencement and extension of detention are decided by the court and the end point is also clearly prescribed, in that no third independent neutral institution or judicial body is involved at all in the stages of commencement and extension of detention.

(b) First, regarding the issuance and execution of detention orders, the deportation procedure for foreigners under the Immigration Control Act is structured such that immigration control officials apprehend and investigate suspects, the head, etc. issues a detention order and immigration control officials execute it, the head, etc. examines and decides whether to deport, then issues a deportation order and detention order, and immigration control officials execute them. Accordingly, although, formally, the investigation procedure and the review procedure are separated and the entity issuing the detention order and the executing agency are separated, in reality subordinates and superiors within the immigration office together conduct suspect investigations and issue and execute deportation orders and detention orders. In other words, the head, etc., who makes the detention decision is not an independent third institution but merely a superior within the same executing agency to which the immigration control officials belong, so the institutions cannot substantively be said to be separated, and because there is no room for external institutions such as the judiciary to intervene, it is difficult to say that procedural control by an objective and neutral institution is achieved merely by having decisions made by a superior in the same executing agency.

Although the provision subject to review is phrased as a permissive clause stating that a person may be detained, in practice, when a deportation order is issued, detention orders are issued simultaneously with or immediately after the deportation order, without any special review of the detention order itself such as the necessity of detention or the risk of flight, and there has been no case in which a detention order was not issued for a person subject to deportation who could not be immediately repatriated. However, because a person subject to deportation cannot always be deemed to be at risk of flight, a separate determination of the necessity of detention is required, and unless a neutral institution capable of ensuring fairness and objectivity intervenes, the current structure in which a detention order is issued almost automatically upon a deportation order is unlikely to change.

By way of reference, in Germany, both pre-deportation detention for examination of deportation and secured detention for execution of deportation are subject to a judge-issued warrant requirement, so judicial control is exercised from the commencement stage of detention.

(c) Regarding ex post remedies or control procedures, the detainee may file an objection with the Minister of Justice against a detention order or a deportation order, and the head, etc. may extend detention with prior approval from the Minister of Justice where the detention period exceeds 3 months.

However, the Minister of Justice is in reality merely the supervisory authority over the administrative agency issuing and executing detention orders, and thus it cannot be said that a review system by an external neutral and objective institution is thereby secured. Indeed, there has not been a single case in the past five years in which an objection against a detention order or deportation order was granted, and prior approval by the Minister of Justice for extension of detention is also almost invariably granted in reality when the head, etc. submits the application documents while deportation execution is delayed, so even from this perspective it is difficult to regard the Minister of Justice’s review and determination as having substantive significance as a control procedure to ensure the legality of detention.

In addition, the detainee may file an administrative action against a deportation order, detention order, or a decision dismissing an objection, but general and ex post judicial control methods such as administrative litigation are insufficient to adequately secure the freedom of the person of a foreigner who is unfamiliar with the Korean judicial system and not proficient in Korean.

(d) Since one of the important procedural requirements that can be derived from the principle of due process is to give the parties an opportunity to submit opinions and materials, such opportunity must also be guaranteed to the detainee in detention under the provision subject to review.

However, the Immigration Control Act contains no provision requiring that the person concerned be given an opportunity to submit opinions before issuance of a detention order under the provision subject to review. Article 22(3) of the Administrative Procedures Act provides that when an administrative agency issues a disposition imposing obligations on a party or restricting rights and interests, the agency shall give the party, etc. an opportunity to submit opinions; however, dispositions concerning the entry and departure of foreigners are excluded from the scope of the Administrative Procedures Act, and no system such as a pre-arrest judicial review of suspects exists under the Criminal Procedure Act. Therefore, the person subject to a detention order has no opportunity whatsoever to make statements or submit opinions favorable to him or her. At the stage of objection to detention, the Minister of Justice is merely authorized at his or her discretion to hear the statements of the parties concerned if necessary, and prior approval by the Minister of Justice for extension of detention is also conducted only through review of documents submitted by the head, etc., without giving the detainee an opportunity to state opinions or submit materials.

(e) Considering these points together, the provision subject to review violates the constitutional principle of due process because there is no control procedure by a fair and neutral institution at the stages of commencement or extension of detention, and no opportunity to submit opinions is guaranteed when physical restraint is imposed administratively.

(3) Conclusion

The provision subject to review violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and the principle of due process, thereby infringing the detainee’s freedom of the person, and is therefore unconstitutional.

5. Conclusion

Since the provision subject to review is not in conformity with the Constitution, a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution shall be rendered, and the provision shall be provisionally applied until remedial legislation by the legislature is enacted, with 2025. 5. 31. as the deadline. In addition, Constitutional Court Decision 2017HEONGA29, in which the Constitutional Court had previously held, in a view different from this decision, that the provision subject to review does not violate the Constitution, shall be modified to the extent inconsistent with this decision. Except for the dissenting opinions of Justices Lee Eun-ae, Lee Jong-seok, and Lee Yeong-jin, the opinions of the Justices participating in this decision were unanimous, and with respect to the constitutional opinion of Justices Yoon Nam-seok, Lee Seok-tae, Kim Gi-yeong, Moon Hyeong-bae, and Lee Mi-seon, there is a supplementary opinion by Justice Lee Mi-seon as set forth in Section 7 below.

6. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Lee Eun-ae, Lee Jong-seok, and Lee Yeong-jin

We conclude that the provision subject to review does not violate the Constitution, and state our view as follows.

A. Precedent of the Constitutional Court

In Constitutional Court Decision 2017HEONGA29 rendered on 2018. 2. 22., the Constitutional Court held, for the following reasons, that the provision subject to review does not violate the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction or the principle of due process and therefore does not infringe freedom of the person.

The Court reasoned that the provision subject to review has a legitimate legislative purpose, that the detention is a temporary compulsion with substantive and temporal limits, that international and comparative materials do not require an upper limit in every case, that various release and objection procedures exist, and that alternative measures cannot fully substitute for detention. The Court also reasoned that due process is not violated because immigration detention is part of administrative discretion, there is some opportunity to contest the measure through objection and administrative litigation, and the overall procedure, including prior investigation and notice, provides sufficient procedural protection.

B. Whether there is a need to recognize a change of precedent

Article 23(2) No. 2 of the Constitutional Court Act allows the Court, if supported by at least 6 Justices, to change an opinion previously expressed by the Constitutional Court regarding the interpretation or application of the Constitution or statutes. However, in order to change precedent, in addition to the formal requirement of such a qualified quorum, it must be recognized that there is a need to change the position of the precedent, for example because there is a legal error in the precedent’s reasoning or because circumstances have changed. Also, from the standpoint of foreseeability, legal stability, and the protection of trust, it must be shown that there is a need to change the position of the precedent, namely that there has been a change in normative or factual circumstances such as changes in social institutions or culture, changes in the public’s legal sentiment or consciousness, or changes in the content of other laws or the legal principles concerning them, and that for this reason the position of the precedent must be changed.

The constitutional opinions of Justices Yoon Nam-seok, Lee Seok-tae, Kim Gi-yeong, Moon Hyeong-bae, and Lee Mi-seon and the constitutional opinion of Justice Lee Seon-ae regarding the provision subject to review held that detention without an upper limit is beyond the limits of detention as a temporary and provisional compulsory measure; that, in light of numerous foreign examples that set upper limits on detention periods, it is difficult to regard the absence of an upper limit on detention period as inevitable; that the objection system against detention orders, the Minister of Justice’s approval system for extension of detention periods, and the temporary release from detention system alone are insufficient to properly control the detention period and alleviate excessive restriction on the body; that execution of deportation orders can be secured through various alternative means such as restrictions on residence or reporting, designation of a surety, a security deposit system, or observation or supervision through supervisors; and on those grounds held that the provision subject to review violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction. The constitutional opinions also held that the provision subject to review violates the principle of due process and infringes freedom of the person because no third independent neutral institution or judicial body is involved at all at the stage of commencement or extension of detention, because the detainee is not guaranteed a procedural opportunity to state opinions and submit materials from before the issuance of the detention order through the stage of objection, and because ordinary administrative litigation procedures cannot be regarded as guaranteeing swift and effective judicial relief. However, it is doubtful whether the reasons set out in the constitutional opinions truly amount to a change in normative or factual circumstances that would justify changing the precedent.

The average detention period in the record was around 10.1 days in 2018, 9.6 days in 2019, and 16.9 days in 2020, which suggests that in practice detention is usually executed within the substantive and temporal limits of its purpose. The Act also supplements the system through objection, prior approval for extensions, and temporary release. Moreover, after the precedent, the Ministry of Justice and practice have been 개선, including expansion of departure orders, substantialization of objections, and more active temporary release. Thus, there is no sufficient changed circumstance to alter the precedent.

C. Conclusion

Since the Constitutional Court stated in its 2018. 2. 22. 2017HEONGA29 decision that the provision subject to review does not violate the Constitution, the normative or factual circumstances surrounding the provision subject to review do not appear to have changed so drastically as to require a stricter determination than before regarding whether the provision is unconstitutional, and no other new necessity for reinterpretation can be found. Rather, the Ministry of Justice, the competent ministry, has continuously improved the relevant systems and practices since the above 2017HEONGA29 decision was rendered. Considering that immigration control administration is an area in which legislative policy is determined to a certain extent, there remains doubt whether it is desirable, after only about 5 years, to change the precedent and thereby eliminate through a Constitutional Court decision the room for voluntary and gradual institutional improvement by the legislative and executive branches.

The precedent’s position that the provision subject to review, which is established to conduct immigration control administration as a sovereign state, does not violate the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction or the principle of due process remains valid even at this time, there is no error in that judgment, and no necessary and sufficient changed circumstances justifying a change of precedent can otherwise be recognized.

Accordingly, the provision subject to review does not violate the Constitution.

7. Supplementary Opinion of Justice Lee Mi-seon to the Constitutional Opinion of Justices Yoon Nam-seok, Lee Seok-tae, Kim Gi-yeong, Moon Hyeong-bae, and Lee Mi-seon

In addition to the constitutional opinion of the five Justices that the provision subject to review violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and the principle of due process, I wish to state as follows that it also violates Article 12(6) of the Constitution, which provides for the right to request judicial review of the legality of arrest or detention.

Article 12(6) of the Constitution provides that any person arrested or detained shall have the right to request a court to review the legality of the arrest or detention. Thus, it establishes the system of judicial review of arrest or detention. This is an ex post remedial procedure intended to promote prompt and effective relief by allowing a person whose freedom of the person has been restricted by arrest or detention by public power to request judicial review by a court, and to obtain immediate release not only where the physical restraint was unlawfully commenced but also where continuation of the restraint is unlawful.

Because the freedom of the person guaranteed by Article 12 of the Constitution may be directly restricted not only by investigative agencies but also by other state institutions, including general administrative agencies, arrest or detention in Article 12(6) of the Constitution must also be interpreted broadly. Therefore, Article 12(6) applies to all cases in which any public power exercising agency restricts freedom of the person by means of arrest or detention. Furthermore, Article 12(6) is a provision that guarantees at the constitutional level a procedure by which the person concerned may request a court to review the legality of the arrest or detention itself, separate from the final judicial determination procedure regarding the causal relationship that led to the arrest or detention. Because this right to request judicial review of arrest or detention has an independent status at the constitutional level, the legislature has an obligation to provide persons concerned, through the overall legal system, with at least one opportunity to properly exercise the concrete procedural right. Furthermore, Article 12(6) of the Constitution states that any person has the right to request a court to review the legality of arrest or detention, thereby recognizing that right also for foreigners.

Accordingly, with respect to a foreigner detained pursuant to the provision subject to review, there must be provided at least one opportunity to request judicial review of the legality of the detention itself.

However, the provision subject to review and the Immigration Control Act, including the provision subject to review, do not establish a procedure by which, in the event of detention pursuant to the provision subject to review, the legality of the commencement or continuation of detention may be requested to a court for review. In addition, the Habeas Corpus Act, which provides for court remedies concerning bodily liberty, excludes persons detained pursuant to the Immigration Control Act from the scope of its application, so foreigners detained pursuant to the provision subject to review cannot, unlike other forms of administrative physical restraint, file a petition for relief under the Habeas Corpus Act.

In shaping the procedure for realizing the right to request judicial review of arrest or detention, the legislature has relatively broad legislative power and may make various choices regarding the concrete contents and nomenclature of the law in the course of legislation, and the detainee may file an administrative action seeking cancellation of the detention order or a motion for a stay of execution thereof. However, the purpose of guaranteeing the right to request judicial review of arrest or detention separately from the right to file a judicial action under Article 27(1) of the Constitution is to enable a person who has been physically restrained by public power to request judicial review of the legality of the commencement or continuation of the physical restraint, thereby establishing a prompt and effective remedy. Yet, in the current situation where no court involvement whatsoever exists at the stage of commencement or extension of detention under the Immigration Control Act, it is difficult to say that such ordinary administrative litigation procedures alone guarantee a swift and effective judicial remedy. Also, even where detention was lawfully commenced but continuation of detention became unlawful due to the disappearance of the necessity for detention, it cannot be said with certainty whether proper and effective relief can be provided in an action to cancel the detention order or in a motion for a stay of execution. The Immigration Control Act provides an ex post remedy by allowing an objection to detention to be filed with the Minister of Justice; however, it is obvious that such an objection system cannot constitute part of the system of judicial review of arrest or detention under Article 12(6) of the Constitution, the core element of which is court review. Furthermore, ex post control by the Minister of Justice, who is merely a supervisory authority rather than a neutral and objective institution, or other procedures prescribed by the Immigration Control Act, such as prior approval by the Minister of Justice for extension of detention, presentation of the detention order to the person concerned, and detention notices, cannot be regarded as supplementing the system of judicial review of arrest or detention.

As noted above, the legislature has relatively broad legislative power in shaping the procedure for realizing the right to request judicial review of arrest or detention, but considering the purpose of Article 12(6) of the Constitution in guaranteeing that right, a procedure must be secured whereby the legality of the state of detention itself under the provision subject to review may be requested to a court for review; and this is equally true even if detention under the provision subject to review is carried out as part of immigration control administration, because the detention causes a serious restriction on freedom of the person.

Taken together, the provision subject to review, which does not establish a procedure for requesting judicial review of the legality of the commencement or continuation of detention from a court in the event of detention under the provision subject to review, violates Article 12(6) of the Constitution."}
